en: Having received the full precepts,
he was then designated as a Great Bhikṣu; he was endowed with the two hundred and fifty precepts,
including the four *pārājika* dharmas and the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas.
The two *aniyata* dharmas; the thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas;
the ninety *pāyattika* dharmas; the four *pratideśanīya* dharmas;
the one hundred *śaikṣa* dharmas; and the seven *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* dharmas.
The section on "Possessing the Precepts" concludes with the *Mumoku* (Table of Contents).
The enumeration of the names and numbers of the full precepts (*upasampadā*) appears scattered throughout various sources; therefore, they have been omitted here.
*A Concise Annotated Version of the Essentials of the Śrāmaṇera Vinaya*, Volume One.
Compiled by the Bodhisattva-Precept Disciple, Śramaṇa Zhuhong of Yunqi Temple;
annotated by the Bodhicitta Bhikṣu, Śramaṇa Hongzan of Dinghu Mountain.
This present essential abridgment was compiled by the Great Master of Yunqi from such works as the *Śrāmaṇera-daśa-śīla-sūtra*.

The meaning of this is most essential, yet the text is concise and brief, intended to facilitate the study and practice of novice *śrāmaṇeras* who are beginners, so that they may perceive it as clearly as seeing fruit in the palm of their hand.
According to the classification of *śrāmaṇeras*, there are three grades. First, from the age of seven to thirteen, they are called "crow-scaring" (*kākavācanaka*) *śrāmaṇeras*;
this means that because they are young and not yet capable of other duties, they are only required to guard the grain and wheat for the Sangha. And...
In places such as the refectory or during seated meditation, one should drive away crows and birds to perform a small measure of labor on their behalf;
this simultaneously generates merit and virtue, ensuring that one does not sit idly consuming the offerings of the faithful or spend one's time in vain. Second:

from the age of fourteen to nineteen, one is called a *dharmānulomika-śrāmaṇera* (a śrāmaṇera in accordance with the Dharma), meaning that his age is precisely in accord with two dharmas: first, he is able to serve his teacher.
1. They perform manual labor and service. 2. This is because they are able to practice meditation and recitation. 3.
From the age of twenty until seventy, they are called *nāma-śrāmaṇeras* (nominal śrāmaṇeras).

This means that although they have reached the age of twenty and should receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), they are either dull-witted by nature or late in entering the monastic life, such that they cannot suddenly uphold all the precepts; thus, although their age qualifies them as bhikṣus...
One who holds the status of a śrāmaṇera is called a "śrāmaṇera by name. Although there are three categories [of śrāmaṇeras], they all receive the ten precepts;
thus, they are collectively termed "one dharma" and are identical to śrāmaṇeras. One who has shaved their hair and beard but has not received the ten precepts is called a "śrāmaṇera by appearance.

Although their physical appearance is the same, because they lack the restraint of the precepts, they do not belong to the number of the five assemblies (pañca-saṃgha). Here, we exclude those who are identical only in appearance.
The method of their ordination is the same.

The Sanskrit term *śrāmaṇera* is translated here as "Cessation and Compassion" (*xīcí*), meaning to cease evil and practice compassion; that is, to cease worldly defilements and compassionately rescue sentient beings.
It is also called "Diligent Encouragement" (*qíncè*) and "Seeking Quiescence" (*qiújí*).
"Brahma-language" refers to the sounds of the people of India; because it is identical to the language of the Brahma Heaven, it is called "Brahma-language.

Long ago, when the world was first formed and no humans yet inhabited it, the light from the earth shone upward. The hosts of the Brahma Heaven in the Form Realm followed this light down to observe the new land.
Having consumed the essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*), they lost their celestial radiance and supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-pāda*) and could no longer ascend.

He thus became the progenitor of humanity. His descendants resided for generations in India; thereafter, as people moved with the land, their pronunciations diverged into various forms, while only those in India remained unchanged.
Consequently, their speech is the Sanskrit language and their script is the Sanskrit script, both of which are not found in other countries.
Regarding the term "this" (此): it means that the expression "East Flower Cessation-Love" (東華息慈) from this land is used to translate the title "Śrāmaṇera" from India.
This interpretation originates from the *Biography of Yaśas*. To explain the two characters "Cessation-Love" (息慈), it is said that one "ceases evil and practices love.
Fearing that beginners might not yet know what evil is to be ceased and what love is to be practiced, [the text] further explains "cessation of worldly defilements" (息世染).
To examine in detail how one compassionately saves sentient beings: it is because ordinary beings, from time immemorial, have had their true nature shrouded by ignorance;
they give rise to various deluded thoughts and cling to sensory objects, becoming emotionally stained by the five desires of the world.
Through body, speech, and mind, they commit various transgressions, falling into the three miserable realms and wandering through the six destinies without any prospect of escape. It is as follows:
Therefore, out of compassion for them, he established the ten precepts to cause them to cease the transgressions of body, speech, and mind, and to realize the holy fruit of quiescent nirvana.
Yet, although their evils may have been stilled, if they lack a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, they cannot practice the six pāramitās to provide universal succor to the four modes of birth;
consequently, they fall into the limited and partial [vehicles] and cannot be called virtuous, let alone attain awakening.

Great Bodhi. Having attained equal and perfect enlightenment, one therefore practices compassionate salvation to fulfill the myriad practices and proceeds directly toward the precious destination, rather than lingering at the provisional city.
Thus, the *Zhi guan* (Calming and Contemplation) states: "One should know that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are likewise considered 'evil.
It is only when a bodhisattva of the six perfections provides universal relief through compassion that this is called 'good. This is the meaning of 'resting in compassion' (*xi ci*). To this end:

This refers to what is called the *śrāmaṇera* (勤策, *qínsè*), also known as the seeker of tranquility (*sāmanera*). The Sanskrit term is *nirvāṇa*, which in this language is translated as "perfect stillness" (*yuánjì*).
It is termed "perfect" (*yuán*) because it is endowed with both wisdom and virtue; it is termed "stillness" (*jì*) because the afflictions, habitual tendencies, and obstacles have been exhausted.

This refers to a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*) who, having first resolved to leave the household life and received the ten precepts, diligently cultivates and exerts himself to sever the afflictions and habitual tendencies, seeking to realize *nirvāṇa*.
This is because it is the wondrous fruit of the *pātra*.
Regarding the *vinaya* (discipline): it refers to the ten precepts and various codes of decorum.
Beginning from the precept against killing up to the tenth precept against handling gold, silver, or precious objects, these are called the "ten precepts. Hereafter...
Twenty-four matters are enumerated and termed the various *īryāpathas*.

The preceding section, the Gate of Precepts and Vinaya (*śīla-vinaya-mukha*), was originally compiled as this essential summary; its text is divided into two parts, the Upper and the Lower. Now, first, the Upper Section, the Gate of Precepts and Vinaya, is explained.
"Chapter" (*piān*) refers to a scroll; furthermore, "chapter" implies "pervasive. This means that it reveals principles and unfolds events, making them clear and comprehensive.

"Precept" (*jiè*) refers to prohibitive precepts, while "code" (*lǜ*) refers to legal statutes. Although the names "precept" and "code" are identical, their meanings differ slightly. To prevent wrongdoing and cease evil is called "precept";

to adjudicate degrees of gravity, and to distinguish between what is permitted or prohibited, and what constitutes observance or violation, is called "code. "Gate" (*mén*) takes the sense of "ability to pass through," meaning that—
The ten dharmas, beginning with non-killing, all emerge from the single gate of the precepts;

they are the path traversed by the noble ones of the Three Vehicles, leading universally to the city of Nirvana. Thus we know that these ten precepts are truly the stairway for transcending the world and the gateway to Nirvana.

The Buddha established that those who have left the household life must devote themselves exclusively to the Vinaya for five summer retreats (*pañca-varṣa*) prior to that; only after five summer retreats is it permitted to study the teachings and engage in Chan meditation.

This clarifies the sequence of the three untainted trainings (*trīṇy-aśravāṇi śikṣāṇi*): morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). Should one transgress this order, then concentration and wisdom—
There is nothing from which he arises. "Buddha" is the title for the Great Enlightenment of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata was born in the kingdom of Kapilavastu in the Central Heaven (Madhyadeśa), within the house of King Śuddhodana.
This was in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, the year of Jiayin (463 BCE). He was born at dawn on the eighth day of the fourth month. When he reached the age of nineteen...
He left home in Yuecheng and attained enlightenment at the age of thirty. His parinirvāṇa occurred in the year Ren-shen, the fifty-third year of King Mu of Zhou.
During that interval, he preached the Dharma for forty-nine years, instructing the holy multitudes of the three vehicles and establishing the various prohibitions and precepts.
He commanded all bhikṣus to rely upon a teacher to study the Vinaya for five summer retreats, even if it were for only a single night.
One must not dwell apart from one’s preceptor. Only after one has mastered the Vinaya Piṭaka should one study meditation and recitation.
If one is a śrāmaṇera, one must remain in dependence for the rest of one’s life, regardless of the number of *varṣa* (rainy-season retreats) spent; this is detailed in the Mahāvinaya.

Although these are matters pertaining to *bhikṣus*, they are things that a *śrāmaṇera* must know. Regarding the term "prescription" (*zhi*), it refers to the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, who, concerning the Dharma, himself...
In order to exhaustively comprehend the karmic nature of sentient beings, he established the various codes of discipline (*vinaya*) and commanded his disciples to rely upon and practice them;
through this, they attain liberation from birth and death. This is not something that other sages are capable of accomplishing.

Just as worldly rites and music are not established by anyone other than the Son of Heaven, so too these great transmundane regulations cannot be instituted by anyone other than the Buddha. Thus, it is known that the *vinaya* was personally promulgated by the Tathāgata himself; as for all others...

The Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas merely recounted [the teachings] rather than composing them; thus, when Mañjuśrī descended, he did not permit anyone to add a single word of their own, and Upāli, in his compilation, did not dare to expand upon it by even a single character.
Among the boundless assembly of sages in the human and celestial realms, [there was no deviation].
They are all governed by one and the same discipline and are collectively upheld; therefore, they should be especially revered.

Regarding those who have "left the home" (renounced the world), there are two kinds: first, those who bid farewell to their kin, sever their attachments, abandon the secular world to enter the Way, shave their hair, and don dyed robes—this is called leaving the household of the mundane world.
Second, those who eradicate delusive afflictions and realize the fruit of non-arising—this is called leaving the household of the triple world. This constitutes true renunciation.
"Family. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Now, those who have left the home life do so for the sake of unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). This is precisely it.
As for the term "summer" (*kṣetra*), it refers to having left the home life and transcended worldly customs; one does not reckon years by the secular calendar.

Therefore, during the three months of summer, one exerts oneself, intensifies one's efforts, and strives for progress—either ascending to the fruits of sainthood (*āryaphala*) or increasing the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*). Because one receives this name based on the merit of such exertion, it is called "summer retreat" (*varṣā*). That is to say...

The fifteenth day of the seventh month is designated as the end of the *lābha* (the ritual of giving). Regarding the term "exclusive and refined": "exclusive" means being single-minded and not mixing in other studies;
"refined" means scrutinizing the text to clarify its meaning and fully elucidating its subtle and profound points. Therefore, one is required to do so during the five summer retreats.

One who studies the *Vinaya* and is well-versed in the distinctions between what is permitted and prohibited (*kai-sha*), as well as what constitutes an offense and its non-offense (*ji-han*), is said to possess the characteristics of the lineage (*gotra*). The *Mahāvinaya* states:

"Even if one has attained the three types of supernormal knowledge (*traividyā*) and the six higher powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), if five summer retreats (*pañca-varṣa*) have not yet been completed, one must still remain in dependence upon a teacher.

Even if the five summers have been completed, if one does not know the prohibitions regarding what is permitted and prohibited, or those of natural and conventional offenses (*prakṛti-prajñapti-śīla*), one must still depend upon another for the rest of one's life. For this reason, Vinaya Master Xuanchang—ten... [text continues]
Taking one's seat to listen to the *Vinaya*: Master Huixiu heard the *Vinaya* for his entire life. What kind of person am I to suddenly propose that my studies depart from the teacher?
Only after one has thoroughly exhausted the *Vinaya-piṭaka* and completed five summer retreats (*pañca-varṣa*) is it permitted to listen to the teachings and practice meditation.

"Listening" (*ting*) refers to receiving instruction from another; "teachings" (*jiao*) refers to the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata throughout his single lifetime, which is divided into twelve categories.
Regarding the categories of the scriptures: it is because the ailments of sentient beings are not uniform that the dispensing of the medicinal Dharma has many methods;
thus, the divisions of the teachings are opened into twelve types. First is the *sūtra* (契經), which refers to those among the various scriptures that are spoken in prose directly.
Second is the *geya* (重頌), which generally refers to all verses in the various scriptures that restate the meaning of the prose sections. Third is the *vyākaraṇa* (授記), which refers to...
"Coming to bestow the prediction of Buddhahood upon the various disciples. "Four gāthās" refers to the verses found within the various sūtras;
"mutually speaking for oneself" means that although no one asks the Buddha, the Tathāgata observes the capacities of sentient beings and proclaims the teaching spontaneously.
"Six causes and conditions" refers to those instances in the various sūtras and vinayas where the Buddha preaches the Dharma based on events arising from specific persons and circumstances.
7. Jātaka (Birth Stories): These refer to the accounts of various deeds performed by the Bodhisattvas in their past lives, as taught by the Buddha. 8. Itivṛttaka (Past Occurrences):
These refer to the accounts of the previous lives and other matters concerning the Śrāvaka disciples, as taught by the Buddha. 9. Vaipulya (Extensive Teachings).
It is also called Vaipulya (Extensive Teachings), referring to the Mahāyāna sūtras whose meanings are vast and whose measure is equal to space.
Tenth, Adbhutadharma (Marvelous Events), referring to the extremely rare and wondrous dharmas taught by the Buddha within the various sūtras.
Eleventh, Avadāna (Parables), wherein the Buddha, when teaching the Dharma to sentient beings of dull faculties, uses the language of parables to instruct and enlighten them.
Furthermore, there are twelve types of doctrinal exegesis (*śāstra-artha*), which refer to the detailed explanation of meanings provided by those who answer various questions.

Regarding what is called "meditation" (*dhyāna*), although its gateways are immeasurable, to speak of them in essence, they are only two: first, cultivation through contemplation (*vipaśyanā-bhāvanā*); second, direct pointing. What is now referred to as "investigation" (*cān*)—
This is Direct Pointing Chan; it is precisely the direct pointing to the human mind to see one’s nature and attain Buddhahood. Zichi says:

"The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* stipulates that a bhikṣu, for five summers or less, must devote himself exclusively to the Vinaya-piṭaka. Only after he has mastered what constitutes an offense and its non-offense, and is capable of managing the affairs of a bhikṣu, may he then proceed to study the Sūtras and Śāstras.
To bypass these stages and study prematurely results in a loss of proper sequence in practice, which hinders entry into the Way."

There is no such basis. The Great Sage’s reprimands are never in vain. Nowadays, as soon as one has received the elements of the precepts, one immediately proceeds to listen to the teachings and practice Chan.
Regarding the conduct and decorum of a monk, one understands nothing at all;

moreover, one treats the restraint of the precepts with contempt, slanders the *vinaya*, disparages the study of the rules as "Hīnayāna," and neglects the observance of the precepts as being "clinging to appearances. Thus, one fails to fathom the intent of the Sages and errs.
If you understand the True Vehicle, then the precepts must be capable of being disregarded; why then do you ascend the altar to receive them?

If the Vinaya must be capable of being violated, why do you shave your head and don the dyed robes? Thus, to disregard the precepts is entirely to disparage yourself, and to violate the Vinaya is likewise to bring about your own ruin.
Delusive attachments are easily cultivated, while the Ultimate Way is difficult to hear. To transcend the mundane and rise above the masses—such a person is but one in ten thousand.
I pray you examine the sagely instructions closely; can you not follow them?
Therefore, when a śrāmaṇera shaves his head, he first receives the ten precepts and subsequently ascends the altar to receive full ordination.
Now, although he is called a śrāmaṇera, the foolish are茫然 (máng hū) ignorant of the precepts they originally received, while the reckless neglect them and fail to study.
They then attempt to leap over the stages, having no intention of aiming for the lofty and far-reaching. This is truly lamentable.

"Is guo zhe" (is-hence) is a phrase used to connect what precedes with what follows. It means that among the three types of untainted training (*anāsrava-śikṣā*), the discipline (*vinaya*) is primary;
and for the five groups of renunciants, the ten precepts (*daśa-śīla*) come first. Therefore, as soon as one begins by shaving the beard and hair, one is immediately required to receive them.

Because the holy life (*brahmacarya*) remains unimpaired, only then is one permitted to ascend the altar (*maṇḍala*) to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). The "altar" refers to the ordination platform (*sīmā-maṇḍala*); on this platform, the *saṃgha*...
It is accomplished through the formal ritual of *karmavācanā* performed in common. Were it not for this assembly, the precepts could not be obtained.
To be "fully endowed" means to receive the two hundred and fifty major precepts of a *bhikṣu*; one thereby becomes fully endowed with the sublime cause of *nirvāṇa*.
This is also called *upasaṃpadā*. "Complete" (*yuan*) refers to *parinirvāṇa*; it signifies that these great precepts are not far removed from *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding what is now called a *śrāmaṇera*, as for the precepts originally received: this refers to receiving a name by tracing it back to its source.
Because one originally received the ten precepts, one now receives the name "śrāmaṇera. Since the name is derived from that source, one ought to study and diligently uphold them;
yet there are two kinds of people who neither study nor uphold them: first, the ignorant; second, the insane. The ignorant lack the eye of wisdom and thus do not discern this.
This is not so. Consequently, regarding the various characteristics of the precepts, they are utterly ignorant; with arrogant and deluded views, they do not follow the proper sequence.
Thus, they neglect and fail to study the holy regulations established by the Tathāgata, intending instead to leap over the stages.

"Leaping" (*lè*) means to overstep; it refers to the hierarchy of levels. The *Xuéjì* (Records of Learning) states: "The young listen but do not question; learning does not leap over stages. If one does not follow [this principle]...
Regarding the ranks of ordination, he then desired to leapfrog and advance, which is precisely what is meant by "attaining a shaven head in the morning and overstepping the senior monks by evening.
This stems from his deluded views and ignorance of the sequence of the Dharma-characteristics and the categories of the precepts;
thus, he recklessly attempts to leapfrog, wishing to equal the sages of old. As the *Śata-avadāna-sūtra* says: "Long ago, there was a foolish man who saw another..."
The wealthy man’s triple-storied pavilion was high, spacious, and magnificent. He immediately summoned a carpenter and ordered him to construct the very top, the third story.
The craftsman said, "How can one build the second story without first constructing the bottom one? Without constructing the second, [the third] cannot be made."
He was able to construct the third story. The fool stubbornly said, "I do not need the first two; you must build the top story for me.
When the people of the time heard this, they were struck with wonder and laughter.

It is like the fourfold assembly of disciples who do not diligently cultivate reverence for the Triple Gem, but being lazy and indolent, desire to seek the fruit of the Path while refusing the first three fruits and wishing only to obtain the fourth.
One who produces no fruit will likewise be ridiculed by the people of the time; such a person is no different from that fool.
It is the same if one does not follow the sequence of the three vehicles and first studies the Mahāyāna. As the *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* says:
One who does not first study the Hīnayāna and subsequently studies the Mahāyāna is not a disciple of the Buddha.

Now, one who does not study as a śrāmaṇera yet desires to receive full ordination, or who does not maintain pure precepts yet desires sudden enlightenment, is no different from that fool; how could there be any distinction?

To harbor such deluded thoughts of loftiness and distance is also lamentable. "Deluded thoughts" (wǎngyì) refers to being dark, ignorant, and lacking knowledge; it means to falsely equate oneself with those who came before.
"Philosophy" (*zhe*) refers to the lofty and remote. "Lofty" (*gao*) refers to the *bhikṣu*; "remote" (*yuan*) refers to the *bodhisattva*. "Lamenting" (*kai*) is an expression of sorrowful sighing.
Furthermore, the "lofty and remote" is also the ground realized by the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Because one studies with wild negligence, one loses the clarity of wisdom;
because one loses the clarity of wisdom, one has nothing to know; because one has nothing to know, one does not recognize the principles of teaching and practice.
Regarding the sequence of the three trainings, to recklessly leap over to such lofty heights as to attempt to equate oneself with the Buddhas and Patriarchs is truly pitiable;
hence it is said, "it is also lamentable."
Because he received the ten precepts, I have provided a brief explanation of a few words.
It is brief rather than extensive; hence, it is called "a few words.
This is intended to enable those who are still in their studies to know the direction in which they should proceed.
For those who have newly entered the Path, this is thus called "Elementary Learning.
Out of concern that the wild and ignorant are entirely unacquainted with the precepts and laws, I have excerpted the ten precepts from the *Śrāmaṇera-vinaya-sūtra* and provided a brief explanation.

This is intended to instruct those who have not yet heard them, so that they may be freed from the suffering of ignorance and those who have newly entered the Path may have a point of focus for their minds. Thus it is called "Turning Toward the Direction. As the treatise says: "The three evil [realms]..."
Being burned, the heavy beatings of camels and donkeys, and the hunger and thirst of hungry ghosts are not what is called suffering.
Rather, it is being shrouded in the darkness of ignorance, lacking learning, and unable to discern the directions that is truly called suffering.
Those who have left the household life with a sincere heart must apply themselves wholeheartedly to its practice and act with great care not to transgress it.
You have not done so out of being coerced by royal power, nor for the sake of seeking a livelihood through improper means, nor to avoid toil and seek ease, nor to escape the hardships of debt.
Rather, it was fundamentally because you sought the True Dharma that you entered the gateway of the Dharma through faith. This is...

It is said: "One leaves the household life with a sincere heart. If one seeks to escape birth and death, one receives and upholds the prohibitive precepts; therefore, one is able to observe and practice them with earnest intent.
The precepts are the life-preserving float for crossing the sea of suffering, and the jeweled necklace that adorns the Dharma-body."
Therefore, one must be prudent and careful, ensuring that not even the slightest fraction of a hair is violated.
Only then will it serve as a stepping stone for the bhikṣu precepts in the near term, and as the very foundation for the bodhisattva precepts in the long run.
Thereafter, one proceeds from the lower to the higher. This means that the ten precepts serve as the staircase for a bhikṣu and the root of a bodhisattva;
they are like a three-tiered multi-storied building, hence they are called a "staircase. They are like the crown of a tāla tree, hence they are called the "root.
A śrāmaṇera is adjacent to a bhikṣu and is thus termed "near," yet because he is still separated from full ordination (*upasampadā*), he is termed "distant. This refers to the first stage.
If one violates them, it becomes difficult to progress further; once the root is impaired, the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits all fall away.
Therefore, a sutra states: "If one breaks a grave precept among the five lay precepts, there is no way to receive the five precepts again, nor even the bodhisattva precepts.
If one breaks a grave precept among the ten precepts, there is no way to receive the ten precepts again, nor the bhikṣu precepts, nor the bodhisattva..."
Furthermore, it is impossible for wisdom not to arise from concentration, nor for concentration not to arise from precepts.

By means of the precepts, concentration is born; by means of concentration, wisdom is developed. In this way, one may hope to accomplish the Noble Path and not fail the resolve of leaving the household life.
"Shujī" (庶幾) is a term signifying "near attainment. Because the precepts are pure, the determined nature (*niyāma*) manifests, whereby untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) arises.

Through this wisdom, one seeks only to sever all afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), thereby restoring original purity and luminosity; hence it is said that one "accomplishes the Noble Path" (*āryamārga*).
This is because the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*) support one another like the three legs of a tripod; thus, one is able to accomplish the Noble Path. The Noble Path...
This refers to the bodhi of the three vehicles—the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas. One leaves the household life with the primary aspiration for bodhi;
if one then excels in the three trainings, one will not be far from the Way, and thus the resolve to leave home is not in vain.
Master Danyue said: "The teachings of the Buddhas of the three periods take the precepts as their foundation. If one does not cultivate this foundation, how can the Way be far off?"
If one delights in extensive study, one should naturally peruse the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. "Delight" (*lè*) means desire;

"peruse" (*lǎn*) means to look at; and "peruse" (*yuè*) refers to examining and viewing thoroughly. The complete Vinaya Piṭaka consists of the *Sāmaṇera-daśa-śīla-dharma* (The Ten Precepts for Novices) along with the *Vinaya-vidhi-sūtra* (Scripture on Dignified Conduct) and so forth.
This present abridgment is intended to facilitate those who have newly entered the path, so that they may come to know [the essentials].
Regarding the coarse aspects of observing and violating the precepts, if one wishes to fully understand the subtle details of their practice, one should personally consult the complete texts.
The subsequent ten precepts are from the *Śrāmaṇera-daśa-śīla-sūtra*, which the Buddha commanded Śāriputra to expound for Rāhula.
As for the latter ten precepts, they begin with the abstention from taking life and extend to the tenth, the abstention from handling gold, silver, or living images.
Their appearance in the *Śrāmaṇera-daśa-śīla-sūtra* demonstrates that this is not a mere speculative theory; it is also corroborated by other sūtras. "Buddha" refers to Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
"Decree" (chì) is like an imperial edict issued by a Son of Heaven; as the Buddha is the Dharma King, he established the precepts and codes as his command.
Śāriputra spoke for Rāhula. In the Sanskrit language, *śāri* means "body" (*kāya*) or "śāli" (a kind of bird);
*putra* means "son. His father was the Indian Brahmin teacher Tiṣya;
his mother’s name was Śārī, who possessed a beautiful form and eyes as clear as those of a śāli bird. He received his name from his mother, and is thus called Śāriputra.

Upon hearing Daoxiang’s account, he then prepared offerings for the assembly, just as Daoxiang had seen. There were more than thirty people who had received retribution for their sins.
Within seven days, Daoxiang died thirteen times; each time he saw a Bodhisattva point out his karmic retributions, and he related these accounts to the people.
Thereupon, each was compensated, and the prison records were accordingly cleared. This is recorded in the *Sengjing lu* (Mirror of the Sangha).
Thus, a sutra says: "It is better to have one's hand cut off than to take what is not rightfully one's own.

That which is not obtained through righteousness is called "what is not one's own" (*asvaka*). To protect the precepts and not take what is not one's own, even if one’s hand were to be severed, one would simply—

This constitutes one lifetime. If one takes what is not wealth—that is, violates the precepts—one will fall into the three miserable realms and receive the retribution of being handless life after life.

As the ancients said: "One does not associate with those who are not good; one does not take things that are not righteous. If taking what is not one's own wealth harms oneself, and malicious speech injures others, this is true even for the Confucian scholars of the world;
how much more so for the sons of the Śākya, who regard gold and jade as mere rubble? (From the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-samuccaya*).
A sutra states: When the Buddha was a poor man in a previous life, he said, "I would rather die in poverty while upholding the Way than live in wealth and honor while lacking the Way."
Alas! Should one not be cautious? The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "If a person steals another's property and is seized by the owner, they will be sent to the authorities for punishment and confined in prison;
their hands and feet, ears and nose may be severed, or even their head may be cut off."

They are struck with arrows and subjected to various forms of agonizing torture until they are killed. At the end of their lives, they are reborn in the hells, where fierce fires burn their bodies, molten copper is poured into their mouths, and they suffer in boiling cauldrons, glowing embers, and charcoal furnaces;
upon mountains of knives and trees of swords; through pits of hot ashes and excrement; and by being ground down or pounded in mortars and pestles.
They undergo various kinds of piercing and agonizing pain beyond measure. Even after hundreds of thousands of millions of years, there is no foreseeable end to their release.

Once their karmic retribution in hell is exhausted, they are reborn among the animals—such as elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, camels, donkeys, and dogs—and for hundreds of thousands of years they must repay their debts through the power of others.
When their animal retribution is exhausted, they are reborn among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), suffering from the torments of hunger and thirst. It is beyond description...

He spoke in detail: "For hundreds of thousands of years, one undergoes such suffering. Once the retribution for the sin is exhausted and one becomes human again, two kinds of retribution are received:
first, poverty, such that clothing does not cover the body and food does not fill the mouth;
second, being constantly plundered by water, fire, kings, ministers, and wicked bandits."
△ Third, non-lust:
the mutual union of two bodies is called lust.

The commentary states: Among the five precepts for laypeople, only sexual misconduct is prohibited; among the ten precepts for those who have left the home life, all sexual desire is completely severed.
To violate the wives or concubines of others, excluding one’s own, is called sexual misconduct. The five precepts for laypeople are the path to the realms of humans and devas;
therefore, the Buddha restricted them only to prohibit improper and illicit sexual conduct.

The ten precepts for those who have left the household life are the pure cause for proceeding toward Nirvana and the life-preserving float for crossing the ocean of suffering. If this float is once destroyed, one will sink into the turbulent waters of suffering; thus, [Nirvana...]
The *Pán jīng* (Discourse on the Crossing) says: Suppose there is a rākṣasa who, following those crossing the sea, asks them all for their life-preserving bags (*uḍupa*).
The crossers reply, "We would rather sacrifice our bodies and lives than give up these bags. The rākṣasa speaks again, saying, "If you are unwilling to give them entirely, please grant me half.
That person is likewise unwilling to give. In this manner, the request is made in succession until it is reduced to the size of a single mote of dust; yet that person [still refuses].
He likewise refuses to give it away. It is the same with the Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts.
When the rākṣasas of afflictions and broken precepts exhort the Bodhisattva to violate the heavy precepts while guarding the remaining light ones, the Bodhisattva does not comply.

Even when exhorted to violate the light precepts, the Bodhisattva likewise does not comply. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva reveres both the heavy and the light precepts in his observance of them.
It is profoundly firm and without distinction; how much more so for a śrāvaka who urgently seeks liberation from birth and death—how could such a person be subject to disparagement?
Yet, to violate any man or woman in the world is entirely termed a breach of the precepts.
"Khan" (干) means "to commit an offense," and it also signifies "to encroach upon. It is another term for sexual desire. "The world" refers to the world of sentient beings.
"Men and women" refers to men and women of the four castes, and even those who are male or female among ghosts, spirits, and animals.
To engage in impure acts at the three locations—the anus, the urinary tract, and the mouth—with any of them constitutes an offense that cannot be [atoned for].
One must repent for one's transgressions; therefore, it is said that all such cases are termed "breaking the precepts.

If a śrāmaṇera is forcibly violated by another and his own mind experiences pleasure, he commits an offense that cannot be repented of (an-avaśeṣa). If his mind does not experience pleasure, the offense may still be repented of.

What constitutes experiencing pleasure? It is like obtaining food when hungry, or obtaining a drink when thirsty. What constitutes not experiencing pleasure? It is like hot iron entering the body, or like a blade [of steel].
Regarding the nature of this transgression, a sutra states: "One who violates this precept is no longer a śrāmaṇera.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* records the case of the bhikṣuṇī Padmottarā, who secretly engaged in sexual misconduct. She claimed that sexual desire is neither killing nor stealing, and thus carries no karmic retribution;
consequently, she was struck by fierce flames erupting from her body and fell directly into hell.
"Born-entrapped" means that without waiting for the death of the body, the soul falls into it; rather, in this very life, the earth cracks open and one sinks into Avīci.

After these words were spoken by the bhikṣuṇī, a great, fierce fire first arose from her female organ, and subsequently, fierce fires burned through every joint of her body as she fell into the Avīci Hell.
"Avīci" (the Uninterrupted) is synonymous with Avīci (the Incessant). This means:
Sinful beings fall into this hell and undergo the sufferings of being burned and boiled, without a single moment of respite or joy.
Although there are many hells, they are generally subsumed under three categories. First, there are the eight hot hells, which lie beneath this continent of Jambudvīpa;
the Avīci Hell is at their very bottom. Each of these eight hells is surrounded by sixteen minor hells. Second, there are the cold hells.
There are also eight [types of cold hells] located at the base of the Cakravāḍa Mountains, where sinners undergo the suffering of freezing cold.
Third are the peripheral hells (*prādeśika-naraka*), which are briefly of three kinds: first, those in mountain ranges; second, those by the water’s edge; and third, those in the wilderness.
These involve the mixed experience of both cold and heat, such as those seen by Mount Tai’s Lord of the Underworld, as well as by Saṃgharakṣita and Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa. This...
The names, characteristics, and distinctions of the various hells, as well as the details regarding the retributions received therein, are explained extensively in the sūtras and śāstras.
Since worldly people lose their lives and ruin their families because of desire, how could those who have left the secular world to become monastics commit such transgressions again?
Kings, ministers, scholars, and commoners alike are all called "worldly people. King Zhou lost his state, and Duke Xian of Jin lost his house;
licentious women rode upon their necks and the ancestral temple consumed them by fire—all of which resulted from lustful desire.

From antiquity to the present, those who have been deluded are not few, and those who have suffered harm are beyond counting. As the *Aṣṭācārya-sūtra* states, the Buddha told a Brahmin: "The wife of a lecher..."

A woman may be discovered by her husband or his kin, meeting with calamity at that time; she may be subjected to punishment with blades and staves, having her hands and feet severed, and the disaster may extend to her family and clan.
Or she may be arrested by royal law and cast into prison, where she is tortured and interrogated with cruel severity;
she herself must bear the guilt, dying and entering hell, lying upon an iron bed or embracing a copper pillar while the wardens kindle fires.

Because he burned his own body, once his retribution for hellish offenses is exhausted, he shall receive the form of an animal. Even if he should obtain human birth, his family life will be licentious and chaotic;
he will distance himself from the Buddha and violate the Dharma, not associating with sages or worthies. He will constantly harbor fear, facing much peril and little peace.
Furthermore, he spoke in verse: "Lust is an impure practice; through delusion one loses the Right Path. The physical form wastes away and the soul is terrified; it injures one's life."
Yet they die young, suffering the punishments of stubborn ignorance and delusion; after death, they fall again into the evil realms.

Because I fear this, I have abandoned my home to find joy in the mountain thickets, leaving the secular world to become a monk. How could I ever transgress again? This refers to knowing the faults and afflictions of the five desires.
Therefore, one renounces them and leaves the household life, especially discarding even tears and spittle; how could one ever eat such things again? Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
"One who enters the Path with a sense of shame and modesty holds the alms bowl to gather in sentient beings. How can they indulge in the dust of desire and sink into the five sensory passions?
Having already abandoned the pleasures of the five desires and cast them away without looking back, how could they wish to obtain them again? It would be like a fool eating his own spittle."
The root of birth and death is desire; it is the foremost.
That all sentient beings possess bodies is entirely due to the inversion of their first thought upon seeing others in union.
By means of a lustful mind, one enters the mother’s womb and forms the physical faculties; therefore, this is called "birth.
That all sentient beings realize their nature and life through sexual desire is precisely what is meant by this. Since that which is born must inevitably perish, it is called "death.
Thus, we know that the root source of birth and death has sexual desire as its primary cause; hence, it is said to be "the foremost" of desires.
To eliminate birth and death, one must sever the mind of lust. Thus, a sutra says:

"If the beings of the six realms in all worlds have no lustful minds, they will not follow the continuity of birth and death. If the lustful mind is not eliminated, one cannot escape the realm of dust."
One must ensure that the mechanism of lust is severed in both body and mind, such that even the nature of this severance is non-existent. Only then can one hope for the Bodhi of the Buddha.
Thus, a sutra says: "Though one may live a life of lewdness and dissipation, it is better to die in chastity."

*Yi* (pronounced *yì*) means licentiousness and unrestrained indulgence. Although one may be born with licentiousness and indulgence, the body of precepts and the life-force of wisdom have already perished;

consequently, one falls into the three miserable realms and will no longer attain a human form. Although one may die in chastity and purity, the body of precepts and the life-force of wisdom remain ever-present;
through successive births and rebirths among humans and devas, one cultivates and realizes Bodhi. Therefore, the Mahā-vinaya states: "It is better to be bitten by a venomous snake..."
He died with [the organ] in his mouth; he was born thus because it did not enter into the female organ.
Long ago, in the country of Andhra, there was a bhikṣu of few desires who sent a śrāmaṇera to a household of pure faith to fetch food.

At that time, the entire family of that person of pure faith had gone to a gathering, leaving behind only a single daughter, sixteen years of age, whose appearance was upright and beautiful, yet she was [possessed by] lustful desire.
The fire burned. Prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, the śrāmaṇera said, "I possess immeasurable treasures; you may deign to accept this house as your own.
I shall provide for all your needs and serve you. The śrāmaṇera thought to himself, "I would rather give up my life than [accept this]."

Without violating the prohibitions and precepts, he immediately entered his room and closed the door. Kneeling on his right knee with palms joined, he made this vow: "I shall not forsake the Three Jewels or the true precepts;
may I be born into a tranquil family, exhaust all outflows, and attain the Way. He then cut his own throat and died. When the king heard of this, he marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
He went in person to pay his respects and placed the corpse upon a precious chariot, making various offerings.

They were nourished [with offerings] and cremated after piling up various fragrant woods. Thus, the *Daśa-śīla-sūtra* says: "Though one may live a life of lewdness and dissipation, it is not as good as dying in chastity and purity.
This is what that refers to. The details are as found in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*.
Alas! Should one not be cautious?

The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "It would be better to eat poisonous snakes and insects, or even molten copper, than to break the prohibitions and precepts while consuming the food and drink of the Saṃgha.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If a person who has broken the precepts wears the Dharma robes..."
These are sheets of hot copper and iron with which their bodies are wrapped. If they hold an alms bowl, it is a vessel for molten copper;
if they eat what is offered, they are swallowing hot iron balls and drinking molten copper.
If they receive offerings and provisions from others, these are the ox-headed hell-wardens of the hells; if they enter a vihāra, they are entering the great earth of hell.
Prison. If one sits upon the monastic bed, it is as if sitting upon a bed of glowing iron, as described in the sutras and treatises. How can one not stand in awe?
△ Fourth: Do not speak falsely.
When the mind and speech are at variance, it is called false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*).

The commentary states: There are four types of false speech. The first is lying (*anṛtavāda*), which refers to taking what is right as wrong, taking what is wrong as right, saying one has seen what was not seen, or saying one has not seen what was seen;
such things are empty, false, and unreal.
Taking what is right as wrong, one says "I do not see" when one actually sees; taking what is wrong as right, one says "I see" when one does not see.
Because these are false and deceptive, they are unreal. Furthermore, seeing belongs to the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*); "and so forth" refers to hearing, touching, and cognizing.
Hearing belongs to the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*); touch pertains to the three consciousnesses of nose, tongue, and body; and knowing pertains to the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*).
Thus, there are eight types of false speech in total: namely, to say one has seen what was not seen; to say one has heard what was not heard; to say one has touched what was not touched;

to say one knows what was not known; to say one has not seen what was seen; to say one has not heard what was heard; to say one has not touched what was touched; and to say one does not know what was known. If...
If one desires to delude others, performing any one of these [four] constitutes lying. If one has seen, heard, touched, or known something, one says that one has seen, heard, touched, or known it;
if one has not seen, heard, touched, or known it, one says that one has not seen, heard, touched, or known it. These are called the four noble statements (*āryavāda*).
Although such speech may be virtuous, if it lacks sincerity, one ultimately does not belong to the ranks of the sages.

The second is frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*). This refers to the embellishment of empty, idle, and flowery words; seductive songs and passionate verses that incite desire, increase sorrow, and dissipate the human will.
"Qi" (綺) means brocade; "mi" (靡) means beautiful. It refers to the adornment of empty and unsubstantial speech, such as—
Woven brocades and fine silks dazzle the eyes and minds of people; the passionate lyrics of sensual songs are all capable of leading people toward love and desire, and increasing their sorrow.
Furthermore, these sensual songs are melodies that delude the human ear, such as those so-called "靡靡" (mi-mi) tunes of the Yang-’a;
the passionate lyrics are the written words that seduce the human passions and desires.

The phrase "and so forth" includes everything up to words of joy, anger, sorrow, pleasure, and lamentation; these are all capable of altering one's ordinary nature and causing one to lose right mindfulness.
Therefore, it is said that they "dissipate the human mind and will. In the past, Chan Master Fayun Xiu said to Lu Zhi:
When His Majesty composed songs of sensuous beauty, they disturbed the lustful hearts of men, causing them to transgress propriety and violate prohibitions;
his sin did not stop at merely falling into evil realms. From this time forth, Lu Zhi never again composed such works.
Third is harsh speech (*pāruṣya*). This refers to using coarse and evil words to revile others and so forth.

To directly confront someone is called "reviling" (*māra*); to speak of them indirectly is called "abusing" (*li*). It means that the mouth utters coarse, evil, and unwholesome words to insult and slander others.
Thus, once the fire of anger arises, it gushes from the mouth and burns the heart, harming the person before one and causing them pain.
To cut with a blade that exceeds the edge [of propriety] truly contravenes the compassionate mindfulness of a Bodhisattva and violates the virtuous intent of one who has left the household life.
When the body dies and the soul departs, one falls into the three miserable realms. As stated in the sutras: if one falls into hell, one’s tongue will be cut off and forced to eat it oneself;
if one falls among the hungry ghosts, maggots and pus will flow from one’s mouth; if one is born as a bird or beast, one will feed upon filth and excrement.
People marveled at his voice. When his retribution was finished, he became a human again, but his appearance was hideous; his breath was foul, and both his lips and teeth were missing.
The Buddha said, "It would be better to have one's tongue cut off with a sharp blade and suffer for many kalpas than to use a single word to revile or slander a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts.
The retribution for such evil is difficult to exhaust. There are two kinds of people who will invariably enter hell. If it is not...

Fourth is double-tongued speech (*paiśunya*), which refers to speaking about one person to another and about another person to this one, thereby creating estrangement between those bound by kindness and righteousness, inciting strife, and so forth.

This includes falsely claiming to have practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*) when one has not, or slandering one who truly practices the holy life by accusing them of not practicing it. These constitute the four [types of unwholesome speech].

"Separate" (li) means to part; "intervene" (jian) means to obstruct. The gracious favors bestowed by a sovereign or a father are called "kindness" (en). The mutual benefit and virtue shared among brothers and friends is called "righteousness" (yi).
To speak of someone to another is to transmit that person's words. To speak to this person about that person, or to speak to that person about this person, is to transmit this person's words.
To speak to another person in order to incite strife and discord is to cause [disorder] for the sovereign... [and so forth].

To cause estrangement between the bonds of affection and righteousness among subjects, fathers and sons, brothers, or friends—should one not merely transmit the words of either party, but instead speak to both sides to incite their separation, this too constitutes double-tongued speech. As the *Guanzi* says:
"To sever friendships and alienate kin is called treachery. This is precisely what is meant by "instigation," which refers to provoking and inciting the words of either party to bring about division.
This gives rise to strife and contention. The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "If one teaches and transforms others with a virtuous mind, even if it results in their separation, no offense is incurred.

However, if one uses an evil mind to cause others to quarrel and be disturbed, this constitutes double-tongued speech (*paiśunya*). This is an offense of the deepest gravity, leading to rebirth in the three miserable realms.
In life after life, one will obtain a base, evil, and disintegrating retinue. This is because one has now sowed discord and caused the destruction of others."
For this reason, they even go so far as to praise in front and disparage behind; to agree with their faces and disagree behind their backs.
That is to say, when in the presence of that person, they extol their virtues, but when behind them, they slander their faults. When that person...
To one's face, they say what they have said is right; behind one's back, they say what they have done is wrong. The *Bao-en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness) states:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "When people are born into this world, calamity issues from the mouth.
One must guard the mouth more carefully than a fierce fire. A fierce fire blazes up and burns worldly wealth; malicious speech blazes up and burns the seven noble riches."

To testify to another's guilt or to proclaim another's shortcomings—regardless of whether that person is actually guilty or innocent—if one does so with an evil mind, claiming they are guilty, one incurs sin for oneself.
To "proclaim another's shortcomings" means to conceal their virtues and broadcast their faults. As Confucius said: "To hide..."
To conceal the virtues of others is what is called "obscuring the worthy. To broadcast the evils of others is the mark of a petty person. Taigong said:
"If you wish to measure others, you must first measure yourself. Words that wound others are those that wound oneself; it is like spitting blood at another—only to soil one's own hands."
First, one defiles one’s own mouth. During the Han dynasty, Ma Yuan, Marquis of Xinxi, admonished his elder brother’s sons in a letter, saying:
"I wish that you all would hear the faults and failings of others as you would hear the names of your own parents—your ears may hear them, but your mouths must not speak them.
To delight in discussing the long and short of others and to recklessly judge the correctness of laws and governance—this is what I greatly detest."
"I would rather die than wish to hear that my descendants have committed such deeds. From the *Sūtra on the Five Paths of Transmigration*, the Buddha said:
"If one delights in spreading the evils of others, after death they shall enter hell. Molten copper will be poured into their mouth; their tongue will be pulled out and ploughed with an ox-yoke.
Thereafter, they will fall among the evil birds; when people hear their cries, none will fail to be struck with terror, and they will cast spells to cause them to die."
All these belong to the category of false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*).
This refers to praising someone previously and later disparaging them, up to and including proclaiming the shortcomings of others; all such acts are subsumed under false speech.

Furthermore, if an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) claims to have realized the state of a noble one (*ārya*), such as saying they have already attained the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna-phala*) or the fruit of a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin-phala*), this too is false speech.
This is called a great lie, and its transgression is extremely grave.
An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is one who has not yet entered the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*).

To claim for oneself that one has realized the state of a noble one means that, while knowing in truth that one has no realization whatsoever, one deliberately speaks falsely, saying, "I have already realized the Dharma of the noble ones," such as that of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).

This is called "entering the stream. It means that one has already completely severed the afflictions of the three realms pertaining to views (*dṛṣṭi-heya*) and has thus entered the stream of the Dharma of the Noble Path.
This is the noble person of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) of the Hīnayāna. *Sakṛdāgāmin* (Skt. is translated here as "Once-returner.

This means that among the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm pertaining to cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), the first six grades have already been severed, while the remaining three grades still persist; consequently, one must still return [to the desire realm] once more.
Taking birth once in the desire realm—these two fruits belong to noble ones (*ārya*).
The term "and so forth" refers to the remaining three fruits and the fourth fruit, or even claiming to have attained dhyāna, samādhi, or the meditative absorption of *samāpatti*.

By such means, they deceive the world, causing devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits to come and take refuge in them, thereby seeking fame, profit, and offerings; their sin is irredeemable, and they shall fall [into hell].

In the great hells, one suffers for long kalpas. The Buddha said: "It would be better to swallow ashes and charcoal, or to consume excrement and soil, or to have one's belly ripped open by sharp knives, than to receive offerings by falsely claiming to have attained the noble Dharma.

Such a person is the greatest thief, for they steal the food and drink of others; therefore, it is said that their transgression is most grievous. The *Adbhuta-dharma-paryāya Sūtra* states that there is [no evil] equal to false speech.
Second: there are two types, the grave and the light. For the sake of making offerings, one manifests outwardly the appearance of diligence while inwardly practicing perversity and turbidity.

To falsely claim to others that one has attained states of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), or to say that one has seen the Buddha, or seen dragons, ghosts, and so forth, is called a great falsehood (*mahāmṛṣāvāda*) and leads to rebirth in the Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, there is false speech that can cause people to be killed, destroy households, or cause one to miss appointed times.
If one makes a formal agreement and causes another to feel anger or resentment, it is called "false speech of the lower grade," and one falls into a minor hell.

In other cases, such as when joking or laughing, or regarding matters of concealment and prohibition, if one says there is something when there is nothing, or says there is nothing when there is something, one does not commit an offense.

Regarding other instances of false speech: there is no offense if one employs skillful means and expedient methods out of compassion to rescue another from urgent distress or to provide them with benefit and relief.
For example, if various birds or wild animals, pursued by a hunter, enter a monastery, and the hunter asks, "Venerable sir, have you seen such-and-such a bird?
at that time, if it is a cold season, one should say, "Long-lived one, you may enter briefly for a moment."
If one is sitting by a fire at that time, and it is hot, one should say, "Please enter briefly to drink some water and rest for a short while.
If the hunter says, "I am not tired; I am asking about the wild beasts," one should immediately examine one's own fingernails first.
He replies, "I see fingernails. If he should further say, "I am not asking about fingernails; I am asking whether there are sentient beings who can be killed—is this permissible?
one should then look in all four directions and reflect thus: "In ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), there are fundamentally no sentient beings.
Then one should reply to him, "I do not see any sentient beings. Furthermore...
For example, King Prasenajit ordered the execution of his chief cook.
Queen Mallikā had someone hide him away until the king’s intoxication had worn off and he felt remorse; she then sent him back to the king. The king was greatly delighted.

Although the queen had received the eight precepts, she did not violate the prohibition against lying in order to save another from peril. This is what is called benefiting others through skillful means and expedient wisdom.
The ancients said that the essential principle for governing oneself begins with refraining from false speech; how much more so for one who studies the Way that transcends the world!
Now, the preservation of virtue and integrity has utmost sincerity as its primary requirement, and the foundation of establishing one’s character has speech and conduct as its priority.
This is why Nan Rong repeated the lines of the "White Jade" three times, intending thereby to exercise caution over his words. Thus, the ancients were careful at the very beginning.
[End. It begins with not speaking falsely. As for the "ancient person," it was Lord Sima (Sima Guang).
The Lord was filial and fraternal, loyal and trustworthy, reverent, frugal, and upright. From his youth until old age, he never spoke falsely.
Therefore, he once said: "The Way of Sincerity is indeed difficult to enter; however, one should begin with not speaking falsely. He further remarked: "I have no qualities that surpass others."
"However, throughout my life, there has never been anything I have done that I could not speak of openly to others.

At that time, Liu An-shi asked the Master, "Is there one word that can be practiced throughout one's entire life? The Master replied, "It is sincerity (*cheng*). He asked, "By what means does one enter into it?
The Master replied, "One enters through refraining from false speech. "The Confucian scholars of the world establish themselves as men of lifelong fame and virtue," [he added].
If this is so, how much more so for a son of the Śākya who studies the supramundane path and cultivates the causes for the future mark of the long tongue—would he not do likewise?
As the Sūtra says: "He who is not careful with his speech is not a śrāmaṇera."
The Sūtras record that a śrāmaṇera once mocked an elderly bhikṣu for reading the scriptures with a voice like the barking of a dog. That elderly bhikṣu was, in fact, an arhat.
Because of this, he instructed the śrāmaṇera to perform an urgent repentance; only thus did he narrowly avoid falling into hell, yet he still fell into the body of a dog.
A single word of evil speech brings such harm as this.
The sūtras record this in more than one place; some refer to him as a śrāmaṇera, while others refer to him as a young bhikṣu.
According to the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* and the *Sūtra on Requiting Kindness*, during the time of the past Buddha Kāśyapa, a young bhikṣu saw an elderly bhikṣu.
He was constantly fond of chanting, yet his voice was dull and muffled. Relying on his own pleasant tone, he said, "Your voice now is like the barking of a dog.
At that time, the elderly bhikṣu asked him, "Do you recognize me? I have now attained the path of Arhatship.
Upon hearing this, the youth was struck with terror and reproached himself; he immediately confessed his transgression before the elder bhikṣu, who then—
"Listen to this confession of transgression. Although he was spared from hell, because of those evil words, he constantly took birth in the body of a dog for five hundred lifetimes.
At that time, there were five hundred merchants who, taking a white dog with them, traveled together to another country.
On the way, they halted to rest. The dog stole some meat; the merchants cut off the dog's four paws, threw it into a pit, and departed. Then Śāriputra—"
With his divine eye, he saw from afar that the dog’s body was hunched and prostrate on the ground, emaciated by hunger and suffering, its life about to end.
He immediately took his alms-bowl of rice and flew to where the dog was. With a heart of compassion, he bestowed the food upon the dog, thereby saving its remaining life.
Having eaten, the dog was filled with joy; [the monk] then preached the Dharma for it. Seven days later, its life ended, and it was reborn in Śrāvastī.
He was of a Brahmin family, named Kunti. When he reached the age of seven, Śāriputra transformed him by leading him to leave the household life.

He preached the sublime Dharma to him, whereupon he immediately realized arhatship and became fully endowed with the six supernormal powers. He then perceived that his own previous existence had been that of a starving dog.
"By the grace of my teacher Śāriputra, I have now obtained this human body and attained the fruits of the Path.
I thought to myself that I should serve my teacher with all my strength for as long as I live, remaining a *śrāmaṇera* forever and never receiving the full precepts (*mahā-śīla*).

Because I had left the household life and maintained the pure precepts in my previous existence, I have now encountered Śākyamuni Tathāgata and attained the state of an Arhat. Thus, one knows that if it were not for..."
If one’s precepts are impure, then liberation will have no foreseeable end.
Thus a sutra says: "When a person lives in this world, an axe is in their mouth; it is by means of evil speech that they cut themselves."
Although this passage originates from the *Mūlasūtra*, it is identical in the *Dharmapada*, the *Āgama*, and the *Mahāvibhaṅga*.

The axe serves as a metaphor for one's own tongue, and malicious speech is likened to the striking of that axe. It is like a person who hurls an axe to strike another, yet when the axe falls, it returns to wound his own body.
When people of the world seek to harm others with malicious speech, they instead bring harm upon themselves. As the *Mahāvibhaṅga* states: "In the past, Devadatta reviled..."
"Śāriputra, for a bhikṣu of evil desires, hot blood shall immediately gush from his nostrils, and he shall fall into the great hells in his very living body.
The Buddha thereupon spoke this verse: 'When a man dwells in the world, an axe is in his mouth;
It is by means of it that he cuts himself— Because of his evil speech. He should revile, yet instead he praises; He should praise, yet instead he reviles. He reaps the fruit for himself.'"
Its retribution brings no joy at all.
Alas! How can one not be cautious?
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The sin of lying can cause sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms. Even if they are born as humans,"
In the intermediate state, one receives two kinds of retribution: first, being frequently slandered; second, being deceived by others.
Why does false speech lead to rebirth in the three evil realms? It is because such false and unreal speech causes others to undergo suffering in vain.
Therefore, one suffers death and the pains of hell. Because one’s deception violates the sincerity and trust of others, one is reborn among the animals.
Regarding the retribution experienced in this life: because of their false speech, which arises from greed, deceit, and the sin of stinginess, they further become hungry ghosts.
Because their false speech is not truthful, they are slandered by others; because their false speech deceives and misleads people, they suffer these consequences.
One is deceived by others; having realized that false speech brings these four great karmic retributions, how could one not exercise restraint?
Fifth: not drinking alcohol, which confuses the mind and obscures wisdom—this is called *madya*.
The commentary states: "To drink alcohol" refers to drinking any kind of intoxicating liquor. In the Western Regions (India), there are many varieties of wine;
it can be made from sugarcane, grapes, or even a hundred kinds of flowers. In this land (China), there is only that made from grain.
Neither is permitted to be drunk.
The Western Regions refer to India; this region refers to China. Although there are many varieties of wine, they do not exceed two types:
first, grain wine, which is brewed by mixing the five grains with yeast;
second, wood wine, which is distilled from roots, stems, flowers, and fruits, combined with various medicinal herbs—such as sugarcane, grape, and the hundred-flower wines.
These include lotus-root syrup and the like. These two types of liquor must not be swallowed; therefore, it is said that both are undrinkable.
Generally, if a substance possesses the three characteristics of the color of liquor, the fragrance of liquor, and the taste of liquor—whether lacking one or two of these—it can cause intoxication.
To drink such a substance constitutes an offense. If one consumes dregs, eats yeast, or cooks food mixed with liquor, one commits an offense in every case. If there is none...
Regarding the flavor, aroma, color, and scent of alcohol: it shall not intoxicate, nor shall one consume it.
Except in cases of serious illness where there is no remedy other than wine, one must inform the assembly before partaking. Without such cause, not even a single drop may touch the lips.
The Buddha said: "If you take me as your teacher, you must not drink alcohol, nor give it to others to drink, nor store it;
you must not even place a drop of alcohol on the tip of a blade of grass and let it enter your mouth. Regarding those with 'serious illness,' this refers to conditions that are not minor or slight.
'Nothing but alcohol can cure it' means that other medicines fail to heal it, and the physician instructs [the patient to use alcohol]."
If alcohol is used as medicine and no other means can cure the ailment, one must inform the assembly so that they are aware;
only then may it be consumed. In this way, one avoids the fault of selfishness. "Without cause" refers to being without illness.

It is only for serious illnesses or chronic conditions that a temporary, provisional allowance is granted; this does not mean consuming it habitually over long periods. If one is without illness yet feigns it, or has only a minor ailment, [it is forbidden].
To carry a heavy load [of alcohol] constitutes an offense for both parties.
Furthermore, one must not smell wine; one must not stay in a tavern; and one must not give wine to others to drink.
"Smell" refers to smelling with the nose. "Must not stay in a tavern": "stay" means to stop there temporarily, and "tavern" refers to a place where liquor is sold.
Regarding taverns and liquor shops: for the sake of preventing two matters, they are not permitted to be established. First, to prevent scandal and suspicion; second, to avoid excessive intoxication.
One who does not drink alcohol themselves, knowing it to be wrong, how could they give it to others?

For a Bodhisattva acting for the benefit of sentient beings, drinking oneself is still a minor matter, but giving it to others to drink is a grave offense, as it uses intoxicants to delude sentient beings and causes them to lose the seed of wisdom.
It is for this reason.
Yi Di created wine, and Yu consequently forbade it in grief.
Yi Di was a man of the Xia dynasty who was skilled at brewing fermented liquors. Yu was the sovereign of Xia. The *Zhan Guo Ce* states that Yi—
Yi Di brewed wine. When Yu drank it and found it sweet, he said, "In future generations, there will surely be those who cause their states to perish because of wine.
He consequently distanced himself from Yi Di and, out of deep remorse, renounced fine liquor. Long ago, Bing Yuan of the Han dynasty abstained from drinking;
when someone asked him why, Yuan replied, "I was originally able to drink, but because it distracted my thoughts and caused me to neglect my studies, I have severed the habit."
This is all they do. Worldly scholars still fear the neglect of their studies; how much more so for one who studies the Way that transcends the world?
King Zhou constructed a wine pond, and his state perished as a result. For a monk to drink alcohol is even more shameful than that.

Zhou was the youngest son of Emperor Yi, named Shou, also known as Xin. His ancestors had established their capital at Yin. According to the *Shifa* (Canon of Posthumous Titles), one who "harms righteousness and injures the good" is called Zhou.
He first fashioned jade cups and ivory chopsticks; he constructed the Lu Terrace and built the Palace of Jade.
Its jade gates were three li wide and a thousand chi high. There, he fed humans like beasts and turned wine into a moat, hanging meat to form a forest. Men and women...
They went about naked, chasing one another through the courtyards; within the palace were nine markets where they indulged in drinking bouts throughout the long night.
They devised the "frying-grid" torture, disemboweled pregnant women, and hacked at people's shins. When Prince Bi Gan remonstrated with him, he said in anger: "I have heard that a sage..."
The heart has seven apertures. [King Wu] subsequently killed Bi Gan to examine his heart. Thereupon, King Wu addressed the feudal lords, saying, "The Yin dynasty has committed grave crimes;
it must not fail to be punished. He then marched east to attack Zhou. Zhou fled and ascended the Luk Tai terrace, where he dressed himself in pearls and jade, set himself on fire, and died.
Yu said that there would surely be those in later generations who cause their states to perish through wine; this is an example of that.
Therefore, the warnings against licentiousness in the *Shi* and *Shu* all originate with wine.
Thus, when King Zhou was immersed in drunken debauchery, Wei Zi composed a "Gao" (Admonition) to inform Ji Zi and Bi Gan before departing.
Because King Li of Zhou was steeped in wine, Duke Mu of Qin composed the "Da Ya" (Greater Odes) to lament and wept with flowing tears. Later, in the state of Qin...
Fu Sheng was the ruler. He drank day and night without ceasing; while intoxicated, he committed many acts of slaughter, and his ministers and subjects feared him.
Fu Jian, the King of Haedong, led an army to invade him. While Sheng was still sleeping in a drunken stupor, the soldiers killed him. Fu Jian subsequently proclaimed himself Emperor.

When Emperor Jingzong of the Tang Dynasty was eighteen years old, he drank heavily with eunuchs at night and played the ball game; suddenly the candles went out, and he was assassinated. For this reason—
The perils of the past and those of the present all stem from wine and women. From the ancient sages to the later worthies, all achieved renown by severing their attachment to these things.
Having left the household life to become monks, one’s mind and body transcend the secular world; thus, one should not bring shame upon the ancient sages by following in their perilous footsteps.
Therefore, it is said that this is most deeply shameful.
In the past, there was an upāsaka who, because he violated the precept against intoxicants, subsequently broke all his other precepts as well.
Among the thirty-six faults, the single act of drinking was fully present; thus, the transgression was no small matter.
Upāsaka; this is translated as "male lay follower. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: Once there was a lay follower who was by nature benevolent and virtuous.

Having received and maintained the five precepts, he was diligent and never transgressed them. Later, at another time, he returned home from a long journey. His family members had gone to attend a gathering.
Pressed by thirst, he saw a vessel containing what appeared to be water but was actually wine; he took it and drank it. Then...

He violated the precept against intoxicants. At that time, a neighbor’s rooster entered his house; he stole it, killed it, and ate it, thereby further violating the two precepts against stealing and killing.
A neighbor’s daughter followed the rooster into the house; he coerced her into sexual intercourse, thereby further violating the precept against sexual misconduct.

When the neighbor’s family reported this to the authorities, he denied it and refused to confess, thereby further violating the precept against false speech. Thus it is said that he subsequently broke all the remaining precepts as well, totaling thirty.
Regarding the six losses, the *Sūtra on the Arising of Good and Evil* states: first, the loss of wealth and resources; second, the manifestation of many illnesses;
third, engaging in strife and contention; fourth, the increase of killing and harm; fifth, the increase of hatred and anger; sixth, the frequent failure to achieve one's intentions;
seventh, the gradual diminution of wisdom; eighth, the non-increase of merit and virtue; ninth, the further decrease of merit and virtue; tenth, [the manifestation of] manifest faults.
11. Secrecy; 12. Failure to accomplish one's undertakings; 13. An abundance of sorrow and suffering;
14. Obscurity and dullness of the faculties; 15. Dishonoring one’s parents; 16. Lack of respect for śramaṇas;
17. Lack of faith in brāhmaṇas; 18. Lack of reverence for the Buddha; 19. Lack of reverence for the Dharma and the Saṅgha; 20. Associating with evil friends.
21. Abandoning virtuous friends; 22. Neglecting food and drink; 23. Failing to maintain physical modesty;
24. Intense lust; 25. Displeasing to others; 26. Excessive talkativeness and laughter;
27. Disdain from one’s parents; 28. Resentment from one’s kinsmen; 29. Upholding what is improper.
29. Abandoning the True Dharma; 30. Lack of respect for the virtuous and good;
31. Committing transgressions and faults; 32. Being far removed from Nirvāṇa; 33. Increasing madness and insanity; 34. Distraction of body and mind;
35. Engaging in evil and negligence; 36. At the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one falls [into the lower realms].
In the great hells, one suffers without end. These thirty-six calamities arise from the violation of the precept against alcohol;
thus it is said that "a single sip brings them all. Since the calamities number thirty-six, it is said that "the transgression is no small matter."
Those who are addicted to drinking fall into the Hell of Boiling Excrement after death; life after life they remain ignorant and deluded, losing the seed of wisdom.
As the *Sūtra* says: "If one is fond of drinking wine and becomes intoxicated, upon death one enters the *niraya* of boiling excrement."

Later, they fall among the *xingxing* apes; later, when born as humans, they are foolish and ignorant, having no knowledge at all. The *Jiaohua didiyu jing* (Sūtra on Teaching and Transforming Those in the Hells) states:

Bodhisattva Xinxiang addressed the Buddha, saying, "Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are sometimes dazed or insane, or foolish or idiotic, unable to distinguish between the beautiful and the ugly.
What sin has caused this? The Buddha said, "In a previous life, because they sat and drank [intoxicants]..."

Intoxication leads to disorder and incurs thirty-six transgressions; furthermore, one acquires a deluded body like that of a drunkard, failing to recognize the honorable from the lowly and the beautiful from the ugly, and thus incurs this retribution.
Nevertheless, good and evil do not fail to correspond; there must be a result for every cause.
