"Biqiu" (Bhikṣu) is translated here as "the mendicant" (*qishi*). "Mendicant" (*qi*) is a term for begging or seeking; "gentleman" (*shi*) is a designation for one who is refined and pure.

This refers to one who internally cultivates refined and pure virtue and externally remains free from the four types of wrong livelihood, seeking only the requisites for sustaining the body in order to fulfill that refined and pure virtue and to bring benefit to sentient beings.

The Vinaya Master said: "As for those who beg for alms (bhikṣu), internally they beg for the Dharma to cultivate their nature; externally they beg for food to sustain their bodies.
Parents are one's closest kin, yet they are the first to be relinquished. Hair and beard are what the world prizes, yet they are completely shaved away.
Wealth overflowing with the seven treasures is discarded as if it were mere weeds. Even the highest rank of nobility is viewed [with indifference]..."
How much more so than mere mist and clouds! Utterly weary of impermanence and profoundly investigating the root of existence, one who wishes to elevate their aspirations must humble their person.

Holding a mendicant’s staff is no different from grasping a withered gourd; carrying an alms bowl is no different from holding a broken vessel. With tattered robes draped over the shoulders, one wears nothing but worn-out rags;

He then asked the people, learning that the princess had come; his desires unfulfilled, he was consumed by grief, resentment, and vexation, and the fire of lust breaking out within him, he burned himself to death.

○ The Lower Section: Gate of Dignified Conduct (*Īryāpatha*).

Regarding "dignified conduct" (*īryāpatha*): it means there is a majesty that inspires awe and a decorum that merits reverence. Because one maintains pure precepts and is fully endowed with the holy life (*brahmacarya*), the physical appearance of a monk is majestic and grand;
his manifold virtues are solemn and awe-inspiring, thereby causing others to feel a sense of reverence. His movements and stillness are in perfect accord with the proper rules.

Dignified and worthy of admiration, his deportment was upright and manifesting rectitude; thus he inspired reverence in all. This constitutes the constituent qualities of the path for one who has left the household life, serving as a model for both humans and devas.
It is said that his pure conduct was perfected in his ritual observances, and his stainless integrity was complete in the precepts.

His spirit towered above the stars and the Milky Way; his majesty was as solemn as wind and clouds. Within, he harbored the virtue of a lion; without, he manifested the appearance of a king of elephants.
Its majesty is extolled and received by humans and devas alike; divine dragons look upon it with reverence and submission. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"To fully receive and uphold the teachings on dignified conduct (*vīryāpatha*) is that which enables the Three Jewels to remain uninterrupted.

Now, this lower section consists of twenty-four chapters, all emerging from the single gate of dignified conduct. This is the chariot track of the śrāmaṇera, the very beginning of transcending the world.
This is a step [in the process].

The Buddha established a rule that when a śrāmaṇera reaches twenty years of age and wishes to receive full ordination (upasampadā), if he is unable to answer fully when questioned regarding his conduct as a śrāmaṇera, one should not grant him full ordination.
One should say: "When you were a śrāmaṇera, you did not even know the duties of a śrāmaṇera..."

"Regarding what Maitreya has practiced: the duties of a śramaṇa are difficult to perform. You should first go and study them thoroughly; once you have fully heard and understood them, you shall receive the full ordination (upasaṃpadā).
Now, although I am conferring the full ordination upon you, people say that the Buddha-dharma is easy to practice and that being a śramaṇa is easy to do;
therefore, you must first inquire [into these matters]."
When a śrāmaṇera wishes to receive full ordination, the preceptor should inquire about the ten precepts and various matters of deportment;
if he is unable to answer fully, one should not grant him full ordination. "Your Honor" is a title of respect, used as a ruler addresses a minister.
To say that one does not know what a śrāmaṇera should practice means that one is unacquainted with the ritual observances and the actions a śrāmaṇera ought to perform.
Furthermore, that which is most difficult for a śramaṇa to accomplish refers to the two hundred and fifty precepts of a bhikṣu, which are extremely difficult to practice and maintain.
To be "thoroughly learned" means one should diligently train in the ten precepts as well as all the rules of decorum (vīryā).

To "fully hear and know" it: "hearing" refers to extensive inquiry of those who have prior knowledge; "knowing" refers to internal realization through one's own mind. Thus, people say the Buddha-dharma is easy [to understand].
It is said that practicing as a śramaṇa is easy because one does not understand that the Buddha-way is supremely subtle; thus it is called "easy practice.

It is said to be easy to perform because one does not recognize the workings of transgression and merit, nor the interplay of the laws and regulations. Therefore, anyone who acts as a teacher should first inquire by means of these points.

The following rules have been excerpted from various sūtras concerning the deportment of śrāmaṇeras, as well as from the *Ancient Pure Regulations* (*Gǔ qīngguī*) and the *Modern Model for Śrāmaṇeras* (*Jīn shāmí chéngfàn*).

Furthermore, although the *Practicing the Protection of the Vinaya Code* (*Xíng hù lǜyí*) by Vinaya Master Xuánzàng was intended as an admonition for newly ordained bhikṣus, those sections applicable to all have likewise been excerpted.
This is because the dispositions of people in this Dharma of the Final Age are largely characterized by indolence; they grow weary when hearing too many details. Therefore...

This work deletes the redundant and extracts the essentials; it further classifies the material to facilitate study. Where there were occasional omissions, one or two items have been supplemented according to their meaning.
The "rules below" refer to the twenty-four rules of deportment for śrāmaṇeras. *Śrāmaṇera-Ācāra*.
The "Various Scriptures" refers to the *Śrāmaṇera-daśa-śīla-sūtra*, the *Dharma of Serving the Teacher*, the *Sūtra on Ritual Standards*, and so forth.
The "Ancient Rules of Purity" refers to the *Baizhang Qinggui* and the admonitions and regulations composed by ancient masters.
The *Śrāmaṇera Chengfan* was compiled by the Ming dynasty Chan Master Xixian Yuexin based on the ten precepts and other laws. As for the "Practicing and Guarding Dignified Conduct," it is...
This was compiled by Master Daoxuan of the Tang dynasty; however, it is not entirely precise. Why?

Because within it there are one or two points that do not accord with the Vinaya texts. "Prolixity" means abundance. This refers to the fact that we live in the age of the Final Dharma (mappō), when people are generally indolent.
Due to this mental indolence, they feel weary upon hearing something prolix. Consequently, regarding the aforementioned sutras and vinayas...
From within the *Qinggui* (Rules of Purity), redundant texts have been excised; each section has been abbreviated to extract its essential core, while still being divided into twenty-four categories.
This is because the ocean of the Vinaya is vast and profound, such that one cannot find its source through mere exploration; and the celestial expanse of its meaning is so high and wide.

Looking up at it, one cannot reach its summit. Therefore, I have abridged that extensive literature and condensed it into this essential summary, so as to facilitate the initial study and training of beginners, enabling them to know the direction they should take.
As for the additions included here, they were penned by the Great Master himself;
whenever there was anything incomplete within the protocols of deportment and ritual practice, he supplemented it according to its respective category and meaning.
Those who delight in extensive study should consult the complete text for themselves.

Within the *Śrāmaṇera-daśa-śīla-dharma*, there are seventy-two types of dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*). Should one wish to understand the details and meanings extensively, [one must refer to the full work].
One should personally examine that text, as well as the various *śrāmaṇera* precepts and so forth.
△ Regarding the first point of revering the Great Śramaṇa:
one must never address the Great Śramaṇa by his personal name.
The Sanskrit term *śramaṇa* is translated here as "diligent labor" (*qín láo*), meaning that one exerts great effort and merit in cultivating the Path.
It is also called "restraining and resting" (*lè xī*), meaning that through diligent cultivation of wholesome qualities, one brings all evils to rest.

Furthermore, it is called "restraining and proceeding" (*lè xíng*), meaning that by diligently practicing wholesome dharmas, one proceeds toward Nirvāṇa. The *Śūramgama-samādhi Sūtra* states: "One who quiets the mind reaches the fundamental source; therefore, he is called a śramaṇa."
"Gate. Great Śramaṇa. 'One who has received full ordination. 'Name' refers to a personal name; 'to call' means to address.
This means that one must not utter those two syllables [of his name]; rather, one should say 'Venerable So-and-so' or 'Elder So-and-so.
The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states: The Buddha told the bhikṣus, 'You should dwell with reverence; you should always bind the mind [to mindfulness]; you should always be fearful.'"
Be careful! If one is not reverent, does not focus the mind, and lacks fear and circumspection, yet wishes to have one's deportment complete—this is impossible.
If one’s deportment is not complete, yet wishes to fulfill the training in the Dharma—this is impossible.
If the training in the Dharma is not fulfilled, yet wishes to have the fivefold Dharma-body complete—this is impossible. The fivefold Dharma...
One whose body is not complete cannot possibly attain *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
One must not eavesdrop on the Great Śramaṇa when he recites the precepts during the *poṣadha*, nor when the *vinaya* is being expounded; a *śrāmaṇera* must not go there in secret.
Eavesdropping brings upon oneself grave offenses and shall forever preclude one from receiving the full precepts; one must therefore exercise great caution.
If one sees two or three great śramaṇas conversing in private within a room, one must not enter abruptly. If there is an urgent matter, one should snap one's fingers to make a sound before entering.
This applies equally to the private conversations of others, excluding only bhikṣus, lest [the secret] be leaked.
To judge right and wrong brings calamity upon oneself, for it disrupts right mindfulness.
One must not go about speaking of the faults of the Great Śramaṇa.
If a bhikṣu has made an error or omission, one must not speak of his shortcomings behind his back, nor may one do so in private.
He stood reviling the Great Śramaṇa and mocked him with laughter, imitating his speech, appearance, and gait.
The Mahāvinaya states: "Whatever words a person who has left the household life utters should all be for the benefit [of others]; one must not privately speak of others out of resentment.
The Śāstra says: "If one speaks of a bhikṣu’s transgressions to a layperson (avadātavasana), then that person..."
Within the Buddha-dharma, there is no lack of faith and reverence. It would be better to destroy stupas and damage images than to speak of the faults and evils of a bhikṣu to others.
If one speaks of such transgressions, one destroys the Dharma-body.
One must not remain seated and fail to rise when seeing a great śramaṇa passing by, except during the time of reciting scriptures, when ill, while shaving the head,
while eating, or while performing communal duties.
If one sees a bhikṣu passing by, one should immediately stand up; however, there are five exceptions where one need not rise, and in those cases, failing to rise is not an offense.
If one encounters him on the road, one should immediately step aside onto the path and stand upright, waiting until he has passed before proceeding.

Whenever one receives instruction or benefit, one should join the palms in reverence and stand listening until it is finished, then perform a prostration to express gratitude. If one is reprimanded, one must not stare back with wide eyes; rather, one should...
One should speak with gentle words and repent for one's transgressions, drawing others' shortcomings toward oneself. The *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* states:
"If one treats the Saṃgha with contempt, that person shall fall into a poor and lowly family. Wherever they are born, their physical faculties will be incomplete;

they will be hunchbacked, short-statured, and ugly. After casting off this body, they will again be born into a place where they suffer from many ailments, emaciation, and wasting, with hands and feet that are cramped and paralyzed."
There is pus and blood filling and flowing over his body, and his flesh falls away; for hundreds of thousands of millions of years, he undergoes this retribution of suffering.
Xinghu says: "Those with five summer retreats or more hold the rank of ācārya; those with ten summer retreats or more hold the rank of upādhyāya. Although...
A *śrāmaṇera* should anticipate the affairs of a *bhikṣu*.

"Summer" (*kṣa*) refers to the summer retreat; "summer-ordination age" (*kṣa-lakṣa*) means having received full ordination (*upasampadā*) and having already undergone that many years of summer retreats. "Upādhyāya" is a foreign term;
here it is translated as "Power-Born" (*li-sheng*), meaning that by the power of the teacher, one's body of precepts (*śīla-kāya*) is born. If based on the Sanskrit...
In speech, one says *upādhyāya*, which means "preceptor" (*ācārya*), signifying that the disciple receives instruction directly from him.

Although in this case [the recipient] has not received the precepts or instruction directly from him, he is nonetheless of great virtue and high standing due to his seniority in the monastic order (*vassa*).
Therefore, they share the same rank as the teacher (*ācārya*). *Ācārya*, or alternatively *ācārya*, is translated here as "Model Teacher" (*guifanshi*).

This refers to one who can instruct disciples in the proper methods and regulations. There are five such types: first, those who confer the ten precepts; second, those who confer the full ordination (*mahāśramaṇa*);
third, those who provide instruction; fourth, those who provide reliance (*niśraya*); and fifth, those who transmit the scriptures.
△ Second, regarding serving the teacher:
one should rise early.
To "serve the teacher" means to attend to them from beginning to end without ever becoming separated; this is what is meant by "service. They are the model for all people.

One who instructs others through the Way is called a *śāstṛ* (teacher), or alternatively a *gurusthānīya* (senior teacher). This means being the elder among people and providing the rules for training beings.
Some call them *śāstr-pitṛ* (teacher-father); "father" refers to the standard of conduct, for they teach their children according to the Dharma.

The Vinaya states: "When a disciple attends upon the *upādhyāya* (preceptor), he should maintain four mentalities: first, affection; second, reverent compliance; third, awe and caution; and fourth, respect."

In attending and serving [the teacher], one should act as a minister or a son serves a sovereign or a father. In this manner, by successively showing mutual respect, veneration, and care, one can cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time and increase in greatness.
Within the Buddha-dharma, a single night is divided into three periods: the beginning, the middle, and the end.
During the first and last periods, one should attend to the teacher, or perform prostrations, recitations, and seated meditation; it is only during the middle period of the night that...

When resting, if it is past midnight, one should rise first; having washed and rinsed one's mouth, one should then prepare tooth-sticks, water for rinsing, and other necessities, awaiting whatever the teacher may require.
When wishing to enter a room, one should first snap the fingers three times.
If entering the teacher’s quarters, one must snap the fingers three times outside the door; only after the teacher has been alerted should one enter.
If one commits a transgression, the Upādhyāya or Ācārya may instruct and admonish them; one must not respond with contrary words.
If one has personal faults and the two masters instruct and reprimand them, they should receive the instruction with bowed head and must not oppose the teachers' words.
After departing, one should especially reflect upon them and act according to their instructions. Chengfan says: "Śrāmaṇeras..."

One should always maintain reverence and awe toward the teacher, comply with the teacher’s intentions, and constantly cultivate a sense of shame and remorse. One should keep in mind the repayment of the four debts of gratitude and provide support for those within the three realms of existence.
One should regard one’s *upādhyāya* and *ācārya* as one would regard the Buddha.

"Beholding" refers to gazing upon [the teacher]. Because the teacher is able to propagate the model for the three realms, proclaiming the teachings on behalf of the Buddha, and because he gives birth to one's body of precepts and nurtures one's life of wisdom, one should regard him with reverent attention as if he were the Buddha. Chengfan says:
"If there are many disciples, each should fulfill their duty; this extends even to the offering of a single cup of tea, a single whisk, or a single desk."
If one must go out to dispose of impure vessels, one must not spit, nor should one harbor anger or resentment.
"Anger" (*krodha*) refers to the state of being provoked; furthermore, harboring a grudge is called "anger," while the outburst of indignation is called "resentment" (*pratigha*).

Regarding "impure vessels," this refers to receptacles for feces and urine, as well as spittoons and the like. "Must not spit" means that one should not give rise to a sense of loathing while spitting phlegm or saliva.
One should reflect with earnest mindfulness that this foul body composed of the four great elements is something that neither the noble nor the ordinary, neither oneself nor others, can avoid.
When the teacher is seated in meditation, one should not prostrate; when the teacher is walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*), one should not prostrate;
when the teacher is eating, preaching the sutras, brushing his teeth, bathing, or sleeping, one should in all such cases refrain from prostrating. Furthermore, when the teacher closes the door...
One should not perform prostrations outside the door. When wishing to enter the door to perform prostrations, one should snap the fingers three times; the teacher should then respond by leaving.
As for cleaning the teeth, this involves using a toothpick, a comb, or a brush to scrub and rinse the teeth. None of the aforementioned activities constitute a time for performing prostrations.
Therefore, one should not perform prostrations. Regarding the phrase "and so forth": it may be that the teacher is shaving his head, washing his feet, or chewing on a tooth-stick;
or the ground may be impure; or the teacher may be occupied and have no leisure; or there may be guests and the like.
When carrying food and drink for one's teacher, one should always support it with both hands. When the meal is finished and the vessels are being gathered, one should do so slowly;
supporting them with both hands is the manner of showing respect. "Slowly" is the etiquette of caution. "Gathering" (liǎn) means to collect and put away. The Vinaya states:
"Whenever presenting food and drink, one should ensure it is neither too cold nor too hot. The *Chengfan* says: "In preparing food for one's teacher, there should be no..."

Regarding the discussion of coarse and fine [utensils], both must be refined and clean; they must certainly suit the teacher’s disposition. Whenever serving tea or soup, one must not insert a finger into the bowl.
Instead, one should bend the four fingers of both hands and hold the belly of the bowl with the sixth finger (the thumb), lifting it level to present it to the teacher.
When the tea is finished, receive the bowl back as before. The attendant says: "Whenever offering medicinal tea, salt, or any food..."
Regarding foodstuffs, one should eat them all; they must be given out according to the time and not given in excess so that any remains overnight. One must be extremely careful of this.
If one offers fresh fruit to the teacher, it must first be purified—either by touching it with fire or by cutting it with a knife.
Alternatively, one may peel it with the fingernails. If the fruit is unfit to serve as seed, it need not be purified. For sugarcane, the joints and sprouts should be removed;
for willow branches, the sprouts should be removed. Alternatively, they may be purified by fire. Non-seasonal fruits and juices must be strained to remove the pulp and clarified;
they should then be sprinkled with water for purification before being offered to the teacher.
When attending to one's teacher, one must not stand directly facing them; nor should one stand at a high elevation; nor should one stand too far away.
One should position oneself so that the teacher’s soft voice can be heard without straining their venerable strength.
"Attendant" (*shi*) means to serve in close proximity. To stand directly facing [the teacher], at a high elevation, or too far away all violates the decorum of respect.

If one is too distant, the teacher’s words will not be heard, necessitating repeated speech and thus taxing the venerable one’s energy. The Vinaya states: "One must not remain more than seven paces from the teacher.
The *Chengfan* says: "One must not stand in the teacher’s shadow; one must not turn the body away, lower the head, speak in a low voice, or laugh lightly. One should maintain a respectful posture."
With a solemn and reverent mind, stand facing [the teacher]. One must not stand with hands hanging down. Regarding conduct while in the teacher’s presence:
one must not scratch an itch, nor rub the face with the tips of one's fingernails. One must not put on socks or wash one's feet in the presence of the teacher.
If you wish to inquire about the causes and conditions of the Buddha-dharma, you should adjust your robes, prostrate, join your palms, and kneel with your right knee on the ground.
When the teacher speaks, listen with a clear and attentive mind, contemplating the words deeply.
"Circumstances" (*nidāna*) refers to the accounts of causal conditions explained in the Sūtras and Vinaya, or the spiritual encounters (*jīyuán*) of ancient masters;

because deluded thoughts do not arise therein, it is called "clarifying the mind. To listen attentively is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); to contemplate is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*);

to penetrate deeply is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Furthermore, there are three grades of listening: listening with the spirit is superior; listening with the mind is middling; [listening with the ears is inferior].
Listening with the ears is the lowest [form of inquiry]. When the teacher is sitting alone, or when he is walking, or when his countenance is serene, one should immediately ask.

One must stand to one side, with a relaxed expression and a tranquil mind, asking questions with utmost sincerity. Each word should be articulated clearly, and one should listen and receive the teaching with an open mind.
If asked about matters of daily life, there is no need for prostrations or kneeling; one should simply stand upright beside the teacher and report the facts as they are.

"Matters of daily life" refers to the ordinary, routine affairs of the monastic community. "Reporting the facts as they are" means to present the matter directly and truthfully according to its actual state.

If following the *Mahā-vinaya*, one must likewise perform a single prostration, kneel with the right knee on the ground (*hu-kuei*), and request permission before speaking. For instance, if one wishes to...

Regarding the announcement at the time of eating: one should perform a single prostration before the teacher, kneel with the right knee on the ground (hukuei), and announce: "Venerable Teacher, please attend to me. I now make this formal announcement:
having washed my hands and the vessels, I wish to partake of food. I do not know which food it would be appropriate to serve. This applies to all other matters requiring an announcement.
One should understand that it is the same for other similar cases. If there are many matters to report at once, one may do so together.
If the teacher is weary in body or mind, one should leave as instructed; one must not show displeasure in one's heart or manifest it on one's countenance.
Whenever one asks about the scriptures or engages in dialogue, one should wait for the teacher’s intent and must not seek one's own convenience.
If the teacher’s body or mind is fatigued and they have no leisure to respond, and the teacher instructs you to depart, you should immediately comply with the teacher’s instruction and leave.
You must not harbor feelings of displeasure, as this would bring about your own transgression. As the *Fifty Verses* states: "One should always admire the teacher’s virtue; one should not..."
To look for minor faults leads to failure; by following [the teacher's guidance] one attains accomplishment.
To seek out faults will surely bring self-injury. The *Śīla-saṃvara-sūtra* states: The Buddha said, "A disciple must not speak harshly toward the teacher.
When rebuked by the teacher, one should not retaliate. If the teacher does not..."
Question: One must not speak rashly. Whenever you are commanded, do not disobey the order.
If one does not show respect toward the teacher, or speaks of the teacher’s faults and shortcomings, that foolish person shall be dealt with according to the law.
Even if the teacher actually has a fault, one must not speak of it; how much less so when there is none. If one is disrespectful toward the teacher, [the consequences will follow].
There is another minor hell called *Tui-po* (The Beating). One shall fall into this place, possessing a single body with four heads;
the entire body is likewise thus, appearing like a mass of fire that emits great, fierce flames, burning incessantly within that hellish realm.

Furthermore, there are hook-jawed venomous insects that constantly bite the root of the tongue. Upon emerging from hell, they are born among the animals, where they perpetually consume excrement and urine.
After casting off that body, even if they are born among humans, they are always born in border regions, their skin not resembling that of human beings.
They cannot possess the complete physical form of a human being; they are constantly subjected to contempt, slander, and humiliation.

Separated from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, they are perpetually devoid of wisdom. After dying there, they fall back into hell, further encountering immeasurable and boundless states of suffering and affliction.
Whenever there are matters such as violations of the precepts, one must not conceal them. One should immediately go before the teacher and piteously beg for repentance.
If the teacher grants permission, one should disclose everything with full sincerity and reform with earnest devotion; thus, one shall regain purity.

Because one does not disclose [one's faults] oneself, it is called "concealment" (*paticchādana*). "Vigilance" (*appamāda*) means a mind that is focused and single-minded; "sincerity" (*sacca*) means ultimate honesty without delusion;
"repentance" (*vippaṭisāra*) means confessing what has been transgressed; and "reform" (*paṭikamma*) means changing one's former errors so as not to commit them again.
Therefore, it is said: "One thereby regains pure conduct and protection. If one is reviled or scolded, one must reproach oneself and offer an apology with gentle words.
One should practice mindfulness and cultivate precepts and meditative concentration to repay the kindness of the teacher. Chengfan says:

Whenever there is an error or transgression, and the teacher displays anger or reprimands one in various ways, one must not use clever words to gloss over the fault. As soon as one sees the teacher’s anger, one should immediately feel awe and fear;

with a composed countenance, one should kneel before the teacher and, harboring a sense of shame, accept the reprimand. If there is a fault, one must reform it; if there is no fault, [one remains steadfast].
Remain silent.
Before the Master has finished speaking, you must not speak;
this means that until the Master’s instruction is complete, you must not state your own words to disrupt the Master’s teaching, for to do so would bring loss upon yourself.
Furthermore, one loses respect and may not dispute for victory based on reasoning.
One must not sit playfully upon the teacher’s seat, nor lie upon the teacher’s bed, nor wear the teacher’s robes, hat, or other belongings.
Because one lacks a mind of reverence, there may be instances of sitting or lying down playfully.
When acting as a messenger for a teacher to deliver letters, one must not privately open them to read them, nor should one show them to others.

Upon arriving at the destination, if questioned, one should answer truthfully if it is appropriate to do so; if it is inappropriate, one should skillfully decline to answer. Even if the recipient wishes to detain one, one must not remain.
While staying there, one should focus the mind on the teacher with the hope of returning.
To look for oneself would violate the principle of reverence; to have another look would be an improper act.
Even if others attach letters or correspondence, one must not open them, so as to maintain a path of profound integrity and avoid causing error to others. If someone opens [a letter]...
One must not privately pry into letters. Formerly, when Fu Bi was an envoy to the Qidan, he received a family letter but did not open it;
instead, he burned it, saying, "It would merely disturb the mind. If one does not even open a family letter, how much less so other correspondence?
When entering another's home, one must not look at their writings, ledgers, or records. To respond appropriately means that one’s reasoning is consistent and one’s speech is [proper].

Regarding those who seek benefit, one should respond to them according to the facts. As for those whose questions should not be answered—whether because their reasoning is obscure or the matter is hidden—one should avoid giving rise to suspicion, lest it cause harm to the Buddha-Dharma;
in such cases, one should decline them with skillful means and appropriate speech.

One who contemplates the Master’s reputation and return should do so like a filial son mindful of his compassionate mother, never forgetting her presence at his side for even a moment. As the Sūtra says: "One should be straightforward..."
When returning from a journey, one must recognize what the teacher has said and also recognize the words with which others have reported back to him.
Whether the teacher is facing guests, standing in his usual place, beside him, or behind him, one must ensure that one’s ears and eyes remain in close contact with him,
waiting for whatever he may require.
Neither distant nor near, their ears and eyes are thus joined; body and mind thus respond to one another.

Therefore, there shall be no failure in providing what the teacher requires. Chengfan said: Whenever a guest arrives, one should give rise to reverence and not harbor feelings of aversion or arrogance.
One must wash the cups, boil tea, and so forth.
When the Master was ill, [the attendant] applied his mind with single-minded care to treat him. This included the chamber, bedding, medicines, and gruel.
The chamber and bedding were for regulating the external; the medicines and gruel were for treating the internal. The term "etc.
refers to all medicinal foods appropriate for the illness, as well as suitable utensils and the like. The term "eṛ" (to ingest) refers to everything that is...
This refers to medicinal food that can regulate the illness. Xinghu said: "Constantly recite the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and pray for the Master’s recovery.
Chengfan said: "Prepare a solemn chamber, avoiding windy or damp locations; the bedding must be thick and soft. Observe the Master’s complexion and assist him with a staff when entering or leaving.
Prepare soups, decoctions, and medicines by boiling them according to the proper methods. Once he has recovered slightly, joy shall arise."

Rejoice. One should always serve [the teacher] with a filial heart and a harmonious countenance. When guests come to visit and inquire after him, you should skillfully represent the teacher in conversation;
do not speak clamorously or gather in crowds, but remain solemn and tranquil. If the teacher falls seriously ill, one must not weep or wail. Upon the teacher’s parinirvāṇa...
One must not disobey the instructions and admonitions of one's teacher, but should follow and practice them exactly as taught.
Matters such as wearing robes, offering shoes, washing, laundering, and drying are detailed in the Vinaya; they are not recorded here at length.
When taking up the teacher’s robe, one should slowly push it upward with one hand while grasping the bottom with the other, then stand upright and place it upon the teacher’s left shoulder.
Once the teacher has put it on, one should again inspect whether the upper and lower patterns are aligned according to the rules. When folding it, one must not hold it in the mouth;
rather, one should watch the upper and lower edges so that it does not touch the ground, then return it to its usual place and cover it with a clean cloth.
One must not cover them with other garments. When handing over shoes, one should first shake them out and brush off the dirt;

one must not make a loud noise. One should inspect them and arrange them in order. Only after washing one's hands should one take up the garments. In all washing, one must ensure they are clean. One must not waste water.
When drying the dharma-robes, one should wait for them to become dry. If there is urgent business to attend to, [one should depart].

If it is forgotten, one should entrust it to another person. Once the task is completed, it should be returned immediately. Other matters concerning the washing of the bowl and its accessories are fully detailed in the *Daśa-śīla Sūtra*;
as the text is extensive, I have not recorded them here at length.
Appendix: In all cases of attending upon one’s teacher, if not commanded to sit, one must not dare to sit; if not questioned, one must not dare to respond.

Unless one has a matter of one’s own that one wishes to ask, one must not sit down on one’s own initiative, nor answer or respond on one’s own initiative. Only when one has a personal matter that one wishes to report may one then inquire.
In all instances of standing in attendance, one must not lean against a wall or rest upon a table. One should maintain an upright posture with feet together and stand at a slight angle.

Regarding the attendant: the *Sūtra on the Descent from Tuṣita* states that an attendant possesses eight qualities:
first, firmness in the faculty of faith; second, a mind that seeks progress; third, freedom from physical ailments; fourth, diligence; and fifth, possession of mindfulness.
Sixth, the mind is free from arrogance. Seventh, one is able to achieve a concentrated state of mind. Eighth, one is fully endowed with the wisdom of learning.
If one wishes to perform a prostration and the teacher stops them, it is appropriate to comply with the teacher’s command and not prostrate.
Ritual propriety (*li*) is the outward expression of reverence. If one can accord with the command, that itself constitutes reverence.
Whenever a teacher and a guest engage in discussion, all discourse concerning the Way that is beneficial to the body and mind should be committed to memory.
Engaging in conversation while traveling on the road is itself the discourse of the Dharma. To take up labor and serve others builds the foundation of one’s own merit;

hearing the Dharma and committing it to memory moistens and nourishes the ground of the mind. Is this not truly the meaning of serving one's teacher? Chengfan said: "Sometimes the teacher questions a guest, and [the disciple] provides the answer."
If someone asks the teacher a question and receives a reply, one must not hear it with feelings of strangeness or alarm, nor see it with laughter.

One should follow the laughter and discern the meaning of the words and their underlying principles. Examine and savor them with a sincere heart. If you should attain a point of insight, you must present it again to the teacher.
When the Master issues a command, one should perform it promptly and without delay. "Performing" (*bian*) means to prepare;
"contrary" (*wei*) means to be uncompliant; "arrogant" (*man*) means to be disrespectful—or, alternatively, to be indolent.
In all instances of sleeping, one must not precede the teacher.
When the consciousness becomes dull and heavy, it is called "sleeping" (*śī*); when the five sensory faculties are shrouded in darkness, it is called "slumbering" (*miān*).

Because this obscures both body and mind, wholesome dharmas do not arise, and one remains long submerged within the three realms. Therefore, one should sleep little; it is appropriate to rise before the teacher and lie down after the teacher.
Furthermore, there are five faults of excessive sleep: first, having many bad dreams; second, the devas being displeased; third, the mind not entering into the Dharma;
fourth, failing to contemplate the signs of light; and fifth, frequently discharging impurities.
When anyone asks about the teacher’s taboo name (*huì*), one should say, "The first character is so-and-so, and the second character is so-and-so.
A taboo name consists of two characters and refers to the Dharma-name. If asked about the style name (*zìhào*), one should simply say, "Venerable So-and-so," or "My original teacher, So-and-so.
If asked about the Ācārya’s style name, one should say, "My preceptor, So-and-so. If...
One who is not one of the five types of *ācāryas* shall not be addressed as "Teacher. The Fifty Verses states: Furthermore, regarding the name of the teacher, one should not casually mention it;
if someone should insist on asking, one should show only a single character. If they ask about the teacher’s seniority (*yuanla*), [one should respond accordingly].
As well as the names of the prefectures and counties—one must answer each and every one.
Generally, a disciple should select an enlightened teacher and remain close to them for a long time; one must not leave the teacher too soon.
If the teacher is truly not enlightened, one should seek another excellent guide.
The Sanskrit term *śiṣya* means "one who is taught. In older translations it was called "disciple" (*dizi*). One is named a "brother" (*di*) because their learning follows that of the teacher;

one is named a "son" (*zi*) because they understand [the Dharma] by following the teacher. If the teacher’s insight into the Way is clear and penetrating, one should serve them for the remainder of one's life.

However, if the teacher lacks such clarity, it is appropriate to seek out another spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). A *śrāmaṇera* originally has no rule for departing from a teacher; it is only because the teacher lacks clarity that [one must leave].
Seek out a true guide separately, for a true guide is one capable of leading others to the ultimate Way. Thus, a sutra says:

"By following and learning from a virtuous teacher, one attains the vision of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Do not, by any means, revere a monkey as Śakra or take a clod of earth for a bright pearl.
To take a clod of earth as such is to be ignorant of the Dharma; to revere a monkey as such is to be ignorant of people.
If one does not recognize the Dharma, the eye of wisdom is lost; if one does not recognize people, one falls onto a deviant path. Thus it is said:
"Since your teacher has fallen, you too shall follow him in his fall. This is precisely what that means.

Even if one is separated from the teacher, one should remember the teacher’s instructions and must not indulge one's own whims or act according to one's own will. One must not follow the worldly stream to perform improper deeds.

Because one does not remember the teacher’s instructions, one indulges one's own whims and acts according to one's own will; because one follows the worldly stream, one performs improper deeds. [End of middle section]
The Heart Sutra says: "The Buddha said that those who know their teacher's kindness shall serve them when they see them; when they do not see them, they shall contemplate the teacher's instructions.
This is precisely what is meant.
Nor should one dwell in marketplaces or bustling places.
A "market" (*shi*) refers to a place where goods are gathered for trade; in antiquity, markets were established at water-wells, hence the term "market-well" (*shijing*).
Because the marketplace is clamorous and chaotic, it is called "bustling. Even if a location is not a market, one should likewise avoid all other bustling places.
One may dwell [there], but one must not dwell in spirit shrines or in sacrificial altars where blood is offered;
these are not places where those who have left the home life should reside. Even Brahmā and Śakra do not show them respect, let alone others.
To serve spirits of wine and meat is a great violation of the holy teachings; such persons are not disciples of the Buddha.
They must not dwell in civilian houses, nor may they reside near nunnery sites.
Because there must be a distinction between male and female, they do not stay near nunnery sites. Since monastics and laypeople must remain separate, they do not live in civilian houses.
First, there is the fear that emotions will arise and lead to gradual defilement; second, there is the concern that it will provoke the ridicule and slander of the laity.
Therefore, one must not dwell apart from the teacher while committing any evil deeds within the ways of the world.
Engaging in trade for profit, forming alliances and frequenting social circles, relying on worldly power and influence, training in extraordinary arts, being employed as actors or performers,
serving as envoys to the four quarters, and cultivating crops for gain— all these are called evil deeds.
△ Third, when following the teacher on a journey, one must not pass through or visit lay households.
To go from one house to another is what is meant by "passing through. Even if one passes through the homes of one's parents or patrons (*dānapati*), the teacher [must not permit it].
Even if you hear [a call], you must not enter.
You must not stop by the side of the road to converse with others.
This is the rule for the road. If you encounter relatives, friends, or acquaintances, you should politely decline them; do not engage in conversation, lest you lose [your composure].
As an attendant, one must not look left or right; one should keep the head lowered while following behind the teacher.
To look around would scatter the mind and cause a loss of decorum; to keep the head lowered ensures the mind is upright and manifests inner rectitude.
Upon arriving at the house of the *dānapati* (donor), one should stand to one side. When the teacher instructs one to sit, one should sit;
"standing to one side" means attending and standing by the teacher's side. *Dāna* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "giving.
This refers to one who is able to practice giving, thereby crossing over the ocean of suffering of poverty.
Upon arriving at the temple, the master bows to the Buddha, either bowing himself or having others do so; he must not strike the *qing* gong or the wooden fish block (*tan*) on his own authority.

This is because such actions imply personal autonomy, yet each temple has its own presiding authorities. Guest and host must be distinguished; therefore, one must personally assume the etiquette of a guest and refrain from acting on one's own initiative.
If traveling by mountain, one should carry a sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) along with them;
whether it be a *niṣīdana*, a rush mat, or whatever object is used for sitting, one should carry it as appropriate to facilitate the teacher’s seating.
If traveling a long distance, one must not be separated from the teacher too far away;
if too near, one’s feet may tread upon the teacher’s shadow or stir up dust with one’s steps; if too far, one will not hear the teacher’s calls or instructions.
Otherwise, one may incur further faults. The *Fifty Verses* states: "If one steps upon the shadow of one's teacher, the offense incurred is equal to that of destroying a stupa.
When crossing water, one should carry a staff and proceed slowly to test its depth."
If the water is shallow, one should assist the teacher across; if it is deep, one should request someone else to carry the sedan chair.
Details regarding the carrying of the water jar, the staff, and so forth, are fully set forth in the Vinaya; as the text is voluminous, they are not recorded here.
In the *Daśaśīla-sūtra*, there are fifteen matters concerning the carrying of the teacher’s water flask (*kamaṇḍalu*) and seven matters concerning the carrying of the mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*).
Because the text is extensive, it is not recorded here; those who wish to study this should consult the *Śīla-sūtra* themselves.
Appendix: If one happens to travel separately, one should meet at a designated place and must not arrive late.
"Happening" means by chance. "Must not arrive late" means that one should arrive first at the designated teacher's location to wait;
one must not arrive after the teacher.

When the Master receives the *zhāi* (fasting meal), the attendant should stand in attendance during the *chūshēng* (offering of food). When the meal is finished, the attendant should stand in attendance while the *qīn* (donations) are collected.
Regarding the *chūshēng*: this refers to the food offered to various ghosts, spirits, and sentient beings; it must be placed in a clean vessel and set in a clean location.
*Qīn* refers to the items bestowed by the donor (*tānyuè*). Chengfan says: "Wait until the Master has finished the meal, then collect the Master's donations."

*Dakṣiṇā*. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Giving clothing and other articles after a meal is called *dakṣiṇā*. This is correct. Examining the character *dān* (嚫), it originally followed the "mouth" radical;
its current form with the "treasure" radical is a corruption. The Sanskrit term is fully *dakṣiṇā*, which means "giving. In terms of the Dharma, it is called "Dharma-giving" (*dharmadāna*);
in terms of material wealth, it is called "material giving" (*āmiṣadāna*). Laypeople should practice material giving; those who have left the household life [should practice Dharma-giving].

People should practice the gift of Dharma. As it says in the *Yilan*: "Only when the two gifts of wealth and Dharma are accomplished, and both merit and wisdom are perfected, does one become a Buddha.
△ Fourth: Entering the Assembly.
One must not dispute over one's seat;
one must show respect and yield to others.
One must not call out, speak, or laugh from afar while seated.
If there is urgent business, one should snap one's fingers to awaken others and speak softly to inform them. One must not call out from afar, as this violates decorum and disturbs the assembly.
To laugh in such a manner is a transgression that is no small matter.
If there are those among the assembly who fail in propriety, one should conceal their faults and proclaim their virtues.
By concealing faults, one’s own virtue grows; by proclaiming virtues, the ocean of the Sangha increases in excellence.
One must not disparage the labor of others to manifest one's own achievements.

To perform meritorious deeds is called "labor" (láo); to claim one's own achievements for oneself is called "boasting" (fá). This means that one must not be arrogant or boastful about one's own abilities in order to manifest one's own merit.
Laozi said: "Because he does not boast of his own achievements, he possesses true merit. Therefore, the gentleman does not boast of his goodness.
In all places, when sleeping one does not do so before others, and when rising one does not do so after others.
First, this is to distance oneself from indolence; second, it is to avoid disturbing the minds of the assembly; therefore, one does not occupy the front or the rear.
In washing one's face, one must not use excessive water.
First, to spare it for those who follow; second, to cherish one’s own merit. An ancient saying goes: "Hot water is obtained by burning wood; cold water is obtained by drawing from the well.
If one does not understand the practice of cultivation, even blessings as vast as the sands of the Ganges will be exhausted. The *Qinggui* (Rules of Purity) states: "One must not wash..."
Regarding the head: there are four ways it may be disadvantageous to oneself and others: first, soiling the basin; second, using a greasy towel; third, having dry hair; and fourth, damaging the eyes.
When brushing teeth and spitting water, one must lower the head to direct the water downward; one must not spray or splash water upon others.
Because it is drawn downward by water, it does not splash onto others. The *Qinggui* states: "Dip the right hand into the tooth-cleansing powder and rub the left side;
dip the left hand into the powder and rub the right side. One must not dip again, for fear that the disease of the gums or foul breath might be transmitted to others."
One must not blow one's nose or spit loudly.
That which issues from the nose is called "mucus" (tì), and that which issues from the mouth is called "spit" (ǒutù).
One must not discharge mucus or saliva in a temple, a stupa, a clean room, a clean pond, or pure water; one should do so in a secluded place.
Spittle is emitted from the mouth; it is not a place where purity is maintained. It is called a "secluded spot.
When drinking tea or soup, one must not bow to others with only one hand.
To bow while drinking tea or soup is improper for the occasion; to bow with only one hand is a breach of etiquette.
One must not rinse one's teeth facing a stūpa, nor facing one’s *upādhyāya*, *ācārya*, and so forth.
"Stūpa" here includes sacred images; "and so forth" refers to elders, senior monks (*sthavira*), honored guests, and the like.
Whenever you hear the sound of the bell, join your palms and silently recite: Hearing the sound of the bell, afflictions grow light; Wisdom increases, and Bodhi arises.
Leaving behind hell, escaping the fiery pit; May we attain Buddhahood and deliver all sentient beings. Oṃ karateye svāhā.
Initially, within hearing, one enters the stream and forgets the object; thus, afflictions become light and wisdom grows long, and quiescence manifests before one. Hence it is said that Bodhi arises.
Transcending both the mundane and supramundane, it is said that one leaves the prison and exits the pit. When the ten directions are perfectly luminous, this is called becoming a Buddha.
Attaining these two forms of excellence, it is called saving sentient beings. It transcends names and words, and is free from essence and characteristics.
Therefore, it is said: *Oṃ karateya*. Not abiding in nirvāṇa, not abiding in saṃsāra, therefore it is said: *Svāhā*.
If, while lying down, one hears the sound of a bell, one should immediately rise and silently recite [the mantra]. To remove illness, one may remain without rising; there is no offense.
If the bell rings of its own accord, one should first recite the vow: "May this sound of the bell transcend the dharma-realm," followed by this verse. Furthermore, whenever striking [the bell]...
When striking the bell, it must be done slowly; only when the preceding sound is about to fade should the subsequent sound be continued.

This was as when, in the past, Master Zhigong lent his spiritual vision to Emperor Wu, who thereby beheld the suffering of the hells. The Emperor asked, "How can this be stopped? Zhigong replied, "Only by hearing the sound of the bell."
[They] shared in suffering and found brief respite. Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued for all monasteries throughout the realm to strike the bells, allowing the sound to linger and resonate.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (or *Dharmapada-saṃgraha*) also commands that the sound be made to extend for a long duration. The *Ekottarika-āgama* states:

"When the bell is struck, may the various sufferings of all evil realms be brought to a complete halt. If one hears the sound of the bell while reciting verses of praise, one shall attain liberation from them."
The heavy sins of birth and death for five hundred billion kalpas are described in a verse from the *Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra*:

"If one hears the bell yet remains lying down and does not rise, the protective deities of the stupa will become angry. Due to the meagerness of present conditions and fruits, one will receive the body of a snake as retribution in the future.
Wherever the sound of the bell is heard, those who are lying down must surely rise; joining their palms and generating a virtuous mind, all the worthy sages will rejoice."
One must not laugh excessively. If one laughs loudly, yawns, or stretches, one should cover the mouth with the sleeve of one’s robe.
To laugh excessively causes the loss of right mindfulness; to laugh loudly is contrary to dignified decorum (*īryāpatha*).
A yawn—also called *khañja*—is a manifestation of weariness and fatigue. The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states that there are two kinds of breath: the upper and the lower. The upper breath...
When wishing to exit, do not leave with your mouth wide open facing others; rather, turn your face toward a place where there are no people.

When the downward wind (flatus) wishes to escape, do not allow it to be released among the assembly. One must employ a skillful means to go outside, release it in a place where there are no people, and only then return inside.
Do not cause the assembly to feel contempt or disdain. When entering a stūpa or a temple hall, one should not release [it].
One must not pass wind or make a sound in the presence of a *ho-shang*, a *ta-te*, or an *shang-tso*.
If there is an urgent illness within the abdomen, one should go outside to relieve oneself; do not cause others to give rise to feelings of loathing or contempt. The *Mahā-vinaya* states:
If a sudden wind arises from downwind, one should restrain it; if it cannot be endured, one should step outside the path and release it downwind.
If one sneezes while inside a meditation hall, one must not allow oneself to sneeze excessively.
When a sneeze occurs, one should restrain it, covering the nose with the hand while sneezing, ensuring that mucus or saliva does not escape.
One must not walk hurriedly. One must not take the Buddha’s lamp for private use.
If one lights a lamp, it should be properly covered with a shade to prevent flying insects from entering.
In all movements and stillnesses, one must guard the dignity of one's physical conduct. When taking a step, one should look at the ground so as not to harm insects or ants.

To privately use the Buddha’s lamp constitutes a cause for falling into the Dark Hell; in every successive birth, one will lose the clarity of wisdom. The prohibition against covering the lamp is explained as before.
When offering flowers to the Buddha, select those that are fresh and fully blossomed. One must not smell them beforehand. Only after removing the withered ones should one offer the new ones.
Withered flowers must not be discarded on the ground or stepped upon; they should be placed in a secluded location.
This means one should select those that are fully blossomed and perfect; do not take those that are half-open or nearly withered. To smell them first or to trample upon them is a lack of respect.
A secluded place is one where no people pass, nor is it a defiled location.
As the *Yāo yòng jīng* (Sūtra on Essential Uses) says: "One who smells the fragrance with the nose diminishes its scent and lacks merit; for their retribution, they shall fall."
In the Padma Hell, one shall lack the faculty of smell and never perceive fragrances for life after life. The *Riyun jing* (Sūtra on the Clouds of the Sun) states:

"If one extinguishes incense smoke before it has finished burning and casts it upon the ground, one commits the offense of *vyatikrama*. For five hundred years, one shall fall into the Hell of Excrement. Why is this?"
Regarding "withered" due to a negligent mind: this refers to flowers that have been left overnight. The Sūtra states: "The incense burner and the vase must both be wiped clean.
When taking flowers and willow branches, one should offer prayers to the deities of the mountains, marshes, and trees; one must not pull them up by their roots or stumps.
One should go and return directly, and must not speak with arrogance, indolence, laughter, or jesting."
One must not fail to respond when called. Whenever one is called, it is appropriate to respond by reciting the Buddha’s name.
The character for "respond" (應) is pronounced in the departing tone (*qùshēng*); it is a word of reply. One may respond with "Namo Buddha," or "Amitābha Buddha," or simply "Ā.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "One should respond by saying 'Yes' (*nuò*)."
Whenever one picks up a lost article, one must immediately inform the administrative monk, or the administrative official, or one's own teacher;
or else, one should place it in the monastery's storehouse and wait for the owner to arrive.

Regarding the principle that one’s speech and actions must correspond to reality: if one finds something, it should be returned; it must not be kept private or concealed. Long ago, Yue Yangzi found some lost gold and gave it to his wife.
His wife said, "I have heard that a man of resolve does not drink from the 'Thief's Spring,' and a person of integrity will not accept food brought with the words 'Alas, here!
How much less would he pick up lost wealth or profit to defile his conduct? Yangzi was ashamed and subsequently discarded the gold.
In the wilds, if one acts with such private concealment, they are not even equal to a single woman.
Appendix: One must not form friendships with young śrāmaṇeras.
Unless they are of the caliber of Dao’an or Sengguang, they are unfit to be friends. As the Sūtra says: "Do not befriend those who are not worthy. Do not...

The Sages do not honor such persons. A son who is unfilial, a person who is addicted to alcohol, one whose aspirations are perverse and whose conduct is treacherous—these are not to be associated with.
Their coming and going defiles the arts [of the community] and causes damage to one’s spiritual practice. Chengfan says:

"If one privately associates with evil teachers and evil friends and repeatedly practices heedlessness, thereby causing various kinds of provocation and distress to one's primary teacher, and the teacher does not permit repentance, one shall undergo [further] training."
He earnestly and persistently entreated [the teacher], but the teacher firmly refused him.

He should quickly request the teacher’s close friends and long-standing virtuous elders to intercede on his behalf to seek compassionate repentance, forever severing base and evil ways so as not to commit them again. Therefore, O worthy one, there are three things to be feared:
an evil teacher, evil companions, and evil arts; these can obstruct the Right Path and lead one onto deviant ways. It would be well if you were to awaken to this early.
If one does not know how to return [to the path], then while alive there will be no small benefit, and at death there will be long-lasting sorrow;
one will not even be able to maintain the three robes in a simple manner.
These are the three robes of a bhikṣu; even an upāsaka is made to possess them so that he may keep in mind the characteristics of the field of merit.
This is the robe of liberation; how much less could a śrāmaṇera permit it to be merely makeshift or deficient?

Its original purpose is to enable one to recognize the characteristics of a field of merit and to ensure that it is available when the time for full ordination arrives; it is not intended for one to wear it at all times. Should one be too poor to afford it, [it need not be acquired].
This reasoning is also without fault. In this present age of the Final Dharma, there are teachers who are unacquainted with the Vinaya scriptures and ignorant of the Tathāgata’s regulations;
they all cause śrāmaṇeras to wear five- or seven-paneled robes, leading lay men and women who have received the five precepts to likewise wear them indiscriminately.
This is profoundly unlawful and incurs no small transgression, as will be demonstrated in detail below.
One must not make many robes; if there are any in excess, they should be discarded.

To make many is to create many burdens and to indulge the illusory body. Therefore, it is said that one "adorns the body to advance on the Path. Only when one is always lacking in three respects can one be called a practitioner of few desires.
If one personally recognizes impermanence and is mindful of the poverty of others, then whatever remains [in excess] should immediately be...
Abandon them.
You cannot afford to procure exquisite whisks, playthings, and the like to adorn your body upon the rivers and lakes; you would only be laughed at by those who understand.
Failing to recognize that this is merely a skin-sack of the four elements, you prepare such finery and delude your right mindfulness, thus learning to adorn yourself in imitation.
This is improper; therefore, it invites derision from those who understand. It is not permissible even for a brief moment, let alone to indulge in it throughout one's entire life.
This refers to what is said: "The enjoyment lasts but a moment, while the sorrow endures for a long time. As for those who are unencumbered, they say:
"A 'man roaming rivers and lakes' (jianghu sanren) is precisely one who travels about, lodging wherever he may be."
One must not wear dyed garments or attire similar to that of worldly people.
"Dyed garments" refers to colors such as vermilion, purple, yellow, green, and white; one should instead wear robes of ruined color (*kasāya-varṇa*), such as black.

Regarding "attire similar to that of worldly people," this refers either to a similarity in color or a similarity in style and ornamentation, such as small collars, narrow sleeves, and cloud-patterned toes.
When handling items such as footwear, one must not do so with unclean hands while wearing the robes;
one should revere the robes as one would a stūpa, and therefore must hold them with clean hands. Whenever holding shoes, socks, undergarments, or a *kaṣāya*...
If one touches the head, the feet, or an impure vessel, one must wash them thoroughly before handling other pure objects.
Whenever ascending the hall, one must fasten one’s trousers and socks; one must not act according to one's own whims or neglect proper decorum.
Fearing that the pubic hair might fall out, it is necessary to bind [the penis]. At other times, or in the case of young children, there is no fault in not binding it.
One must not run about aimlessly, nor speak excessively.
To idly wander about while neglecting recitation is to engage in much speech and let loose one's verbal karma.
One must not sit idly by while the assembly performs labor; to avoid toil and seek personal ease is shameful.
To sit by and watch is a lack of shame, and to shirk labor diminishes merit. As the Sūtra says: "One should exhaust one's strength in performing the affairs of the Sangha."
One must not privately take the bamboo, wood, flowers, fruits, vegetables, all food and drink, or any utensils belonging to the *cātuddisa* Sangha.
In Sanskrit, *cātuddisa* means "the Sangha of the four quarters. Such property belongs to the permanent endowment (*sādhāraṇa*). To take it privately constitutes the offense of theft.

The Sūtra states: "If there is anything one wishes to take, one should inform the person in charge. Regarding the ascetic practices of Master Sengzhao, he was foremost in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
While practicing the *Lotus Samādhi*, he was moved by the Great Being Avalokiteśvara to preach the Dharma for him, whereby he attained unimpeded eloquence (*anāvaraṇa-pratibhāna*).
He also beheld the Great Being Samantabhadra riding a white elephant and emitting light to bear witness to his realization. He once [used] the community of monks...
He took a pinch of salt to prepare for his midday meal; as it was used so sparingly, he paid it no mind.
Later, while performing the Fangdeng (Vaipulya) Repentance Rite, he suddenly saw signs of its presence arise. Over three years, the amount increased to several dozen *hu* (measures).

He then hurriedly sold his clothing to purchase salt to repay the assembly; only then did the signs vanish. Furthermore, Shi Daoxiang died a sudden death and went to the Netherworld, where he saw a placard.
The title reads: This man stole a monk’s apricot tree and cut it into pieces for the material of combs. A temple monk named Dao Guo found a remaining piece of wood that was still fit to make a comb;
it was worth eighty coins. [The thief] was destined to fall into the Hell of Burning Flames.
When Dao Guo heard this account, he immediately repaid the debt. Furthermore, in the second year of the Yangdi era, the monk Daoming passed away. It was the same.
Fang Sengxu was traveling through a field at dusk when he suddenly saw a temple. He went there to seek refuge and encountered Daoming, who appeared no different than on ordinary days.
When Xu saw that the monks’ porridge was all the color of blood and that their entire bodies were ablaze with fire, he asked Daoming in fear.
Daoming said, "This is hell. I once took a bundle of the monks' firewood to boil dye, but I forgot to pay for it."
He had been suffering his retribution for a full year. When he lifted his robes, he saw that the area below his knees was entirely scorched black.

He then said, "If you would kindly purchase a hundred bundles of firewood for me to compensate the monastery's permanent assets, and also copy one volume of the Lotus Sūtra, I may be released from this suffering.
Xu agreed to this; upon returning to the temple, he prepared everything according to his instructions. When he went back to search for the monastery, it was silent and nothing could be seen.
When the wise hear this, who would not have their hair stand on end?
One must not speak of the merits or failures of the administration in the imperial court or government offices, nor discuss the strengths, weaknesses, virtues, or vices of laypeople or family heads.

The political affairs of kings and ministers are the formal laws of the state; the long and short, the good and the bad, which constitute the right and wrong of worldly households, all disturb right mindfulness and invite calamity and retribution.
Therefore, it is said that one must not engage in such talk. As the Sūtra says:

"One must not discuss or deliberate upon the political affairs of the state, nor evaluate their merits and defects, nor speak of mobilizing armies, leading expeditions, or the victory or defeat of military conquests."
Furthermore, because laypeople commonly prefer to wear white garments, they are called "white-robed ones" (*baiyi*).
When referring to oneself, one should cite one's two-character Dharma name; one must not say "I" or "this humble monk."
"Sangha" means "the multitude. It is a designation for four or more bhikṣus; it certainly does not apply to a single bhikṣu, much less can it be used for a single śrāmaṇera.
To speak of oneself as "small" is to belittle the assembly, and to say "I" is to demean oneself.
Those who have left the household life are guests beyond the mundane world; even when facing kings or lords, they refer to themselves by their given names.

It was thus. The śramaṇa Sengzhong, upon meeting Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty, addressed him as "poor man of the Way" (*pindao*). The Emperor said, "There is no objection to addressing me by my name. The Emperor then asked Wang Jian:
"When former generations of śramaṇas met the Emperor, what title did they use? Did they return to their seats in the main hall? Wang Jian replied:

"During the Han and Wei dynasties, the Buddha-dharma had not yet flourished; thus we see no records of such matters in the histories. From that time onward, as the Dharma gradually prospered, all [śramaṇas] addressed the Emperor as 'poor man of the Way.'"

Regarding "the Way" (*dào*) and also hearing the term "one who sits in advance": as for the expression "poor practitioner" (*píndào*), "Way" refers to the Way realized by the sages of the Three Vehicles.
Because I am meager in this Way, I call myself a "poor practitioner. The *Lun* (Treatise) states: "There are two kinds of poverty: first, poverty of wealth."
There are two types of poverty: first, poverty of virtue; second, poverty of wisdom. There are also two types of poverty regarding the Dharma. For these reasons, they are not called "ministers.
During the reign of Emperor Suzong of the Tang dynasty, an edict was issued stating that monks and nuns attending court audiences must not address the Emperor as "minister. Hong Juefan remarked:

"Mingjiao Yongzong always sighed that śramaṇas maintain a noble dignity, as they do not observe the ritual of ministerial submission when appearing before the Son of Heaven. It was from the time of Tang Lingtiao that this precedent was first corrupted, and subsequent generations have followed suit."
Thus, he was no longer suspicious. Even the Son of Heaven could not enfeoff those reclusive scholars of the mountains and forests;
how much less so the śramaṇas, whose Way is honored as one of the Three Jewels and who serve as the world’s refuge?

Therefore, at the beginning and end of the *Zhengzong ji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage), the author refers to himself as "Your Subject So-and-so" to preserve historical precedent; however, in the intervening sections where he narrates his own life, he simply uses his given name. At that time...
The high ministers and officials all respected his lofty insight. The *Tongji* states: The *Yi* says, "He does not serve kings or lords; he exalts his own affairs.
The *Ji* says, "Among the Confucians, there are those who do not act as ministers to the Son of Heaven above, nor serve the feudal lords below.

Later, Wang Ruzhong of the Later Han was summoned to have an audience with Emperor Guangwu. When he announced his name, he did not declare himself a minister. An official asked him the reason for this, and he replied: "Heaven..."
There are those whom a son does not serve as a minister: namely, Confucian scholars and recluses, who still know to exalt themselves through the Way;

how much more so for those who have transcended the world to study Buddhism, whose names reside within the Field of Merit—how could they ever serve worldly rulers as ministers and thus bring disgrace upon themselves?
As for Emperor Suzong, he may truly be called one who knows how to honor the followers of Śākyamuni and possesses a profound understanding of the great principles.

One must not engage in disputes over trivial matters. Even when faced with major issues that are difficult to endure, one must maintain a balanced mind and a peaceful temper, resolving them through reasoned argument.
If this is impossible, one should depart politely; to lose one's temper and speak crudely is not the mark of a good monk.
Even if one is falsely accused or slandered through unrighteous means, one should still endure it and defend oneself with reason, without showing anger on one's countenance.
If the person cannot be reasoned with, one should skillfully use expedient words and depart. How much less should one engage in angry contention over a minor matter?
Therefore, a sutra says: "Be careful not to harbor resentment or litigate; attribute rectitude to others and take the crookedness upon yourself."

Furthermore, when one observes those who are disputing, one should bring the two parties together in harmony. The Pure Regulations (Qinggui) state: "Whether they have reason or are without reason, both shall be expelled from the monastery.
Why is this? It is because a monk ought to practice forbearance; if one clings to being right and engages in contention, that is precisely ignorance (avidyā).
Therefore, they were expelled together, so as to quell disputes before they could sprout. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "There are five kinds of faults for one who cannot endure being insulted:
first, ferocity increases; second, there is regret after the fact; third, many people do not love them; fourth, an evil reputation spreads;
and fifth, after death, one falls into the evil realms."
△ Fifth: Partaking of Food in Accordance with the Assembly.
Upon hearing the sound of the *ghanṭā*, one should immediately adjust one’s robes.
Generally, any wooden, stone, copper, or iron object that produces a sound when struck is called a *ghanṭā*. If one hears the sound and does not prepare oneself in advance, [it is a fault].
In principle, one may occasionally fall into haste or error.
When offering prayers before eating, one should always maintain reverence.

One should contemplate the offerings prior to the meal, chant the *saṃghāṭa* at the conclusion of the meal, and recite verses and prayers after eating; in all these instances, one must manifest respect.
One must not allow the mind to become distracted, nor harbor arrogance or indolence that would impair one's own virtue.
Regarding the food served: the rice shall not exceed seven grains; the noodles not exceed one inch in length; and the steamed buns not exceed the size of a fingernail.
To exceed these amounts is greed; to provide less is stinginess. Other items, such as vegetables and tofu, are not served.

Regarding all food: only that which is made from rice or flour may be brought out. As for vegetables and fruits, these are "chewed foods" (*khādanīya*) rather than "eaten foods" (*bhojanīya*) derived from the five grains;
since they do not constitute [proper] food, they are not brought out. "Seven grains" refers to the absolute minimum;
by the power of the incantation and aspiration, it can cause all the spirits and deities to be fully satiated. If there were more, it would be...
"Greed" is a temporary expedient expression used for fear that those lacking discernment might scatter [the food] upon the ground, causing the *dānapati* (donors) to harbor resentment.
If too little is taken, it fails to constitute the proper ritual number and instead results in irreverence; this is certainly not appropriate.
Although the practice of protection (*hugù*) speaks of seven grains, there is no mention of stinginess or greed. The *Qinggui* states: "The rice shall not exceed seven grains. Too much...
In his youth, he was stingy, yet there were no words of greed [regarding this practice]. Regarding "the size of a fingernail," the *Apidamo jing* (Abhidharma Sūtra) states:

"The produced cake is as large as a fingernail. The *Shisao* (Commentary on the Essentials of the Vinaya) says: "The production [of the portion] may occur either before or after the equal distribution of offerings;
it is to be arranged according to one's discretion. According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the Buddha commanded that when bhikṣus eat, they should give food to humans and non-humans alike.
Even down to a single morsel, according to the *Purāṇa-avadāna-sūtra* and the *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, one must not consume food entirely;

one should leave a remainder to universally bestow upon all sentient beings, rather than restricting it to a single class. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* instructs that at the time of first eating, one should first offer it to the Triple Gem.
Later, he bestowed [the precepts] upon the four modes of birth. According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, due to the wilderness ghost (*kāntāra-pretas*), he received the precept against killing;
when he was nearly dying from not being able to eat meat, the Buddha commanded that wherever the Buddha-dharma exists, food must be offered to him.

If there is a residence where food is not offered, those are the retinue of Māra and not disciples of the Buddha. According to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, the Mother of Ghost Children (*Hārītī*) received [the precepts] from the Buddha.
Having finished the precepts, the Buddha commanded all his disciples in Jambudvīpa that at every mealtime they should give food to sentient beings.
At the end of the monks' procession, they were to set out a single plate of food, call out their names, and ensure that the five hundred sons and all other currently existing sentient beings—
including the spirits of the mountains, rivers, streams, oceans, and so forth— were all moved by this intention and fully satisfied.
Causing them to be fully satisfied.
Whenever [food] is produced, place it in the left palm and recite this verse of contemplation: "O hosts of spirits and deities, I now bestow this offering upon you.
May this food pervade the ten directions, shared by all spirits and deities."
The food should be placed upon a clean plate; if no plate is available, place it in the palms of the hands. With the right hand, snap the fingers three times over the clean object.

After reciting the verse, further recite the *Bhikṣā-pariṇāmana-mantra* (Mantra for Transforming Food) and the *Samantabhadra-pūjā-mantra* (Universal Offering Mantra) seven times each. This is most excellent.
Whenever one wishes to eat, one should contemplate five reflections. First, calculate the labor expended and measure the distance from which it came.
"Calculating the labor expended" means that one should contemplate this food in terms of the plowing, sowing, weeding, harvesting, and threshing required to produce it.

It is pounded, ground, sifted, steamed, and boiled. The laborers shed streams of sweat as they gather it together; the food is meager while the sweat is profuse. Such is the heavy toil and bitterness of its production.
Yet, once it enters the mouth, it immediately becomes impure; after a single night, it transforms into excrement and urine—so loathsome that one does not wish to see it.
If I were to harbor craving for it, I would fall into hell and swallow glowing iron balls; upon emerging, I would become an animal to repay my debt.
Regarding his past debts: having observed this, he gives rise to a mind of weary detachment and is then fit to receive food. As for measuring the source from which it comes:
the donor, seeking merit, has reduced their own sustenance and cut into the portions of their wife and children to bring it as an offering.
If one lacks cultivation, even a single grain of rice is difficult to digest; thus it is said, "A grain of rice is as heavy as a mountain.
