Second, one should reflect upon whether one's own virtue and conduct are complete or deficient before accepting offerings.

One should naturally reflect upon and evaluate one's own virtuous conduct. If one does not maintain the precepts, practice seated meditation, recite the sutras, or perform services for the Three Jewels, then virtue will be diminished and conduct deficient;
in such a case, one ought not to receive the offerings and gifts of others, for to accept them would cause one to fall because of those gifts.
Even if one’s virtuous conduct is complete, one must still contemplate the Dharma before being able to digest the faithful offerings. Thus, Tiantai said: "Regardless of..."
When begging for food from the communal alms-gathering, one must always practice contemplation. If one does not enter into contemplation, it merely nourishes the cycle of birth and death;

this is what is meant by "studying the Way without penetrating its principle, returning the physical body to the faithful's offerings. When a tree reaches eighty-one feet in height, it will no longer grow.
As my years have already grown old, mushrooms no longer grow in my garden. Since the teachings contain clear and explicit texts, how could one allow oneself not to believe them?
The three types of restraint prevent the mind from falling into error; their primary purpose is to counteract greed and the like.
This means that this mind is fully possessed of the faults and afflictions of immeasurable ignorance (*avidyā*).

Greed, hatred, and delusion are its root; therefore, they are called its "basis" (*mūla*). A practitioner must guard against them at all times. If the root is eliminated, all faults are instantly abandoned.
Thus, one does not give rise to thoughts of greed regarding fine food, nor does one give rise to anger regarding coarse food, nor regarding that which is... [incomplete].
One should not give rise to deluded thoughts regarding coarse or unwholesome food. Having performed this contemplation, one may then accept the food.
This is as stated in the *Maitreyaparipṛcchā-sūtra-śāstra*: "All unwholesome dharmas arise from greed, hatred, and delusion. Indeed.
The four right endeavors are the excellent medicine for treating the withered body.
This body, composed of the four great elements, is constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst; were it not for food and drink, the body would wither and its complexion would fade.
Without this means, one cannot advance in the practice of the Way. Therefore, food and drink are the essential sustenance for the body and a potent medicine for curing illness;
they are the very mechanism for cultivating practice and advancing on the Path. If one becomes greedily attached to them, they instead become a chronic ailment.
The *Aśokarāja-sūtra* states that Upagupta filled one vessel with milk-rice and [placed] another empty vessel alongside it.
He placed a bowl of milk-rice before a greedy monk and said to him, "You must wait for it to cool; drink it gradually.
However, because the monk’s mind was so heavily possessed by greed, he blew upon it to cool it and then ate it all at once. Guptā said, "Though the milk-rice is cold, your mind remains hot;
you must cool it further, using the contemplation of impurity as water to remove this state of mind."

[The monk] felt a burning sensation. When he saw food and drink, he perceived it as if he were taking medicine. After the bhikṣu had finished eating, he immediately spat it out, filling an empty vessel.
Guptā said, "You may eat more. The bhikṣu said, "How can I eat again what is impure?
Guptā said, "You should contemplate all phenomena as being like mucus and vomit. She then preached the Dharma for him, and the bhikṣu applied himself with diligence.
He reflected and contemplated, and attained the fruit of arhatship.
Fifthly, it was for the sake of accomplishing the Way that he accepted this food;

had he not eaten, his body would have become emaciated and his complexion altered, making it difficult to advance in his spiritual practice. Now, for the sake of fulfilling his spiritual work, he accepts [the food].

Regarding this food: if one does not practice for the sake of the Way, even a single grain of rice will be difficult to digest. Thus, an ancient worthy said: "It is given for the purpose of accomplishing the work of the Way;
if the work of the Way is not yet accomplished, how can it be digested? Whenever receiving food, one should perform these five contemplations.
If one knows for oneself that the work of the Path has not yet been accomplished, one must give rise to deep shame and remorse. Therefore, the *Guhya-ācāra* states:
"In whatever one eats, one must give rise to shame and remorse; one should constantly practice the contemplation of dharmas. The *Mahālaṅkāra-śāstra* states: "When one receives food..."
Recite these thoughts silently with each mouthful. For the first spoonful, recite silently: "May all evil be severed. For the second spoonful, recite:
"May all good be cultivated. For the third spoonful, recite: "I dedicate the roots of goodness thus cultivated to all sentient beings."
All shall together attain Buddhahood.
One must not criticize food as being good or bad,
nor may one find fault with or disdain whether food is coarse or fine.
One must not give food from one’s own portion to others. If one picks out food and gives it to a dog, that object belongs to the Saṃgha;
food is not to be distributed with partiality, and giving it privately constitutes the offense of theft. While the communal meal has not yet concluded, to give to a dog is contrary to the Dharma.
When receiving food, one should properly maintain reverence and practice contemplation; to pick out food and give it to a dog is a violation of dignified decorum.
This is the proper etiquette.
When food is brought to be added, one must not say "I do not need it. If one is already full, one should signal refusal by waving the hand back.
To "add" means to advance or increase. To say "I do not need it" violates the principle of humility; it causes noise and disturbs the assembly.
Reflect: if one yields [the food] to others, one acts with reverence and propriety.

One must not eat with fingernails visible; for if wind causes crumbs to fall into the bowls of one's neighbors, it is improper even when eating alone, let alone when dining with the assembly. There are three faults in this: first, it disturbs the minds of others.
Second, one loses dignified deportment. Third, if one has greasy hands and defiles the alms bowl, one incurs an offense.
One must not speak while food is in the mouth;
even if someone asks a question, one should respond only after swallowing. How much less, then, should one initiate speech oneself?
One must not laugh, talk, or engage in idle chatter;
by maintaining the five reflections in mind, these faults will be avoided.
One must not make noise while chewing food.
When chewing food, one must keep the lips and mouth closed. One should eat cakes and fruits by breaking them into small pieces. Furthermore, one must not slurp while eating soup or congee.
If one wishes to pick at a tooth, one should cover the mouth with the sleeve of one's robe.
If one does not conceal it, one will naturally lose one's dignified demeanor, and furthermore, it will cause others to give rise to feelings of aversion.
If there are insects or ants within the food, one should discreetly hide and cover them so that fellow monks do not see them and become suspicious.
"Neighboring seat" refers to the adjacent seat. If one were to let that person see it, they might give rise to suspicion or resentment, leading to vomiting and an inability to eat again.
One should eat while remaining seated in one sitting. Once the meal is finished, one must not leave the seat and then sit down again to eat;
however, there is no offense if one is ill.
After finishing the meal, one must not use the fingers to scrape food from the bowl or alms-basin.
This is the mark of one who is hungry; it is not the deportment of a renunciant. Furthermore, one must not lick food with the tongue.
In eating, one should be neither too hurried nor too slow.
If one eats too quickly, one loses proper decorum; if one eats too slowly, it disturbs the assembly. Furthermore, one must not leave grains scattered in disorder while eating.
One must not eat with cheeks stuffed, nor eat by snorting through the nose, and so forth.
When food is being served and has not yet reached you, do not give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*).
Food being served is for the purpose of sustaining one’s life; if you maintain the five contemplations in mind and constantly harbor a sense of shame and remorse, then afflictions will not arise.
An ancient saying goes: "Staring about in all directions, greed arises; thinking of the food, one swallows saliva and repeatedly coughs. [This refers to] scooping up rice porridge.
Sipping the soup, one fills the mouth; opening the mat and unfolding the bowl, the sound reaches all the neighbors.
Should there be anything required, one points it out silently; one must not shout or call out loudly.
*Śu* and *xū* are synonymous; they mean "to request. This refers to using one's fingers to point out and instruct so that the other person knows what to take.
One must not allow the bowls or alms-bowls to make noise, as explained previously in the ninth precept.
One must not rise before others have finished eating, except in cases of urgent business, illness, or when one is unable to remain seated for long; in such instances, there is no offense.
If one violates the regulations of the Saṃgha upon hearing the proclamation of the gavel, one must not resist or refuse to comply.
The striking of the mallet is the rule for raising a charge against an offense. To resist is the manifestation of defiance and non-compliance.

If one does not submit, giving rise to anger and discord, one is certainly no good monk. In ancient times, upon hearing virtuous words, people would bow; when informed of their own faults, they rejoiced.
These were all the demeanors of sages and worthies. Why do you not emulate them?
There are grains within the rice; one should remove their husks and eat them.
Life depends upon food for its sustenance, and the Path exists through food. Therefore, one should cherish it and must not treat it with contempt or discard it.
Once, while Master Zhi-feng was sitting in meditation, a spirit knelt before him. The Master asked, "Who are you? It replied, "I am the Spirit who Protects the Precepts."
The Master said, "I suspect that my past transgressions have not yet been extinguished; do you understand this? The man replied, "What sins does the Master have?
There are only minor oversights. The Master asked, "What are they? He answered, "Whenever a bowl is rinsed, the water is also the property of a donor.
You often discard it without hesitation; this is not appropriate. Having spoken, he vanished. From then on, the Master drank all such water.

One must not see delicious food and give rise to a greedy mind, eating to one's heart's content without knowing the faults and dangers of such consumption; thus, they indulge greedily without satiety.

For example, in the past, a certain śrāmaṇera, out of craving for the taste of curd, died and was reborn as an insect inside a jar of curd. Furthermore, another śrāmaṇera, being attached to the fragrant rice of the dragon palace, died...
Later, he became a dragon and sought to seize the dragon palace, killing many of the dragon kin; the harm he caused was no small matter.
Therefore, one must not give rise to a mind of greed regarding food.
One must not consume food by diverting it to a partial portion of the assembly.

If communal property is diverted to a partial portion of the assembly, one incurs an offense according to the rule. If one’s own property is diverted to a partial portion of the assembly, that person is shameless. This applies even before the Sangha has eaten.
One must not taste food beforehand. However, if one is preparing food for the Sangha and wishes to know whether it is salty or bland, there is no fault in tasting it first.
Formerly, in Wengcheng County of Dengzhou during the Tang dynasty, Wang Shi, the wife of Guo Xing, gave birth to a daughter with a crane-like beak. As she was about to die, she spoke of herself.
This is shown to people as a recompense for the merit of having observed the *zhāi* (fasting/retreat) in previous lives.
△ Regarding the sixth prostration:
one must not occupy the center of the hall; that is the station of the abbot.
Even if there is no abbot (*zhuchi*), there is still a supervisor (*jian-si*). Furthermore, one must not obstruct those who come later.

An abbot is one who propagates the True Dharma; he is a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Whenever performing prostrations, one must wash and rinse oneself clean. One should go bareheaded and barefoot.

Upon waking at dawn and during the two meals of gruel and rice, one should chew *yanchi* (willow twigs). If one does not purify oneself according to the Dharma, [one may not perform] the prostrations.
One will then incur an offense.
When someone is prostrating to the Buddha, one must not pass directly in front of that person's head.

"Directly" (逕) means near; it means passing by. To pass directly [in front] results in two things: first, one loses respect for oneself; second, one disturbs the other's meditative visualization (*vipaśyanā*). Thus, one incurs an offense.
It is not a matter of being casual.
Whenever joining the palms, the ten fingers must not be uneven; they must not leave a gap between them; and one must not insert the fingers into the nostrils.
They must be held level against the chest at the proper height.

Irregularity and internal emptiness both belong to negligence and indolence; raising the nose too high or too low means the ritual does not accord with the proper measure and results in a loss of dignified appearance.
One must not perform prostrations at improper times; if one wishes to prostrate at an improper time, one must wait until people have become quiet.

"Improper timing" refers to that which does not accord with the rules of the assembly and thus violates the regulations of the Saṃgha. When others are at rest, one must not cause the assembly to be disturbed in thought.
When the teacher prostrates to the Buddha, the disciple may not prostrate alongside the teacher; rather, they should follow behind the teacher and prostrate from a distance.
These are all the standard protocols for bhikṣus. "Following behind" means remaining behind the teacher's back; one should also not stand too close.
Therefore, it is called "bowing from afar.
When the teacher bows to another person, the disciple must not bow at the same time as the teacher.
If one bows together [with others], the etiquette between the honorable and the humble is lost.
In the presence of one's teacher, one must not perform mutual salutations with one's peers; in the presence of one's teacher, one must not receive salutations from others.
If one performs the same rites as one's peers, one loses the distinction of honoring one's teacher; if one receives the rites of others, one loses the decorum of self-abasement.
When holding a scripture or an image in one's own hands, one must not perform prostrations for others.
The scriptures and images are revered by humans and devas; how could one ever be fit to hold them while paying respects to others?
Appendix: In all acts of prostration, one must cultivate visualization with refined sincerity. One must not fail to know that the teachings enumerate seven types of prostration.
To be unmixed with other thoughts is called *jing* (purity). To pay homage with true sincerity is called *cheng* (sincerity). As for the seven kinds of prostrations: first, the prostration of pride;

second, the prostration for the sake of reputation; third, the prostration of physical and mental reverence; fourth, the prostration of the purity of awakened wisdom; fifth, the prostration of universal entry into the Dharma-realm;
sixth, the prostration of sincere cultivation through correct contemplation; seventh, the prostration of equality within the true mark (*dharmatā*). Of these, the former two are not [proper].

Regarding the ritual prostrations (*namaskāra*), the latter five meanings possess varying degrees of depth, as explained in other passages; they will not be elaborated upon here. To perform the visualization: the latter five prostrations are themselves the visualization.
Alternatively, one may perform this visualization on the emptiness and quiescence of the nature of that which is being prostrated to.
△ Seventh, on Listening to the Dharma:
Whenever you encounter the hanging of the plaque for the morning assembly, you should go to the hall early; do not wait until the Dharma drum is beaten loudly.
If you do not go early, you will be caught off guard at the last moment, losing your decorum and becoming agitated in body and mind, thereby failing to enter into the principles of the Dharma.
Adjust your robes. Look straight ahead and proceed upright.
When the robes are adjusted, the demeanor is solemn; when the gaze is level, the mind is upright; when one proceeds straight, it signifies rectitude.
One must sit with dignified composure.
The physical action is solemn;
one must not engage in idle speech.
The verbal action is solemn.

One must not cough or spit loudly. First, it disturbs the assembly; second, it defiles the ground; third, the transgression incurred is no small matter. These points are explained in detail as set forth in the sutras.

Whenever one hears the Dharma, one should regard it as a hungry person obtaining food or a thirsty person obtaining a drink. One should not waste even a moment and never tire of extensive learning; only then may one be so called.
O Son of the Buddha:
Whenever one listens to the Dharma, one must hear it, contemplate it, and cultivate it.
These are the three wisdoms of hearing, contemplation, and cultivation; none may be lacking. If one hears but does not contemplate, it is like a person planting...
It is like a field where no seed is sown; though one may contemplate it, if one does not practice, and fails to irrigate and weed it, it will never bear fruit.
If the three types of wisdom are established, then the fruits of the Three Vehicles can be attained.
One must not focus solely on memorizing names and terms merely to provide material for conversation.
To focus solely on memorizing names and terms is like a person talking about food, or like counting another's precious jewels.

If used merely as material for conversation to flaunt one’s knowledge and views while seeking no realization of the Principle, it increases the banner of arrogance. When knowledge and views establish further knowledge, they conversely become a poisonous medicine.
Therefore it is said: "The student falls away due to four matters. As stated in the *Lüfa Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Vinaya):
First, the student does not know skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), treats teachers and friends with contempt, lacks single-mindedness, and their mind frequently shifts.

Second, the student excels in the study of texts but possesses no power of the Way (*mārgabala*); they merely crave fame and reputation, hoping for the respect and service of others. Third, the student... [serves... the object of their service.

If a teacher does not undergo diligent hardship, they shall not attain accomplishment. To be vainly ostentatious and arrogant, while ostensibly studying the Way through the four types of excellence, yet instead upholding heterodox arts and comparing them to the profound sutras of the Buddha, claiming that their paths are equal—such evil views are worse than poisonous medicine;
they are harmful to the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom.
One must not claim to have realized what one has not yet realized. "Entering the ear and exiting the mouth" refers to realization;
realization means comprehension and awakening. To claim realization when one has not yet realized it is self-deception and insincerity.

To merely let words enter the ear and exit the mouth without the faculty of awakening is to deceive others. As the ancients said: "The learning of the gentleman enters through the ear and takes root..."
The mind pervades the four limbs and manifests in movement and stillness. The learning of the petty man enters through the ears and exits through the mouth;
between the ears and eyes there is but a span of four inches—how could this suffice to beautify a body seven feet tall?
A young śrāmaṇera whose power of the precepts is not yet firm should further study the Vinaya; he must not attend the lecture hall prematurely.
The "lecture hall" (jiang-xian) refers to the dharma-seat, that is, the place where the sutras are expounded. If the power of the precepts is not yet firm, one's resolve will lack stability.

With feet not yet firm on the ground, one rises and falls with the wind; how much more so for the Great and Small Vehicles and the two schools of Nature and Characteristics—how could they ever be harmonized?
To neither abandon this nor rejoice in that is to deny cause and effect, leading to mutual vilification and the incurrence of the grave transgression of the Avīci Hell;
thus, one must certainly be cautious. In the *Pañcakaṣāya-sūtra*, the Buddha said: "One who truly knows..."

Śāriputra, if you wish to instruct those who are newly learning, you should do so gradually and step by step. First, teach them about the deeds of Māra and cause them to guard against the conditions for Māra.

Make the transgressions and sufferings of birth and death clear, and distinguish clearly the five destinies. Cause them to believe in sin and merit until every matter is fully understood; only then may you speak of the Way.
△ Regarding the eighth [point], the study of the scriptures:
one should first study the Vinaya and subsequently study the Sūtras;

one must not transgress this order. To "study" (xué) is to "awaken" (jué); it means to awaken to that which was previously unknown. Furthermore, "study" is like "adornment. If a vessel is not adorned, [it remains unrefined].
Without it, one cannot achieve a beautiful appearance; likewise, if a person does not study, they cannot achieve sage-like virtue.

Therefore, learning is that which clarifies the spirit and expands the intellect, delights the emotions and rectifies the nature—it is the supreme task of the sages. As the ancients said, "A tree without branches is called a tumor;
a person who does not study is called blind. Since the sages and worthies of antiquity were still devoted to learning, how much more so should ordinary people today?
Is there anyone who becomes a person of accomplishment without study? The Sanskrit term *sūtra* is translated here as "scripture" (*jing*). A scripture is like a path;
it is the trackway upon which those of the Three Vehicles travel to reach Nirvana. Study must necessarily rely upon the holy teachings;
one may not deviate from or bypass the sequence in one's learning. Therefore, the Vinaya comes first and the Sūtras follow, just as one must obtain a cord [to guide the way].
The ink-line and compass are held in hand; first the Sūtras, then the Vinaya. If one lacks these guiding lines, then squareness and roundness will lose their proper measure.
Whenever studying a sūtra, one must first inform the teacher; once that sūtra is completed, one should again inform him that one wishes to study another specific sūtra.
A śrāmaṇera’s insight and vision are not yet broad; he does not know the proper sequence of the Dharma or what is appropriate for his studies.

Therefore, he must first inform his teacher, and only after the teacher grants permission may he study. In this way, he will surely make progress every day, reviewing what is old and practicing what is new. During the intervals between advancing in his studies, [he should engage in other virtuous activities].
He was constantly by his teacher’s side. The Buddha ordained two kinds of training for the great *vinaya*: first, recitation and exegesis; second, meditative contemplation.
Through meditation, one quiets delusion to reveal the truth; through exegesis, one develops sublime wisdom. The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Meditative study is called the opening of wisdom;
lecturing and study are called the unfolding of wisdom."
One must not blow dust from upon the scriptures with one's mouth.
First, the breath is foul and impure; second, it causes the loss of a mind of reverence. One should instead brush it away with a clean cloth.
The *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: "If one uses the mouth to blow away the dust from the implements of adornment and offerings, one will fall into the Utpala Hell."
As a karmic retribution, one becomes a wind-god king;
one must not conceal tea dregs or miscellaneous items upon the sutra table, for this defiles the desk and treats the scriptures with disrespect.
The *Chingui* (Rules of Purity) states: "To privately store tea dregs is to invite derision from onlookers. It also says:
One must not place non-Buddhist texts, impure objects, or even items such as head-caps or fans upon the Buddha’s sūtras and vinaya.
When a person is reading the scriptures, one must not walk back and forth (caṅkrama) near their desk.
One loses one’s own respectful decorum and disturbs the mental focus of others.
Whenever scriptures are damaged, they should be promptly repaired.
As for these sacred texts, if they are damaged, they must be quickly mended so that they do not fall into decay. The sutras are like parents; when parents...
This illness can be quickly cured; do not let it become difficult to treat. It will be too late.
A śrāmaṇera’s primary task is not yet accomplished; he must not study external books, histories, or secular administrative codes.
"Those whose fundamental practice is not yet accomplished" refers to those whose mastery of the ten precepts is not yet pure, whose dignified deportment is not yet complete,

and who have not yet studied the sūtras and dharmas that śrāmaṇeras should learn, such as the Forty-two Sections, the Bequeathed Teachings, the Lotus Sūtra, the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, and secular histories.

"Zi" refers to the various masters of the hundred schools; "Shi" refers to the historical records of the various states. Whenever there has been a sovereign and his ministers of an era, there must necessarily be the history of that era.
History is that by which the traces of what was lawful or unlawful, and of gain or loss, during that time are recorded.
Thus, the virtue of Yao and Shun must be recorded, and the conduct of Zhi and Qiao must also be recorded. [This includes] the phenomena of Heaven and the affairs of men, as well as the good...

Evil deeds, praises, and criticisms are all recorded without exception, so as to warn future generations and ensure credibility for those to come; therefore, it is called a "faithful history" (*xìnshǐ*).
External records include the canons of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, the texts of Confucius and the Duke of Zhou, and even the Four Books and Five Classics.
Through filial piety one governs the family, and through loyalty one governs the state; one cultivates the self and nourishes one's nature, thereby assisting the nation and benefiting [the people].

The people [of the world]. Therefore, it is said that the statutes and codes for governing the world—because their teaching stops at cultivating the self and regulating the family—are called "external.

The sacred teachings of the Three Vehicles, which teach the stilling of mental delusions and the realization of one's own original nature, are called "internal. The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice of the Way) says:

If one studies non-Buddhist texts within the teachings of the Hīnayāna, it is permitted to study non-Buddhist classics for one period out of every twelve periods of the day in order to subdue non-Buddhists.
However, within the Mahāyāna, this is strictly forbidden for a beginner Bodhisattva; rather, they are encouraged to advance directly.

Once they reach the stage of the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*), studying them will not be difficult, nor will it be too late. As the ancient masters said: "Much knowledge..."

It is better to let the mind rest than to engage in affairs; many concerns lead to many losses. It is better to maintain oneness than to harbor many anxieties; when anxieties are many, the will is scattered; when knowledge is excessive, the mind is disturbed.
A disturbed mind gives rise to affliction, and a scattered will obstructs the Way. To possess refined wisdom and artistic talent is called being foolishly exhausted;
a single skill or ability is like a solitary lamp sinking as the sun sets, or a mosquito or gnat in empty space.
Appendix: One must not select scriptures for the purpose of performing rituals at ritual sites (daochang).
Whenever studying a scripture, one must seek to understand its principles; whether through chanting or upholding it, if it is done merely for the sake of ritual performance, it is improper.
One should not study this. As for "responding to invitations" (*yingfu*): it refers to those who take up instruments such as gongs and drums to attend to the affairs of others;

because they respond to the requests of others, it is called "responding to invitations. Within the Buddha's teachings, there was originally no such term as "responding to invitations," so how could there be a sutra titled "Responding to Invitations"?

What is now called the *Yingfu Daochang Jing* (Sutra on Responding to Invitations at the Altar) is merely a scripture used by these "responding monks" (*yingfuseng*) for performing liturgical recitations on behalf of others.

[The texts include] the *Chàn* (Repentance) rituals and the *Shuǐlù kēwén* (Water-Land Liturgical Texts), and so forth. Yet, these sutra repentances are the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure of the Tathāgata;
to uphold even a single phrase or verse thereof causes transgressions to be extinguished and blessings to arise, serving eternally as the seed of Bodhi.
To instead trade them for worldly wealth and profit is truly lamentable. There may be faithful donors who invite monks, desiring to seek merit...
Regarding those who seek benefit in life or death, the Buddha permitted bhikṣus only to recite verses of benediction or even to chant a single sutra;
this was sufficient to benefit them, for there was absolutely no need for [other] ritual responses.
One must not study or practice the fabrication of scriptures,
such as the *Vajra-zuan*, the *Vajra-lun*, the *Xuepen*, the *Miaosha*, the *Jiuku*, the *Fenzhu*, the *Shousheng*, and the *Beidou*.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in three fascicles and others, as well as the dream-bestowed *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, the commentary by Vimalaputra, and the *Taichu yulu*—
all of these are the teachings of Māra.
One must not study or transmit such books.
This refers to the books that employ the principles of yin and yang, the seven celestial bodies, the five phases, and the six stems to divining longevity versus brevity, and success versus failure.
Yet, Heaven possesses calamities that can be averted through ritual, and humans possess misfortunes and blessings that can be transformed.

Thus, practicing goodness brings down a hundred auspicious signs; practicing evil brings down a hundred calamities. Therefore it is said: "A single thought of goodness [brings forth] auspicious winds..."

Harmony arises from a single thought of goodness, while a single thought of evil brings forth demonic stars and malevolent ghosts. A single word of virtue causes even the planet Venus (Hing-hok) to shift its position thrice.

Examining the past and verifying it with the present provides sufficient evidence for sincere reflection. Moreover, as these matters are profound and their principles subtle, few are able to fathom them entirely.
Thus, Han Huan-t’an said: "The Way of Heaven and the nature of life are what the sages find difficult to speak of; from the time of Zi-gong downward, [the commoners] have not [understood them]."

Even those who have attained [the path] find it difficult to hear [such things], let alone the shallow Confucian scholars of later generations—how could they possibly comprehend them? Even if they were able to understand them by comparison, it would truly be unsuitable for a follower of the Śākya;
it would bring harm to oneself and others, corrupt and disrupt the True Dharma, and the calamity would not be small.
Regarding the *xiangshu* (books of physiognomy): these are works that claim to discern fortune and misfortune by examining physical appearance and observing the spirit and vital energy (*shenqi*).

Upon investigating these texts, it is found that they have been transmitted through successive generations, totaling twenty-seven schools. Originally, there was no orthodox tradition; yet, erroneously, Bodhidharma was designated as their progenitor. This was intended—
To deceive future generations and slander the Sage is a sin as vast as the heavens.
Wealth, honor, poverty, lowliness, beauty, ugliness, gain, and loss all arise from the causes of good and evil karma created by oneself in previous lives;

thus, in this present life, one receives various retributive fruits—both general and specific—regarding the primary and secondary bodies (the *shen* and *zheng*). These are transformations of the *xiangfen* (objective aspect) of the eighth consciousness. Since they are...
Once the allotment is fixed, heaven, earth, ghosts, and spirits cannot alter it; only by performing good or evil deeds oneself can one change it.
Therefore, it is beyond what humans can fathom—how could it be known merely by observing physical appearance?
Disciples of the Buddha, do not be deluded by this.

Medical texts refer to books containing prescriptions for treating illnesses. The tradition of Donghua began with Shen Nong, who examined the cold and warm natures of plants and distinguished the principles of the sovereign, minister, assistant, and envoy [in pharmacology], composing medicinal formulas to cure the ailments of the people. The Yellow Emperor composed the *Neijing*...

The Classics record that Yu Fu, Qibo, and Leigong were commanded to examine the Mingtang, investigate the pulses and breaths, and that Wu Peng and Tongjun formulated prescriptions and administered medicinal tonics;
thus, the Way of Medicine was established. Following this, there appeared Hua Tuo, Bian Que, Ge Xian Gong, and Sun Zhenren.

The collections of Zhang Zhongjing and others are all termed medical texts; likewise, the *Jīvakapustaka* and the *Vaidyakasamhitā* of the Western Regions were originally not subjects of study for Buddhist disciples.
Because they distract the mind and obstruct one’s primary duties, if they are applied even once in error, they will harm both oneself and others.
Thus, the Tathāgata suffered the residual retribution of back pain, and [the physician] Bian Que... [and Cang Jie... *(Note: The source text appears to be fragmentary at this point.)*

Your Excellency is facing an unavoidable calamity of punishment; even if you were to obtain the marvelous arts of Jīvaka of the Flowing Water, they truly are not practices appropriate for one who wears the circular crown and square robe.

As for military treatises, such as the *Six Tactics* (*Liùtāo*) of the Grand Duke (Tàigōng), the *Three Strategies* (*Sānlüè*) of the Lord of Yellow Stone (Huángshí Gōng), and the thirteen chapters of Sun Wu’s *Master Sun*, these are all books concerning the methods of conquest and battle formations; they are most certainly not what a son of the Śākya should study. As for...
The *Abhiṣeka Sūtra* records the Buddha’s words: "A thousand years after my parinirvāṇa, there shall be bhikṣus who delight in practicing the arts of war.
They shall associate with kings, princes, ministers, and subjects, thereby destroying my Dharma. Consequently, they shall harbor evil intentions and bring about the extinction of my Dharma;
stupas and images will fall into ruin, and the divine efficacy of the benevolent deities shall cease."
No longer being maintained or protected, it was allowed to fall into ruin. With no one to restrain or govern it, my Dharma transformation gradually perished.
[This includes] the books of divination and astrology.

The tortoise shell is called *bu* (divination by cracks); the milfoil stalks are called *shi* (divination by numbers). The *shi* herb grows with one hundred stems; one uses these to perform divination and resolve doubts.

Hence, they are termed *bushi* (divination and prognostication). Yan Han, a minister of the Jin dynasty, once had Guo Pu wish to perform divination for him. Yan Han said: "One's years are determined by Heaven, while one's position depends on man.
To cultivate oneself yet find that Heaven does not grant one's aims is fate (*ming*). To uphold the Way yet find that others do not recognize it is likewise beyond one's control."
This is one's inherent nature. One possesses one's own destiny; there is no need for the divination of milfoil stalks or tortoise shells.
Even the Confucian scholars of the world are unwilling to do this, so why would a Buddhist monk turn back to study it? This is truly shameful.

Astronomical texts refer to those who look upward to personally observe the celestial phenomena of the sun, moon, stars, and constellations, as well as the anomalies of comets, meteors, and the planet Mars,

in order to prognosticate the prosperity or peril of the state and the calamities or portents affecting the people. Their origins trace back to the Yellow Emperor, Xuanyuan, Chonghu, Tanghe, Gan De, Shi Shen, and others.
Furthermore, these matters are also extensively elucidated within Buddhism, such as in the *Matanga-sūtra*.
Therein, it mentions a candāla named Tiṣya who provides a detailed exposition of the twenty-eight lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and the seven luminaries (*graha*).

For each, he specifies their respective names and numerical counts, their stellar shapes, and their stellar lineages (*gotra*), as well as the requirements for their sacrificial rites and the degrees of the sun’s course.

Furthermore, there are six lunar mansions that travel together with the moon for one day and one night; namely, Bi (Jyeṣṭhā), Jing (Āśvinī), Di (Rohiṇī), Yi (Anurādhā), Niu (Vṛṣabha), and Bi (Mṛgaśirā).

Together with the seven luminaries and Rāhu and the comet, these constitute nine celestial bodies. Moreover, based on the movement of these stars, they are distinguished by their proximity to or distance from the sun.

He discerns the characteristics of good and evil in the persons born under various signs; he further divines the various lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) and their proximity or distance from the sun, discerning the signs of arising, abiding, completion, and destruction.
He further divines which lunar mansion the moon occupies, the amount of rainfall, as well as solar and lunar eclipses, and the affairs presided over by them.
He further divines earthquakes occurring when the sun or moon are situated in specific locations, and the signs of fortune and misfortune. Thereafter...

The Buddha extensively refutes these characteristics [in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*]. In the tenth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the methods of stellar divination are also briefly explained. That is to say:

if the moon reaches the constellations of Mṛgaśiras, Jyeṣṭhā, Āśleṣā, Rohiṇī, Revatī, or Ārdrā, and an earthquake occurs, it belongs to the water-earth spirits; in such a year there will be no rain, and it is not suitable for wheat.

If [the moon] reaches the constellations of Anurādhā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāṅhā, Bharaṇī, Citrā, or Śatabhiṣaj, and an earthquake occurs, it belongs to the dragon spirits; the calamities are the same as before. If [the moon] reaches...
If there is an earthquake when the moon is in the lunar mansions of Shen, Gui, Zhen, Kang, Yi, or when it belongs to the Garuḍa, the calamities will be as previously described.

If there is an earthquake when the moon is in the mansions of Jue, Xin, Fang, Ni, Xu, Jing, Bi, Zi, or Dou, it belongs to the Heavenly Emperor; there will be peace, stability, abundance, and joy, and the five grains will flourish.
The rest is as described in the books of astrology; it is not what is required here, nor does it belong to the tradition of the Śākyas. Thus the Sūtra says:

"One must not look up at the calendar and its calculations, nor deduce the waxing and waning of the moon, solar and lunar eclipses, the anomalies of the stars and constellations, landslides and earthquakes, wind, rain, drought, or floods, the ripening or failure of the harvests, or whether there is pestilence or not. One must not know any of these. There is.
One who violates this precept is no longer a śrāmaṇera.
As for geographical texts,
those that do not clarify the canons concerning the nine provinces, nine circuits, nine mountains, and nine marshes of the kingdom are merely the works of contemporary geomancers (kānyu).
The treatises on selecting sites for birth, dwelling, death, and burial originated with Guo Pu.

Having obtained the *Qing'uzi Qingnang jing* (The Green Bird Master’s Green Sack Scripture), he was thus able to practice divination and geomancy. However, the fixed destiny of misfortune or fortune arises from prior causes (*pūrvakarma*).
Although these prior causes are fixed, cultivating goodness can extinguish remaining calamities, while practicing evil diminishes one's blessings. Cultivating goodness can...
To rectify past errors, how could one allow the accumulation of evil while seeking the three blessings as a reward from the earth?

To fail to cultivate benevolence and righteousness while praying for withered bones to be granted the five fortunes—such a thing has never been seen since the Three Dynasties, nor have even Confucius or Laozi ever spoken of it.
Therefore, the world says: "Wind and water are indispensable in the human realm; they rely entirely upon the mutual support of Yin and Yang.
If wealth and status were obtained through fengshui, even Guo Pu would find it difficult to recreate them. The *Guanding jing* states:
A youth of the Śākya clan asked the Buddha, "For what reason do various ghosts and spirits take up residence in the tombs of ordinary people? The Buddha said, "It is because..."

These are the essences of the five grains; they are illusory transformations of seductive maidens, or ghosts of those who died an untimely death who have no place to attach themselves and rely [on these objects] to manifest as spirits.
Or they are the essences of trees, woods, and mountain forests; because their bones have not yet decayed, they possess a subtle spirit.
If the bones have rotted away, this spirit will immediately perish; it will possess no vital energy or influence, nor can it bring about various calamities or blessings for people.

Perhaps it is the spirit of a local relative who has recently passed away—a person who lacked merit while alive and practiced deceitful wickedness, destined to fall among the ghosts and spirits, or to become the essence of trees or miscellaneous objects, possessing no heavenly merit to receive and not yet having reached hell.

They roam through the world, drifting from village to village among men. Since they lack celestial food and various kinds of sustenance, they eventually terrify people by manifesting various strange transformations and agitating the human mind.
When ordinary people see or hear them, they immediately provide offerings of merit.
As for these so-called "spirits," they are often masters of sorcery and evil who rely upon them as deities to seek various blessings and wish to attain longevity.

Out of ignorance and false views, they slaughter living beings for sacrifice; consequently, after death, they enter the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm, from which there is no time of escape.
One must be cautious of this!
The *Tuchèn* (Diagram-Prophecy) texts are books of talismans and prophecies; they refer to records of past events that have been verified, matching reality without discrepancy.
This extends even to the refinement of alchemical elixirs through furnace fires.
This refers to the arts of cinnabar furnaces and the transformation of metals into gold and silver (*huángbái*).

The *Huáihuán* tradition states that there is a middle section in eight fascicles concerning the arts of immortals and the transformation of metals into gold and silver, totaling more than two hundred thousand words. The *Dàojià liànzhēn jīng* (Scripture on the Refinement of Truth by the Daoists) states:
"If cinnabar (*dānshā*) is refined once, it becomes white silver; if refined twice, it becomes yellow gold. Formerly, the Han dynasty Daoist Li Shao[ling]...

The Emperor said, "I am able to condense mercury and lead to produce white silver, and sublimate cinnabar into gold. Once gold is produced, if one ingests it, one shall ascend to heaven in broad daylight.
The Emperor believed him; however, later, none of these claims were verified. Emperor Wu of the Tang dynasty was fond of seeking immortality.
The Daoist Zhao Guizhen took a golden elixir with him; when the medicine took effect, he became agitated and lost his composure, and subsequently passed away.

These individuals all incurred the crime of deceiving their sovereign. Today there are foolish people who repeatedly fall under such delusions, and those who come to ruin their bodies and destroy their families are not few.
Yet, the sons of the Śākya renounce jade and silk as if discarding spittle; they thus leave the household life to become monks.

The Way consists of the arts for longevity; yet they fail to recognize that this skin-sack of the four elements is but a vessel for discarding one's own mind-nature, seeking instead to become a corpse-guarding ghost—a pursuit that will succeed not once in ten thousand attempts.
Disciples of the Buddha understand that the body is like an illusion and does not endure long in this world;
they awaken to their own original mind, which is truly eternal and never extinguished. How could they, in turn, give rise to greedy attachment and study such a base art? It is truly shameful.
To delude oneself and delude others, thereby bringing disgrace upon the Dharma-gate, is a transgression no light.
Regarding writings on "spiritual wonders" and "ghostly anomalies," such as talismans and consecrated water:

those possessing merit and manifesting efficacy are called *shen* (spirits); those lacking merit yet appearing as malevolent influences are called *gui* (ghosts). Furthermore, *gui* means to deceive; they deceive people.
This is done for the sake of seeking food and drink; it is what is called "summoning spirits" and "summoning ghosts.

Painting talismans, spraying water, curing illnesses, and exorcising ghosts—these various books on heterodox sorcery and illusions falsely expound upon good and bad fortune, calamity and blessing, to delude people and extract profit.

This originated with Zhang Daoling, who styled himself the "Way of the Ghost-Soldiers" (*guizu-dao*) and created the arts of talisman-water and *jiao* rituals. These were transmitted to Zhang Jue. As for Jue...
He taught the people various strange arts through sorcery and used false incantations and consecrated water to treat illnesses.

When the masses saw his eccentricities, they regarded him as divine and marveled at him; thus he was called a "divine spirit and ghostly monster. Later, he rebelled and became one of the Yellow Turban bandits.

This extends even to the *yuánguāng* (halo), the *fújī* (supporting spirits), the *wàidào ānzhái zhòu* (non-Buddhist spells for securing one’s dwelling), the *zhījìe zhòu* (spells for the limbs and joints), the *zhīrén shēngsǐ jíxióng zhòu* (spells for knowing the auspiciousness or misfortune of a person’s birth and death), and the *jiězhū yīnshēng zhòu* (spells for interpreting all sounds).
One should neither perform these oneself nor instruct others to do so. As the *Guǎngdìng jīng* (Sutra of Consecration) states:
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "The words spoken by the Tathāgata are all true and not false. Yet, in the final age, there will be much slander.

Regarding the various sūtras and dharmas previously taught by the Buddha that contain incantations (dhāraṇīs), some say they should be studied, recited, maintained, and practiced, while others say one should not practice such prohibitions and incantations. Within these various sūtras and dharmas, they differ from one another."
Because these matters have been repeated from beginning to end, there are among the bhikṣus of the final age those who practice with faith and those who slander.
For this reason, they have questioned the World-Honored One once more. The Buddha said: "In my sūtras, I have stated that various incantations and arts of prohibition should not be practiced.
These refer to the heterodox and false views of other paths, as well as their magical arts, which delude and confuse the myriad people, serving only for the sake of profit."
To cultivate [the practice] for the sake of sustaining one's own life is something I do not permit.

What I now proclaim—the mantras of consecration, the true incantations originating from the Āgamas and the various mantras within the sūtras—is intended entirely to transform and guide all sentient beings.

It is not like the paths of heterodox sects, which seek material gain; rather, it is solely for the purpose of delivering sentient beings from peril and distress, and for those who have encountered suffering and affliction.
To allow them to find relief, I now grant my permission.

In the future, at the end of the age, there will be disciples of the fourfold assembly who enter my Dharma and receive and uphold the prohibitive precepts, yet they will frequently fail and transgress them;

their minds will not be single-minded, and when faced with urgent calamities or the hardships of illness, they will turn toward the heterodox paths and false views to seek blessings and protection, wishing thereby to escape these manifold difficulties.

Unable to escape, and unaware of their past karmic retributions or the causal conditions of their previous lives, they arrive at the abode of a heterodox teacher, where they kneel, prostrate, and inquire after his well-being, saying, "We pray that you will rescue and protect us. The heterodox teacher says, "I shall grant your wish.

I will offer prayers upward to the Five Officials and speak downward to the Earth Deities, so that you may obtain blessings, be delivered from peril and distress, and no longer encounter suffering. Furthermore...
It may be said that in a previous life you committed various transgressions and evils;

or it may be said that you are led by the calamities and faults of seven generations, to be seized by kings and officials and subjected to various punishments; or it may be said that you are dragged down to the destruction of your family and clan;

or it may be said that your seven ancestors have been ensnared in the Nine Shades of Darkness and their souls reside in Mount Tai. You should therefore use silk fabrics of the colors corresponding to the respective directions to provide salvation.
I shall redeem the souls of your seven ancestors and eradicate the transgressions of your seven generations.
Furthermore, it is said that you have been afflicted by mountain deities, tree spirits, and the gods of the stars, resulting in various illnesses.

You should offer white oxen and white horses, various kinds of rich and delicious food and drink, and provide music, dance, and song for the spirits; thus you may obtain great merit and be freed from [suffering].
"You are in peril. The Buddha told Ānanda: "In the final age, sentient beings will be deluded by various false teachers;

they will take the lives of living beings in an attempt to rescue others from danger and distress. Yet those who kill commit an offense, and neither celestial deities nor terrestrial spirits will consume their offerings.
Therefore, I shall now extensively expound the consecrated verses and the true mantra-techniques to transform those who have not yet gained faith or understanding."
As for the Way, you should propagate it and not allow it to be lost or destroyed.
You must not practice the recitation of scrolls or the striking of verses.
This is the present *Jingang Juan* (Vajra Scroll) of the Unconditioned Teaching: one person proclaims it, and the multitude joins in harmony; this is called "striking" (*da*).
Verse:
One must not study the books of non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika), except when one’s intellectual power is sufficient and one wishes to discern the depth of the internal and external teachings;
in such cases, one may engage with them, yet one must not harbor the thought that they are to be mastered or studied as a primary pursuit.
*Lie* (躐) is also written as *lie* (獵). It means to tread upon. Regarding the internal and external teachings, they have been explained as before. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, "Those who have left the household life should cultivate the study of wisdom and investigate the sūtras; they must not peruse secular books."

After my parinirvāṇa, there will be ignorant and precept-breaking people who abandon the twelve divisions of the scriptures and instead recite various non-Buddhist texts, verses, and literary compositions. They will possess impure items and claim that these are permitted by the Buddha.
Such people trade fine sandalwood for tiles and wood; they exchange nectar for virulent poison. Therefore, the treatise says:
If a bodhisattva abandons what has been taught by the Buddha and fails to study it, instead studying the heterodox treatises of external paths or worldly scriptures, this is called an offense.
However, if one is a person of superior intelligence who is able to receive and study [the teachings] swiftly, attaining unshakable wisdom, there is no offense.
Within the sun and moon [of one's life], one should devote two parts to studying the Buddha-dharma and one part to studying external texts.
If one takes pleasure in worldly classics, heterodox paths, or false teachings and does not abandon them, nor forms the intention to discard them, this is called an offense.
The *Fayuan* states: "If one exclusively abandons the internal [teachings] to seek the external, one incurs guilt. Even if one understands the principles and practices, one may only..."
One may practice briefly to subdue non-Buddhists, yet one must still cultivate revulsion and detachment, advancing in internal practice with a commitment to excellence.

If one becomes biasedly attached, the True Dharma will be ruined; how then could one become a Jewel of the Sangha? If one devotes oneself solely to external classics, singing, lute-playing, chess, or reciting the *Shi* and *Shu*, one merely wastes days and months.
The teachings and medicines of the Inner Dharma take the salvation of sentient beings as their primary urgency; its texts are profound.
The principles are profound, and the phrasing is elegant, secret, and vast; one is able to explain a single phrase and expound upon immeasurable meanings.

Among the new and old sutras and treatises, numbering several thousand fascicles, there is not a single phrase whose meaning has ever been examined by him. Yet he studies the matters of non-Buddhists and secular urgency day and night with diligent effort.
If it is said that laypeople laugh at me for being ignorant and for not studying worldly classics, how does this compare to a common worldly person?
When asked about the meaning of my scriptures, you were unable to answer. To be unacquainted with external matters while dwelling within [the tradition] is not yet enough to cause shame;

but to lack understanding of internal matters while being situated within [the tradition] is a source of even greater humiliation. This is truly because we are approaching the age of the Final Dharma (mappō), and the lifespan of human beings is becoming increasingly shortened.
In this impermanent world, we meet but for a moment; the morning does not plan for the evening. I fear that once one enters the path of darkness, it will be difficult to emerge for many kalpas.

Should one encounter the Buddha-dharma again, there would likely be no way to do so. Although the sutras and śāstras permit a portion of study outside [the Buddhist teachings], this is intended to subdue non-Buddhists;

it is taught for those of superior intelligence and sagacity who first master the internal [teachings] and then come to know the external, so that their eloquence and discernment may be as sharp as a blade.

Your speech draws upon the classics, and you have extensively investigated both internal and external teachings; you are fit to serve as a master. As it is said in the sutras, you should now measure yourself against your own capacity.
You are unable to cope with the affairs at hand; your spiritual consciousness is perpetually closed, while your foolishness is ever-present.

Since you cannot even save yourself, how can you benefit others? With no penetration into form or fragrance, how can you distinguish between beans and wheat? I pray that you will reflect and withdraw from this position. Please take heed.
When studying for oneself, one must not intermingle Buddhist scriptures with secular texts. As the *Mingbao ji* (Records of Karmic Retribution) relates:
Zhao Wenxin of Suizhou was a man of the Tang dynasty who died suddenly in the first year of the Zhenguan era. After three days, he revived and said that he had gone to the abode of King Yama.
The King asked him, "What meritorious deeds have you cultivated? He replied, "Throughout my entire life, I have not cultivated any meritorious deeds."
[The monk] only took pleasure in collecting the literary works of Yu Xin. The King said, "Yu Xin is a great sinner who is currently undergoing suffering.
Have you ever known him? He replied, "Although I have read his writings, I have not known the man.
The King immediately sent someone to bring Yu Xin out; there he saw a multi-headed tortoise. A short while after the tortoise departed, it manifested as a human being.
He came forward and said, "I am Yu Xin. During my lifetime, I was fond of composing literary works;

I falsely cited Buddhist scriptures to intermingle with secular texts, slandering the Buddha-dharma by claiming it did not equal the teachings of Confucius and Laozi. Now I have received this tortoise body as retribution."
This is the height of suffering.
One is not permitted to study poetry or prose.
What the will expresses through speech is called *shi* (poetry); what speech emits through writing is called *ci* (prose). As the *Records* state: "The Book..."

Astrology, divination, and the like, as well as secular classics, prose, and verse, are all worldly matters and not the practice of those who have left the home life; therefore, their study is not permitted.
One must not set one’s heart upon learning characters or seeking proficiency in them; it is sufficient merely to write them with upright and clear strokes.
"Kai" refers to Kai-shu (clerical script). It was created by Wang Cizhong of Shanggu; it is sufficient to proclaim the text and manifest its meaning.
Why then do you further set your mind on seeking excellence in cursive and clerical scripts?

Those who have left the household life nowadays mostly fail to cultivate their primary duties, yet they spend day and night seeking precision in calligraphy, toiling their minds all year long without realizing their delusion. Even if one studies until reaching the level of Zhong [Yong]...."
The subtlety of King [Wang Xizhi] and the ingenuity of Cheng Xu—what do they avail for saving one from birth and death? The Buddhas do not praise them; King Yama does not accept them.
In the end, they become useless things; what purpose have they served? The admonition states: "The Vinaya prohibits the study of miscellaneous arts as they hinder one's primary practice;
therefore, one must not excel in calligraphy. Nevertheless, many eminent monks of antiquity were also versed in various secular studies, some reaching great proficiency.
Among the scribes and clerks, some were skilled in literary composition, some were renowned for their medical arts, and others gained fame through the study of *yin-yang* divination;

yet all of them had thoroughly mastered the Inner Canon (*nèidiǎn*) while peripherally engaging with other schools of thought, none of whom lacked the resolve to protect and uphold the Dharma and assist in the propagation of the Buddha’s transformation.

In the present age, however, the sons of the Śākya have lost both name and reality: those capable of calligraphy are titled "Calligraphic Sages," and those who popularize secular classics [are likewise honored].
What they call "literature" is merely a designation; what they call "mountains and waters" is merely a choice of location; what they call "the three fates" is merely a divination technique.

How could one have expected that, having abandoned worldly affairs to serve the Buddha, one would instead conform to the names of secular trends? One’s original plan was to weary oneself of the world and transcend it, yet one has instead practiced the karma of birth and death.
Seeking fame and profit, aligning with power and boasting of ability—though the outward form is that of a monastic robe, the mind is stained.
To spend one's entire life adrift in worldly vanity is truly lamentable.
One must not defile one’s hands by grasping the scriptures.

The *Sutra on Cause and Effect* states: "If one touches the scriptures with one's hands while requesting them, one shall fall into the retribution of becoming an insect dwelling in a latrine. Ānanda requested the Vinaya.

The treatise states: If monks, nuns, or laypeople, while reading, reciting, or studying the Sūtras, Vinaya, or Śāstras, speak while walking or hold the scrolls in their hands, they will, according to the reckoning of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, undergo two hundred million years of retribution as animals.
They will fall among the species of deer and wild asses, where their backs will be constantly folded over them in suffering that is difficult to endure.
Even if it is for neutral purposes or spoken in jest, grasping the Sūtras, Vinaya, or Śāstras likewise incurs the aforementioned [retribution].

The retribution is as follows: if one places scriptures or images in front of the eaves of the hall or chamber, one will undergo the retribution of an animal for eight hundred years according to the reckoning of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;

for two hundred million years, one will fall into birth among pigs and dogs. Even if one subsequently attains a human body, for one hundred million years one will constantly serve as a tenant, living in squalor and lacking any autonomy.
Toward the scriptures, one must act as one would toward the Buddha; one may not treat them with levity or derision.
The scriptures are the word of the Buddha, and they are also the Teacher of the Buddha. Therefore, one should regard the scriptures as one regards the Buddha.

A single word or a single verse is difficult to encounter even in a thousand kalpas. Even if one does not understand the meaning, reciting them still plants roots of goodness. For this reason, one must accord them special respect.

The Vinaya states: "Be careful never to recite the sutras while lying down. If you feel even the slightest fatigue and thoughts of indolence arise, you should immediately reflect with urgency upon the fact that human life lasts but a breath, as if your head were on fire. How could you afford the leisure for such indolence?"
One must not leave books in disorder upon the table. "Juǎnzhì" (卷帙):
the pronunciation of "zhì" is "yì. A "zhì" refers to a bundle or case formed by binding and arranging sutra scrolls. "Lángjí" (狼藉) means uneven, disordered, and lacking regularity.
One must not raise one's voice so as to disturb the assembly.

In reciting the scriptures, one must understand the punctuation and the rules of intonation, ensuring that both the Chinese and Sanskrit are clearly articulated. When chanting in unison with the assembly, the voice should be harmonious;
one must not rely on one's own prowess. When practicing privately, the voice must be kept low and soft, lest it disturb the thoughts of others.
Furthermore, one must not lend scriptures to others and fail to return them, nor treat them without due reverence, thereby causing them to be damaged.

The Dharma of the scriptures is the parent of those who follow the Three Vehicles; it should be protected with equal care by all, without distinction between self and other. If there is... [text continues]

Those who treat it with disrespect or cause its destruction both incur the offense of arrogance toward the Dharma. To borrow an item and intentionally fail to return it constitutes the offense of theft.
As the Sūtra says: "When borrowing or giving, one must be clear and distinct; do not violate agreements, lest you lose the path of trust."
△ Entering a Temple, Part Nine:
Whenever entering the gate of a temple, one must not walk through the center; one must walk along the left or right side. When walking along the left, the left foot must go first.
When turning to the right, one should first step with the right foot.

To proceed through the center would be a rash intrusion, lacking the etiquette of respect. Just as in the official gatehouses of secular government offices where even subordinates are not permitted to enter directly through the middle, how much more so in the precious palace of the Dharma King?
How could one fail to look back toward the left and right? One should follow this principle.
When entering or exiting through a gate, one should lift the feet while keeping them close together. When following the left side [of the path], first lift the left foot;
when following the right side, first lift the right foot. The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "When walking, first lower the heel and then lower the toes;

look straight ahead and proceed directly. When turning back, turn the entire body as a whole. The *Sītu of Western Country Monasteries* states: "At the time of entering and exiting, one always turns the face [toward the gate]."
When facing the Buddha or paying homage to the Triple Gem, one should always keep in mind that their essence is but one.
Why is this? One who has fully awakened to the Dharma is called a Buddha; the Way that is awakened to is called the Dharma; and those who study the Buddha’s Way are called the Sangha.

Thus, one knows that the essence of all ordinary beings and sages is identical and non-dual. When entering a temple, one should lower the head and look at the ground, not looking upward. Upon seeing the ground...
There are insects; do not inadvertently injure or kill them. One should sing hymns and offer praises. One must not spit upon the ground of the Sangha.
If one sees weeds or filth, they must immediately be removed. As for the term "temple" (*si*), it means "succession. It refers to those who manage affairs, as they succeed one another therein.
Thus, the Son of Heaven has nine temples. In the tenth year of the Yongping era of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, [the monk] Kāśyapa Mātanga from India...

The two Dharma Masters, Dharmaratna and Kālayasas, arrived at Luoyang carrying scriptures and images on white horses. By imperial decree, they were stationed at the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu Si).
In the following year, an edict was issued to construct a separate monastery outside the Yong Gate, named after the white horse to honor its origins;
furthermore, it was called a "si" (monastery), for in the Western Regions, the residence of monks is termed *saṃghārāma*, which here is translated as "Garden of the Community."
This means it is the sprout of the Way that nurtures the sons of the Buddha.
One must not ascend the great hall or wander about without cause.
Since sacred images are enshrined within the hall, one should revere them as if the Buddha were present; how then could one wander about without purpose?
One must not ascend a stūpa without a valid reason.
Even when a stūpa contains no relics or Buddha image, it is still inappropriate to ascend; how much more so when they are present?

If one ascends for the purpose of making offerings such as flowers, banners, or lamps, there is no offense. Thus, the ancient masters said: "Unless there is a specific purpose, one need not ascend the Buddha hall. Etc.
Do not walk through the center of a stupa when it is quiet; do not sweep the ground or add scented water. Even if one possesses merit as vast as the sands of the Ganges, it will be exhausted.
When entering a hall or a stupa, one should circumambulate to the right; one must not turn to the left.

Circumambulating to the right is called auspicious; circumambulating to the left is called inauspicious. When circumambulating the Buddha or a stupa, starting from the east and proceeding toward the south constitutes circumambulating to the right;
it does not mean using one's own hand as the "right. The purpose of circumambulation is to express reverence and longing for the Buddha;
therefore, the Buddha should be positioned to one's right. The *Wenju ji* states: "Turning to the left is eccentric and represents evil; turning to the right..."
It is convenient and serves to manifest goodness. The Buddha’s hair curls to the right, whereas that of ordinary people curls to the left; therefore, one should follow the manner of the Buddha.
One must not spit or discharge nasal mucus within a temple or a stupa.
The *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra* states: "If one spits upon the pure ground of the Buddha or the Saṃgha, by this causal condition, one enters hell.
There, knives amputate one's nose, and one suffers as it is burned by fire without ceasing. This is explained in detail as set forth in the sūtra.
Circumambulating the stupa—whether three times, seven times, or even up to ten or a hundred times—one must know the significance of these counts.
Generally, every number of circumambulations performed out of reverence for the stupa or image has its own symbolic meaning.

Three circumambulations symbolize making offerings to the Triple Gem, eliminating the three poisons, purifying the three types of karma, extinguishing the three evil realms, and attaining the fortune of meeting the Triple Gem. Seven circumambulations eliminate the offenses of the seven branches [of the eightfold path] and attain...

The seven factors of enlightenment. With ten circumambulations, one eliminates the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and attains the ten powers (*bala*) of a Buddha. With a hundred circumambulations, one eliminates a hundred afflictions (*kleśa*) and attains a hundred Dharma gates.
The *Tiwai jing* states: The elder Tiwei addressed the Buddha, saying, "Scattering flowers, burning incense, lighting lamps, and prostrating—these constitute offerings.
What kind of merit is obtained by circumambulating a stūpa? The Buddha said: "Circumambulating a stūpa has..."
There are five merits: first, obtaining a handsome and upright appearance in future lives; second, obtaining a beautiful voice; third, being born in the heavens;
fourth, being born into the family of kings or nobles; and fifth, attaining the path to *nirvāṇa*. By what causes and conditions does one obtain a handsome and upright appearance?
It is because of seeing the image of the Buddha with joy. By what conditions does one obtain a beautiful voice? It is because of circumambulating stupas and reciting the sutras.
Because of these verses: By what cause was rebirth in the heavens attained? Because at the time of circumambulating the stupa, one’s mind did not transgress the precepts.
By what cause was rebirth in the family of kings and nobles attained? Because one turned one’s head to pay homage to the Buddha’s feet. By what cause was the path to nirvana attained?
Because there remains further merit, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states in the verses on circumambulating the stupa:

"When first desiring to circumambulate the stupa, one should wish that all beings practice the bestowal of blessings and bring the aspiration for the Way to full completion. When circumambulating the stupa three times, one should wish that all beings attain a single-minded resolve and never sever the four joys."
One must not lean a rain hat, staff, or other items against the walls of the hall.
It is not the rule for a *śrāmaṇera* to possess a staff; however, one may carry it when traveling far or when old. Upon entering a temple, one must remove the hat and set aside the staff.
If one sees the two teachers, the elders, or venerable seniors, one must place both the staff and the hat on the ground, and only then [proceed].
Inquiring after their well-being: if one is holding a staff for either of the two teachers and the teacher has a question to ask, one must first embrace the staff before responding.

The *Lüshi Chunqiu* states: "Among the disciples of Confucius, some would embrace their staffs when asking about their fathers, lean on their staffs when asking about their brothers, and drag their staffs when asking about their wives and children;
this was because there were distinctions based on rank. If one leans the staff against [a wall or post]...

If one leans against a palace wall, one immediately incurs the offense of disrespect. Thus, in the past, the twenty-fifth patriarch was destined to realize the second fruit [of the path] seven kalpas ago;
however, because he leaned his staff against a palace wall, due to this transgression of pride, he ultimately lost that second fruit.
The *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* states: There was a worthy man who had the marks of a king upon his face. When a physiognomist saw this, he gave his daughter in marriage to him.
Later, when the worthy one entered the temple, he leaned his staff against the temple wall. Because he gave rise to arrogance, he lost the "Wen" chapter of the *Guo Yu* and fell into the Great Hell.
How can one not be cautious?
△ Entering the Meditation Hall and Joining the Assembly, Section Ten:
On the upper bunk, one must not shake one’s robes or bedding to make noise or create drafts that disturb the thoughts of those on neighboring bunks.
This entails three faults: first, it is personally coarse and impulsive; second, it stirs up dust and dirt, defiling others; third, it causes others to become distracted. Furthermore,
Whenever entering the hall, the Vinaya precepts mandate that five rules be observed: first, one must treat others with compassion, respect, and reverence;
second, one should humble oneself and remain modest, like a cloth used for wiping dust; third, one must know the proper timing for sitting, rising, bowing, and looking around;
fourth, one must not engage in idle chatter among the assembly; and fifth, regarding matters that cannot be remedied, one should remain silent.
Descending from the bed, he silently recited this verse: "From the morning dawn until evening, may all sentient beings protect themselves.
If any should lose their lives beneath my feet, I pray that you be reborn immediately in the Pure Land."
Having recited the verse, one should further recite the mantra seven times: *Oṃ dhiri dhiri svāhā*.
One must not speak loudly or with a high voice.
When a śramaṇa utters words, his speech must be respectful and cautious; the tone must be gentle and soft, for only then does it accord with the decorum of a son of the Śākya.
When lifting the curtain with light hands, one must keep the rear hand lowered;
this avoids two faults: first, lack of composure; second, damaging the object. When rolling it up, one must face inward so that both ends are even and neat.
One must not allow sandals to make noise.
Xinghu said: "Whenever wearing shoes or slippers, first ensure the heels touch the ground so that they do not make a sound.
One must not cough or clear one's throat loudly."
Coughing is the expulsion of phlegm with sound; spitting is the expulsion of phlegm without sound.
One must not lean over the neighboring seat to whisper.
Even when discussing the Buddha-dharma, it is inappropriate to whisper; how much more so regarding worldly affairs?
If there are fellow practitioners who regard one with affection, one must not engage in long conversation within the hall;
rather, one should invite them to the woods or by the water to discuss matters with open hearts.
Although it may be granted that one should open one’s heart, this should be limited to matters of the Way; one must not indulge in idle talk about worldly affairs.

As the Zen Master Cishou’s admonition states: "If they are former companions on the path or close relatives from afar, and you are together by the woods or by the water, only then may you open your hearts in discussion.
As for engaging in trade and commerce or attracting miscellaneous people—these are entirely unbecoming of a monastic."
Regarding what is to be done:
if one is reading a scripture, one must sit upright and clarify the mind, contemplating it silently. One must not utter sounds. "Contemplating" (*wan*) means observing and practicing.
This clarifies that the three karmas must be strictly purified: when the body is upright, mindfulness is correct; when the mind is clarified, the principle [is realized].
When the second board sounds, you should promptly enter the hall.
If you arrive early, body and mind will be light and at ease, and all affairs will proceed harmoniously; if you are late, you will be rushed and delusive thoughts will easily arise.
Returning to one's seat, recite the verse silently while sitting upright with the body straight: "May all beings sit upon the seat of enlightenment, their minds free from attachment.
When assuming the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), one should further recite this verse: "As I sit in the full lotus posture, may all beings find firmness in bodhi."
Indeed, one attains the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*).
[Appendix: One must not pass straight through the hall;
one should instead proceed along the front or back. The regulations state: "To pass straight through the hall—would this not be a cause for deep shame? Within the sacred halls..."
When walking, one should fear bringing about meager merit.
Whether on the upper bunk or the lower bunk, one must always conduct oneself with care so as not to disturb the thoughts of those in neighboring bunks.
Indeed, as a śramaṇa and son of the Śākya, one is fundamentally endowed with three thousand modes of dignified demeanor and eighty thousand subtle practices. In all that one raises...
Stop. First, one must be careful with the mind.
One must not write characters alone; this exception applies when the assembly is reading the scriptures and teachings, where "exception" means that it is permitted.
One must not gather together in private to arrange tea, sit through the night, and engage in miscellaneous conversation.
There are three faults in this: first, it stirs discursive thoughts; second, it scatters the mind; third, it violates the prohibition against improper times.
Even if one possesses medicine permitted for improper times, one still ought not to sit through the night engaging in miscellaneous conversation.
