One must not sew or patch clothing and bedding on one’s own bed. One must not lie down or sleep while conversing with those on neighboring beds, as this disturbs the community.
As the Sūtra says: "When eating, do not speak; when sleeping, do not converse. Diligently contemplate the meaning of the teachings and review the old to know the new.
When sitting, practice meditative reflection; when rising, engage in recitation. One whose precepts and conduct are thus is a true disciple of the Buddha.
△ Section Eleven on Handling Affairs:
One should cherish the property of the Sangha.

The *Mahā-vinaya* states: "Guard the property of the permanent Sangha as one would guard one's own eyes. The *Xinghu lü* (Rules for Protecting [the Dharma]) states: "If there is waste or expenditure..."
"Property belonging to the Three Jewels and other such items must be compensated for.

Formerly, at the White Pagoda Temple in Yangzhou, the śramaṇa Daochang was in charge of monastic property, yet he freely embezzled it. Suddenly, several officials from the underworld entered his room during the day."
He dragged Xichang down to the ground, intending to cut off his neck. Startled, Xichang cried out and begged for his life.

The official spoke in a harsh voice, saying, "If you return all the wealth and property of the entire room to the monks, I shall release you and let you live. Xichang prostrated himself and said, "I dare not disobey your command.

He immediately struck the bell to assemble the congregation; they gave away all their clothing and possessions to create images and provide offerings. After three days, the official from the underworld arrived again and saw—

Chang took his single alms bowl and his single robe, departed without a word, and from that time forth exerted himself in diligent cultivation until he ultimately achieved both clear insight and virtuous conduct.
One must follow the instructions of the administrative officials and must not act in opposition to them.
"Contrary" means to act in opposition and lack compliance; "obstinate" means to be stubborn and refuse to submit.
When washing vegetables, one should change the water three times—meaning to replace it.
One should first pick out insects, ants, and the like, and only then wash them.
Whenever drawing water, first wash one's hands. Whenever using water, one must carefully examine it for the presence or absence of insects;
if there are any, one must strain it through a fine cloth before using it. During the severe winter, one must not strain water too early; one must wait until sunrise.
Cold water must be filtered early, for fear that insects might freeze to death. All river and well water must be carefully inspected;

only when it is free of insects may it be used. There are two types of usage: first, for food and drink; second, for washing. The insects in such water are extremely minute and must be scrutinized with great care.
One must not wash one’s hands, face, or perform the large or small excretions therein. There are five kinds of filters: the first...
1. A square gauze filter for secret [mantras]. 2. Two *yīnyáng* (yin-yang) vases. 3. Two *jūnchí* (kunda) vases;

both of these have their openings covered with silk and their necks tied with fine cord, then are submerged in water until full, after which they are drawn out. 4. A water-drawing gauze filter. 5. A five-cornered gauze filter.
Use a square piece of silk about one *zhai* (span) in size; either tie it over the mouth of a jar or place it atop a bowl to filter [the water] before using it.
When building a stove, one must not burn rotten firewood.
Decayed wood contains insects; therefore, it must not be burned. The Sūtra states: "One must not burn green firewood or damp firewood.
Furthermore, when preparing food, one must not have fingernail dirt on one's hands."
The Buddha did not permit the keeping of fingernails; at most, they may be as long as a grain of barley.

If one uses them while they are stained and impure to prepare food, one will receive the retribution of becoming a ghost dwelling in a latrine. The *Piyu jing* (Sutra of Parables) says: There was a śramaṇa who prepared *mopoli* rice.
A bhikṣu, having taken curd and ghee in his hand, wiped it upon a pillar; the pillar immediately split apart. One must be careful! Do not be negligent!

Whenever one discards wastewater, it must not be done in the middle of a path, nor should one lift the hands high to splash it out. One should hold the vessel four or five inches above the ground and discard it slowly.
Wastewater refers to water used for washing vessels or laundering clothes; it must not be poured away in places where people walk.
Whenever sweeping the floor, one must not sweep against the wind, nor must one pile up dust and soil behind the door leaf;
this means that refuse and sweepings must not be heaped up. As the Sūtra says: "When sweeping the floor, one should make it clean so that no tracks remain."
There are those who sweep it away immediately. The *Sūtra of a Hundred Conditions* states: "One gains five merits by sweeping the ground: first, one removes the defilements of one's own mind;
second, one removes the defilements of others; third, one eliminates arrogance; fourth, one subdues the mind; and fifth, one increases merit and is reborn in a favorable realm."
When washing undergarments, one must first pick out the lice before washing them.
The small ones are called *yī* (nits) and the large ones are called *shī* (lice). Only after picking them out cleanly and then washing may one avoid the transgression of harming living beings.
In the summer months, after using a water basin, it must be inverted; if left face-up, insects will breed.
In the summer, insects breed at all times; because there is residual water when the basin is face-up, insects breed.
One must not use a basin used for washing upper garments to wash feet or lower garments, socks, and the like. When drying them on a pole, one must likewise not [use the same pole].
They may touch one another. One must not spray water containing saliva upon the Dharma robes.
One must not pour hot water upon the ground, for this would harm living beings.
Furthermore, one must not extinguish fire by pouring hot water over it.
All grains, flours, fruits, vegetables, and so forth must not be discarded lightly or left in disarray; they must be cherished with care.

If one does not cherish things in this life, there will be nothing to enjoy in future lives. How much more so for the property of the Sangha, which remains permanently—how could one fail to guard and cherish it deeply?
△ Bathing, Number Twelve:
First, wash the face with warm water, proceeding from top to bottom and washing gently.
If there is separate clean water available, it is not appropriate to wash the face with the bathwater. Having finished bathing, one should go outside and use [the following].

Using soap powder or ash and earth, wash both hands thoroughly two or three times, and then wash the face. According to the *Jiǎnwēnshì jīng* (Sūtra on the Warm Bathhouse), bathing can eliminate seven ailments:
first, lightness and ease of the four great elements; second, the removal of wind disorders; third, the removal of numbness and dampness;
fourth, the removal of cold; fifth, the removal of heat; sixth, the removal of filth and impurities; and seventh, clarity of the body and brightness of the eyes. Nevertheless, it also...
One may wash as often as necessary according to the circumstances of the time.
One must not be coarse or impulsive, nor splash hot water or liquid onto one's neighbors. One must not relieve oneself in the bathhouse.
"Relieving oneself" (xiǎoyí) is also referred to as "minor evacuation" (xiǎoxíng), "minor release" (xiǎojiě), "minor purification" (xiǎojìng), or "urination" (xiǎobiàn). [Purification] (jìng).
One must not even neglect the ground, let alone the bathhouse. The *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra* states:
"If a bhikṣu voids excrement or urine on pure ground without choosing a proper place, by this cause and condition, he will enter hell and become a well in a flesh latrine."
They suffer incessantly from being burned by fire. The *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* states:
"If one spits upon ground dedicated to the Sangha, that person will be born as a needle-mouthed insect within a *sāla* tree for twelve years.
If one voids excrement or urine upon ground dedicated to the Sangha, that person will [be reborn] in the great city of Vārāṇasī to void excrement and urine..."
Born among the sharp blades, one becomes a foul-worm. The *Utpalaka-rāja-sūtra* states:
"If one defecates or urinates promiscuously upon the ground within the Gaṇa-dharmadhātu, one will fall into the Bāba Hell for five hundred lifetimes.
For twenty subsequent kalpas, one shall constantly be forced to embrace this defiled earth with one's elbows and hands, even unto the Yellow Springs."
One must not engage in speech or laughter with others. The *Ren-Tian Bao-Jian* states: A certain śrāmaṇera entered the bathhouse and laughed and played;
he subsequently received the retribution of the Boiling Water Hell.
If even the karmic retribution for playful laughter is such as this, the rest may well be known.
One must not wash in secluded places,
specifically those areas used for defecation and urination.
Whenever one has sores or scabies, it is appropriate to bathe last. If there are particularly fearsome sores, one should especially avoid them so as not to prick others' eyes.
"Fearsome sores" refers to malignant ulcers such as carbuncles and abscesses; one must personally avoid them and take water separately for bathing, lest they [infect others].
If one sees others, or if there are people who have already finished bathing, one should bathe last; otherwise, one will diminish merit and incur transgression.
One must not wash at will for a long time, as this obstructs those who follow.
"At will" means to indulge one's passions and let the mind run free. The Sūtra says: "One must not wash clothes therein.
[This refers to] the manner of taking off and putting on clothes; one should do so with composure and ease.
That is to say, one must not be fickle or hasty.
Before bathing, one should first wash oneself clean. One must proceed with careful deliberation; the water used for washing must not be poured into the bath cauldron.
Prior to entering the bath, one should first wash oneself clean according to the Dharma, and having washed one's hands, only then enter the bath. Now...
At that time, there were those who would wash themselves with a little water by the side of the bathhouse, yet fail to wash their hands with ash and earth before entering to bathe;
this was no different from not washing at all. It was extremely filthy, defiling both oneself and others, and the retribution for such an act would not be slight.
When the water has cooled, strike the wooden gong according to custom; one must not shout loudly.
"According to custom" means following the established regulations. Within [the bathhouse], the bathing implements, vessels, and cleansing powder (sādu) and so forth should be arranged properly;
those who use them must also act in accordance with the rules to avoid incurring future calamities, as was seen by Saṃgharakṣita.
13. Entering the Latrine: When one wishes to defecate or urinate, one should go at once;
do not wait until the internal pressure becomes urgent and one is forced to act in haste.
In a sudden emergency, one may easily commit an error of decorum; therefore, one must act promptly.
Hang the *zhiduò* (straight robe) upon a bamboo pole, folding it neatly and securing it with a handkerchief or a waist-cord. This serves two purposes: first, as a marker for identification;
second, to prevent it from falling to the ground.

The *zhiduō* (straight robe). It is traditionally said that former masters, seeing that monks possessed either a *pianshan* (slanted robe) without a skirt (*qún*) or a skirt without a *pianshan*, subsequently combined these two garments into the *zhiduō*.
It should be folded and hung upon a bamboo pole; one enters wearing undergarments beneath it.
According to the Great Vinaya, one must wear a shoulder-covering robe when entering the latrine.
One must remove and change one's shoes; it is not permitted to enter the latrine wearing clean shoes.

One must remove the shoes and put on wooden clogs. If shoes have previously been used for entering the latrine, they must not be worn when treading upon the pure grounds of the Sangha or entering the halls and pavilions.

The retribution one receives shall not be light; the offenses are as described in the sutras. An ancient saying states: "When entering the latrine, do not go bare-chested; when traveling the mountains, do not wear straw sandals;
do not step upon the Dharma Hall; and yield respectfully to the senior monks."
Upon arrival, snap your fingers three times to let those inside know. Do not urge the person inside to come out.
If they do not come out after three snaps of the fingers, you should simply wait for them, or go to another latrine.

Above this, one should again snap the fingers three times and silently recite: "At the time of defecating and urinating, may all sentient beings cast off greed, hatred, and delusion, and eliminate all unwholesome dharmas."

The above refers to ascending to the latrine. These three snaps of the fingers now serve to alert the spirits who consume impurities within the latrine, so that they do not cause offense or mutual harm.
As the *Piyū jīng* (Sutra of Parables) states: There was once a śramaṇa who did not snap his fingers before urinating;
he splashed the face of a spirit in the latrine. The spirit became greatly enraged and intended to kill the śramaṇa. The śramaṇa...
Maintain the precepts; thus, ghosts will find no opportunity.
One must not lower one's head to look down;
looking down may cause impure thoughts to arise. If others arrive later, one must snap one's fingers to alert them.
One must not take grass and draw on the ground,
nor fail to maintain right mindfulness; thus, one may draw on the ground or on walls,
but one must not blow air to make a sound.
First, one loses one's own decorum; second, one disturbs the thoughts of others.
One must not converse with another person through a wall.
The Mañjuśrī Sūtra states: "When defecating or urinating, one must not make a sound with the body, the mouth, wood, or stone."
One must not spit on the walls.
First, for fear of inadvertently touching a non-human being; second, because it causes others to feel revulsion. Furthermore, one must not defile the two edges of the latrine.
When encountering others, one must not perform a formal salutation; it is appropriate to turn the body aside and avoid them.
First, one's own deportment is lacking in reverence; second, the location is an improper place for such conduct.
One must not walk along the road with one's robe or sash tied.
At other times, even when one has removed one's clothes and fastened one's belt, one must not walk along the path, let alone enter the latrine.
Once finished, one should wash one's hands; until they have been washed, one must not handle any objects.

Now, when it says "washing the hands," and does not say "washing for purification," it is an abbreviation. First, one must take the water jar, fill it with water until full, and place it where purification is performed.
If there is no separate place for purification, one may carry it into the latrine; once finished, first wipe with a cloth and afterwards wash with water.
Using the ring finger and little finger of the left hand, scrub and wash until clean, then clench the hand into a fist.
With his left hand [holding the bowl], he draws the robe with his right hand, opens the door, and carrying the water jar, goes out.
Arriving at the place for washing hands, he uses ash or earth to wash his left hand seven times first, then both hands together seven times.

He leaves a small amount of water to rinse the inside and outside of the jar, returns it to its original place, and goes back to his room. There, he rinses his mouth twice or thrice with pure water, and thus the ritual is completed.
This is recorded in detail in the *Mahāvinaya*. Generally, those who act as teachers should instruct according to the Dharma. The Buddha said:
"To wash and purify oneself in this manner brings great benefit. All those who have gone forth, who take refuge in me, and who regard me as their teacher, ought to wash and purify themselves.

If one does not wash and purify oneself according to the Dharma, one should not circumambulate stupas or practice walking meditation, nor is it appropriate for such a person to prostrate to the Buddha."
When reciting sutras, you must not pay homage to others, nor accept the homage of others; you should not consume food, sit upon the monastic seats, or enter among the assembly.
The dhāraṇīs and ritual methods you uphold will all lack efficacy. If you perform offerings for vegetarian feasts, transcribe scriptures, or create images, the merit obtained will be meager and thin.
You all must follow my instructions and teachings; do not deceive yourselves by acting contrary to them.
"Purifying one's karma through indolence and negligence constitutes the conduct of the lowest grade; one shall fall into the evil realms," and so forth.
In the present age, even if there are those who perform ablutions, they do not follow the Dharma at all, but instead result in defilement.
If the master does not instruct the disciple, both will incur transgressions and fall together into the three miserable paths. As the Buddha has taught, how can we not be cautious?
While washing the hands, silently recite: "With water for rinsing the palms, I vow that all sentient beings may obtain pure hands to receive and uphold the Buddha-dharma. Oṃ Cukāraya Svāhā."

Recite the upper verse once; recite the lower mantra seven times. Regarding the mantras for entering the latrine and washing away impurities, each has its own specific incantation, as detailed in other sources.

The *Qinggui* states: According to the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* in the Tripitaka, "If one who ascends the toilet does not recite this mantra, even if they were to wash themselves with the waters of ten Ganges Rivers until reaching the Diamond Realm (Vajra-koti), it would still not [purify them]."
One can purify oneself. Even if there is a small amount of urine in the *vinaya*, one should wash it away as well. Then, using earth, wash the hands once or twice. Appendix:
If one must relieve oneself slightly, one must roll up the sleeves; furthermore, one must not wear a tight-fitting shirt (*biānshān*) while relieving oneself.
If one’s body or robes are defiled by impurities, receiving or offering prostrations will result in an offense. When relieving oneself, one must remain beside the vessel;

one must not relieve oneself inside the vessel, nor make noise, nor emit odors that offend others. A *biānshān* (side-garment) is worn as an undergarment for the Dharma robes and is a garment for performing prostrations;
therefore, it is inappropriate to urinate while wearing it. The *piānshān* (open-fronted robe), moreover, was not originally ordained by the Buddha; rather...

This was created in this region. Formerly, when the Emperor of the Wei dynasty invited monks into the palace for offerings, the palace ladies saw that the monks bared their right shoulders and did not consider it proper.
They consequently fashioned a side-garment (*pianshan*) and attached it to the upper robe (*saṃkakṣikā*) on the left side to cover the shoulder.
Because it covers the right shoulder, it is consequently named *piānshān* (a "partial shirt"). Today, the name "hidden-shoulder-covering garment" has fallen into disuse;
those with two sleeves are generally referred to as *piānshān*. If one wishes to make one, the back seam must be opened and the collar cut away to accord with the original pattern.
△ 14. Sleeping and Lying Down: When lying down, one must lie on the right side; this is called the "Auspicious Sleep. One must not lie on the back, face down, or on the left side.
Whenever lying down, one must use a pillow, or else bend the arm to serve as a pillow. One must not place the head directly upon the mat. To sleep on the back is the manner of the Asuras.
Lying down: covering oneself is the way hungry ghosts lie; lying on the left side is the way those possessed by greed lie. A śramaṇa should lie like a lion king:
with the body aligned, lying on the right side upon the mat, with feet stacked, mouth closed, the head resting on the right hand, and the left hand extended along the body.
Without abandoning mindfulness and wisdom, he should maintain the thought of awakening. Reaching the latter part of the night, he shall immediately rise and sit upright in meditation, reflecting.
One should attend only to one's own karma. Furthermore, one must not lie down making noise. How is it that one lies down like the lion king?
Among all beasts, the lion is foremost in its courage, fortitude, and ferocity.
Likewise, the renunciant is foremost in the courage, fortitude, and ferocity of exerting diligent energy. For these reasons, his manner of lying down accords with the method of the lion king.
It is so. When lying down in this manner, the body is free from agitation, mindfulness is not lost, sleep is not excessive, and one does not see evil dreams;
therefore, it is called auspicious.
One must not share a room or a bed with one's teacher.

If sharing a room is permitted, one must not share a bed, for the purpose of guarding against evil persons and fearing obstacles to the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Therefore, sharing a room is allowed.
Furthermore, one must not share a bed with a novice (śrāmaṇera) who shares the same duties.
"Sharing the same duties" refers to those who perform the same tasks as a novice, or those who study under the same teacher.
For example, when the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita saw two novices in hell lying together, embracing one another, their bodies being scorched by fierce flames and suffering without respite.
The Buddha said, "During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, these two śrāmaṇeras slept together, embracing one another within a single bedding.
Because of this causal condition, they entered hell, where they suffer while being burned by fire, still embracing one another within the bedding, without ceasing even until now."
When hanging shoes, slippers, small garments, and the like, they must not exceed the height of a person’s head or face.
As for all lower-body clothing, they must not be hung high. Appendix:
One must not lie down to sleep while having removed one's undergarments.
The inner robe (*nīveśana*) refers to that which is worn close to the body; whether upper or lower, both are called inner robes.
One must not laugh or speak loudly upon the bed.
While the previous precept forbade speaking while lying down in the meditation hall (*dhyāna-śālā*), this precept forbids making noise while sleeping in one's room.
One must not carry a vessel for excrement or urine past a sacred image or before the Dharma Hall.
"Sacred images" refers to images of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Arhats, or ancestral masters. "Nü" (溺) is equivalent to urine; it refers to urination.
△ Section Fifteen: Around the Hearth.
One must not speak with heads touching or ears whispering. One must not toss soot or grease into the fire.
Head-to-head conversation is the beginning of idle chatter; throwing soot into the fire causes a foul stench to permeate the air. The *Mahā-vinaya* states: "If [hair]..."
If one throws hair, fingernails, mucus, saliva, skin, blood, cakes, fruit, or poisonous medicine into a fire, one incurs an offense in all cases. The *Chinggui* (Rules of Purity) states:
"One must not stir the fire so as to scatter the ashes."
One must not dry shoes or socks over the fire. One must not remain before the fire for too long, lest it hinder those who follow. Once sufficiently warmed, one should promptly return to one’s place.
Both drying oneself and staying too long obstruct others. The *Zhēnguī* (Regulations) states: "When shaving the head and surrounding the brazier, the proper etiquette is as follows..."
[The monks] were modest and yielded. The Buddha said, "There are five faults in warming oneself by a fire: first, it makes one lose one's complexion;
second, it makes one lose one's strength; third, it makes one's eyesight dim; fourth, it causes many people to gather in a noisy crowd; and fifth, it leads to much talk of worldly matters."
△ Regarding dwelling together in a room, the sixteenth [rule] concerns mutual inquiry.
One must know the seniority and juniority [of one's fellow practitioners].

"Inquiry" (pṛcchā) refers to speaking words to ask about one’s age, the number of years since ordination (*varṣa*), as well as whether one’s daily life and activities are peaceful and beneficial, and regarding one’s studies.
Whether progress is made or obstacles encountered, should there be any words regarding gain or loss, I beg that you accept them with joy. Do not let such matters linger overnight.
Do not praise one another behind each other's backs, nor engage in mutual criticism or slander.
If one wishes to enter with a lamp, one should first inform those inside the room, saying, "I am entering with a lamp.
If one wishes to extinguish the lamp, one should first ask the fellow residents, "Is there further need for a lamp?"
When entering, one should announce it beforehand, so as to avoid any breach of decorum or acting with haste. When extinguishing the light, one should inquire in advance whether others may need it.
Furthermore, one must not nail holes in walls or hang lamps or objects thereon; the karmic retribution for such acts is as described in the *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra*.
From time to time, one must inspect the lamps and candles to ensure they do not go out or cause error.
Extinguish the lamp-flame. Do not blow on it with your mouth; chanting must not be done loudly.
Blowing with the mouth violates the ritual decorum and causes a foul odor that offends others, while also harming the insects that feed on the fire.
Furthermore, do not extinguish it by fanning it with your hand. You should instead use an object to snap off the remaining wick and slowly submerge it within the oil. [Chant] loudly.
This is because it moves the thoughts of others.
If there is a sick person, one should attend to them with a mind of loving-kindness from beginning to end.
As a sutra states: "Among the eight fields of merit, nursing the sick is the foremost. In a verse spoken by the Buddha in the *Sūtra on Good Birth*, he said: "A person..."
One should attend to those who are ill and inquire after those in peril and distress. There is retribution for good and evil, just as planting a seed yields fruit.
The World-Honored One is the father; the Sūtras and Dharma are the mother; fellow practitioners are the brothers. It is through these that one attains deliverance.
The Mahāvinaya states: There are five merits in attending to the sick. First, knowing what may be eaten and what may not be eaten; second, [not...]
1. One treats excrement, urine, saliva, and vomit with contempt; 2. one possesses a heart of loving-kindness and compassion; 3. one does not act for the sake of fame or profit; 4.
one is able to provide medical decoctions and medicines until the patient recovers or passes away; 5. one is able to preach the Dharma to the sick, causing them to give rise to joy.
If someone is sleeping, one must not strike objects to make noise, nor speak or laugh loudly;
"noise" (xiǎng) refers to resonance, while "sound" (shēng) refers to the echo of an object.
One must not enter another's room or courtyard without a valid reason.
That is to say, because there is no business [there], one must not enter another’s quarters or courtyard lightly.
△ Upon arriving at a nunnery (seventeenth), one should sit only when there is a separate seat; if there is no separate seat, one must not sit.
"Sitting separately" means not sitting on the same seat as a nun, for men and women must be distinguished and their seats must be divided.
Therefore, one must not engage in untimely discourse.
That is to say, when it is not the appropriate time for teaching the Dharma, one should not speak to them.
Furthermore, upon returning, one must not discuss their merits or faults;
that is, one must not deliberate upon their right or wrong, their good or bad qualities, nor even their physical appearance.
One must not engage in the exchange of letters, nor in activities such as borrowing, cutting, or washing.
"Letters" (shu) are used to convey one's thoughts; "memoranda" (shu) are used to set forth specific matters. "Borrowing" (jia) means to lend; "cutting and sewing" (caige) refers to mending;

"washing and laundering" (xiuan) refers to soaking and cleaning clothes and so forth. All these are prohibited because they are feared to give rise to shame and defilement, as well as to invite censure and slander. Therefore, they are not permitted.
Furthermore, one must not use one's own hands to clean the hair;
that is, one must not personally shave it with one's own hands. Chengfan says: "Nor should one hold the hair while instructing another to shave it."

One must not enter the kitchen to instruct others in the preparation of fine foods unless specifically assigned by one's teacher. Even when passing through the gate of a nunnery, one must not enter without permission.
One must not sit together with a nun in a secluded place.
First, one becomes gradually influenced by worldly attachments throughout one's life. Second, it causes others to harbor doubts and engage in slander.
[Appendix: There must not be two people; one may not enter alone, nor may one exchange gifts with another.
To enter alone invites public censure, and the exchange of gifts is unsuitable for those who have left the household life.
One must not entrust nuns with entering the homes of the wealthy and noble to solicit for alms, nor request that they recite sutras or perform repentance rites.
By requesting such recitations and repentances, one loses one's own purity and loftiness; by entrusting them with soliciting for alms, one invites the derision and suspicion of others.
One must not perform the ritual of bowing to parents, sisters, or fellow practitioners with *bhikṣuṇīs*.
First, this gives rise to worldly suspicion; second, it creates the heavy burden of binding oneself to them in future births and deaths.
This is utterly contrary to what should be done by a son of the Śākya who has left the world.
△ When arriving at a layperson’s home (Chapter 18):
If there is a separate seat, one should sit upon it. One should not sit in a mixed manner;
that is, one must not sit intermingled with the laity, but should instead sit on a distinct seat of one's own. Furthermore, one must not squat.

Sitting cross-legged, sitting with legs spread like a winnowing basket, sitting with legs crossed at the ankles, sitting while swaying the body, sitting while swinging the feet, or rising and sitting repeatedly—when people ask about the sutras, one should know the proper time;
be careful not to give teachings at an inappropriate time.

If the questions are posed in jest or as challenges, one should not speak at all. One must observe the faculties and capacities of the person before them—what kind of Dharma they are fit to hear and how much should be taught—and must not exceed that limit.
The *Yize jing* (Sūtra on Ritual Procedures) states: "To preach the Dharma in a manner that does not accord with the recipient's capacity."
Upon hearing this, his heart was not gladdened; at the end of his life, he underwent great suffering. The Great Sūtra says:

"If there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, copy, or proclaim [the teachings], yet do so at improper times or in improper lands, preach without being requested, with a frivolous mind, showing contempt for others, praising themselves, or preaching indiscriminately in any place—this will instead extinguish the Buddha-dharma, even causing immeasurable people to die and fall into hell. This refers to such persons.
They are evil associates for sentient beings. The *Mahāvinaya* states: there are five kinds of people who inquire about the Dharma to whom one must not speak.

First, those who inquire out of a desire to test; second, those who inquire without doubt; third, those who do not inquire for the sake of repenting their transgressions; fourth, those who inquire without intending to accept the words;
fifth, those who inquire for the sake of refutation and debate. To these, one must not provide answers. However, if the person before one truly possesses a good heart...

If one does not possess the five aforementioned qualities, yet wishes to give rise to the wholesome and extinguish the unwholesome, one may preach with a benevolent mind using skillful means according to the individual's capacity.
However, if one’s own understanding is not yet clear, or if one harbors doubts regarding the Dharma, then one must not preach for others,
lest the preceding person incur the fault of erroneous transmission, whereby both parties would commit an offense.
One must not laugh excessively,
nor laugh foolishly, laugh wildly, or laugh without cause; for all such instances arise from a distracted mind,
whereby one loses self-respect and incurs the derision of others.
When the host provides food, even though it is not a formal dharma assembly, one must not neglect the ritual protocols.
Whenever receiving food, one must maintain dignified deportment and follow the prescribed rules; this should be no different from the procedures for a communal meal during a dharma assembly.
Thus, the *Caryāgīti* states: "When entering the homes of laypeople, one must maintain dignified deportment in sitting and rising; one's speech should be kind and gentle, and one must not be coarse."
Be fierce [in discipline]. Do not speak of worldly matters; you should speak of the Dharma to increase their wholesome minds. Constantly restrain the six sense faculties and do not be negligent.
Do not commit the offense of walking about at night.
At night, do not leave [the monastery]. You must return to the temple early.
One must never sit or converse with a woman in an empty room or a secluded place. This is for two reasons:
first, to fear that one might gradually become defiled and develop worldly passions; second, to avoid causing others to speak ill of you.
One must not engage in the exchange of letters and so forth, as previously stated;

as previously stated. Just as one may not lend items to a *bhikṣuṇī* for cutting, sewing, or washing, if one goes to a layperson’s home to visit relatives, one should first enter the central hall to pay homage to the Buddha, or to the sacred images in the family shrine, and inquire after them with dignified composure.
Inquiry: Next, one should inquire after the health of one's parents and kinsmen, one by one.
This act of inquiry consists merely of joining the palms and bowing the head; a long salutation (changyi) is also acceptable.

If there are images of the Buddha or Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva in the home, one should prostrate before them. If there are images of deities associated with incense and offerings, it is appropriate only to join the palms and bow the head.
When with one's parents and others, one should inquire after their well-being and daily activities.
One must not speak to one's parents of the strictness of the Teacher’s Dharma, the hardships of leaving the household life, or matters such as its solitude, austerity, and bitter toil;
rather, one should explain the Buddha-Dharma for them, so that they may give rise to faith and increase their merit.
If one speaks of matters such as the teacher’s strict discipline and arduous hardships, it causes parents to give rise to feelings of affection for their own children;
consequently, they fail to develop a sense of reverence toward the Triple Gem and thus remain long submerged in the ocean of suffering.

If, however, one explains the Buddha-dharma for them, they will give rise to faith and respect, their merit and wisdom will increase, and they will transcend saṃsāra—this is what is meant by "delivering one's father."
The mother has emerged from the bitter sea of birth and death;
she must not sit or stand for long periods with laypeople or young children, nor engage in miscellaneous conversation or playful laughter.
Furthermore, she must not inquire about the right and wrong, or the good and bad, within her own clan.

To sit or stand with children and laugh with them is not the proper decorum for one who has left the household life. To inquire about the worldly matters of right and wrong, or good and evil, defiles one's own mind-ground.
If you must stay overnight because it is late, you should occupy a single mat alone; sit much and sleep little, reciting the Buddha’s name with a single-minded focus until your task is finished.
He immediately returned;
he must not linger, nor share a bed, coverlet, or mat with children, servants, or slaves. Therefore, he dwells alone on a single couch to guard against obstacles to the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Furthermore, so as to inspire faith and reverence in others, he sits much and sleeps little, thereby remaining detached from the realm of delusive thoughts. Thus it is said.
Single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name and constantly remember the teacher’s instructions, as a child remembers its mother;
therefore, do not linger. Appendix: Do not look to the left or right with a sidelong glance; do not engage in idle chatter.
If you must speak with a woman, do not speak in a low voice or in secret; do not speak excessively.
One speaks without partiality; therefore, one does not speak in low voices or in secret. One’s speech accords with the Dharma; therefore, one does not engage in frivolous talk or excessive speech.
One must not feign dignified deportment or falsely assume the appearance of meditative absorption in order to seek the respect of others.
Although a śramaṇa possesses dignified deportment, he must not feign it to seek respect; although he possesses meditative silence, he must not affect it to solicit fame.
He must not speak of the Buddha-dharma recklessly or answer others' questions in a confused manner, nor sell his own learning to seek the veneration of others.
They falsely expound the Buddha-dharma, claiming it has no systematic foundation; thus, they lose the essential meaning and respond in confusion.
Seeking respect through such confused responses and loss of the essential meaning, they instead incur the contempt of others.
One must not send gift boxes. To engage in the coming and going of laypeople—sending gifts and receiving returns—is the conduct of householders;
it is a worldly entanglement and is not appropriate for a son of the Śākya. As the Buddha said in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*:
"If there are goods belonging to the permanent monastic community from the four directions, or goods belonging to the resident monastic community, [and they are offered by] those of sincere faith..."

If one privately consumes items donated by a donor out of sincere devotion—whether they be flower gardens, fruit orchards, food and drink, necessities of life, bedding, mattresses, sleeping requisites, medicinal decoctions, or anything else required—or if one gives them away to acquaintances, relatives, or laypeople; [this constitutes an offense].
This offense is heavier than the retribution received in the Avīci Hell. Furthermore, a verse says:
"Better to use a sharp blade to cut one's own body—its limbs, joints, skin, flesh, and members—than for a layperson to consume the objects given through faith;
such an act is truly difficult to endure. Better to swallow a great, glowing red iron ball, with flames blazing from the mouth..."
[The Buddha] said: "All food and utensils belonging to the Saṃgha must not be given to laypeople or used for private purposes, and so forth.
Furthermore, one must not use property belonging to the Saṃgha to hoard goods for trade, buying low and selling high to compete with the world for profit.
Nor may one say, 'This is my own property,' and eat apart from the assembly. This is like when in the past Maudgalyāyana took the bhikṣu Puṇya-vardhana [into the assembly]."
While traveling by sea, they saw a great *nyagrodha* tree surrounded by many insects devouring its body, leaving not a single empty space among its branches and leaves.
It let out a great cry that shook the air like the sounds from hell. Puṇyavardhana asked Maudgalyāyana, and Maudgalyāyana replied:
"This tree was once a *karmadāna* (steward) bhikṣu who used the flowers, fruits, and food belonging to the monastic community (*saṃgha*) to send them to others."
"White-robed one, you now receive this retribution of flowers; later, you shall fall into hell. Those insects that devour the tree are precisely those who took the property.
Furthermore, at Shengguang Temple in the Western Capital of Tang, there was the śramaṇa Xiaozhi. His relatives and associates frequently visited him, and he would feed them temple fruits.
Before long, he contracted a disease of vomiting blood. He said himself that whenever the illness was about to flare up, he saw red...

The messenger who had brought the robe led him to the Black Forest (*Kālavana*), where a great wind blew away the branches and joints. A short while later, he was led again toward a terrace and pavilion.
There stood a person of terrifying appearance, who rebuked him in a harsh voice, saying, "How could you feed the fruits of the monastery to your relatives?
Having spoken, he vanished. Filled with dread, Sengzhi immediately calculated the value and repaid it to the assembly of monks. It was more than a month before...
Exempted. Such cause and effect are clearly manifest; how can those who hear this not be afraid?
One must not manage the household affairs of others, for there are three faults in doing so:
first, one develops a dog-like mind; second, the family members harbor resentment and dislike; third, outsiders engage in slander and ridicule.
One must not sit intermingled at banquets where alcohol is served;
this is most unbecoming for those who have left the household life, as all manner of transgressions arise from such occasions.
One must not formally adopt laypeople as one's parents or sisters.
In the present age, there are quite many of such types. All this results from the initial thought of leaving the household life being incorrect;

thus they fall into perversion without realizing it themselves. Therefore, the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says: "To abandon one's kin, cast off affection and love, dwell in an araṇya, and practice samādhi, yet further bind oneself with those of different surnames as brothers, parents, and so forth—this is the height of perversion."
One must not speak of the faults within the Saṃgha.

Since people are not sages or philosophers, who is able to be without fault? When Kāśyapa rose to dance, even Yao and Shun were considered flawed by him. If one lacks the eye of wisdom oneself, how can one examine the errors of others?
The virtues of the Saṃgha are like the ocean, as the Buddha himself praised; if one gives rise to slanderous speech, one brings calamity upon oneself.
The Retribution of Suffering.
△ Chapter Nineteen: Begging for Alms.
One should always be accompanied by an elderly person. If there is no one to accompany one, one must know the places where it is appropriate to go.
There are ten benefits to begging for alms: first, one’s livelihood belongs to oneself and not to others;

second, one causes those who give me food to abide in the Three Jewels before partaking of it; third, one constantly gives rise to a heart of compassion; fourth, one accords with the Buddha’s teachings;

fifth, one is easy to support and easy to satisfy; sixth, one breaks the banner of pride; seventh, one possesses the roots of goodness that are invisible even to the Buddha’s crown; eighth, [one becomes an example for] other virtuous people...
See this and you should emulate it. Ninth, do not associate intimately with men or women. Tenth, beg in sequential order to give rise to a mind of equanimity;
if one is together with elders and senior monks, then faults will not arise. One should avoid the five types of households;

therefore, these are called the places where one may go: first, the household of a public crier; second, the household of a prostitute; third, the household of a wine-seller; fourth, the royal palace; fifth, the slaughterhouse.
Entering the homes of others, one should carefully examine one’s conduct; one must not lose one’s dignified demeanor.
"Conduct" refers here to both movement and stillness. "Carefully" means to attentively observe one's own demeanor so that it remains orderly and composed.
If there are no men in the house, one must not enter the door.
This is for two reasons: first, to prevent others from harboring doubts or slander; second, to guard against obstacles to the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
If one wishes to sit, one should first inspect the seat. If there are weapons or blades, it is not appropriate to sit; if there are precious objects, it is not appropriate.
As for sitting: if there is a woman whose clothing and ornaments are finely adorned, it is inappropriate to sit.
Regarding "observing": this means examining. As for "weapons," these refer to the implements of warfare, such as swords, axes, spears, halberds, bows, and arrows;
if one sits [in their presence], one will certainly be wounded, or it may cause them to give rise to anger; therefore, it is inappropriate to sit. As for "precious objects": [the same applies].
Furthermore, sitting upon such items as women’s clothing invites public censure. Should one later suffer some misfortune, it will give rise to suspicion within oneself;
therefore, it is also improper to sit upon them.
When wishing to preach the sūtra, one should know the proper time for preaching and the improper time.
If there is no man or elderly person nearby, or even when it involves playful questioning and the like, these are all improper times for preaching.
If there is one who possesses faith, for the sake of distinguishing the precepts, concentration, and wisdom, and to cause their faith and reverence to increase—this is the proper time to speak.
One must not say, "Give me food, so that you may obtain merit."
Reflecting upon what virtue or conduct of my own has caused others to obtain merit, and that I myself have gained food through self-praise—should I not feel shame?
Appendix: In all begging for alms, one must not beg piteously or demand with importunity.
To beg piteously is to lose one's own purity and loftiness; to press harshly for alms causes others to feel revulsion.
One must not speak extensively of cause and effect in hopes of receiving much charity, for such a mind harbors expectation.
Even if only a small amount is given, it should not be accepted. This is the constant law of all Buddhas; thus, one should preach the Dharma to them.
After [the donor] has made the offering according to the Dharma, the Buddha does not accept it; how much less could he accept it with a mind of expectation?
If one receives much, do not give rise to greedy attachment; if one receives little, do not give rise to distress.
All food and drink originate from excrement and soil; therefore, do not give rise to greedy attachment. They are intended merely to treat the ulcer of hunger;
obtaining just enough to sustain the body is sufficient, so do not give rise to distress.
One must not exclusively seek food from the homes of familiar donors or from familiar monasteries out of a lack of fear of causing others annoyance.
Because one repeatedly visits such familiar places without any sense of shame, one constantly solicits food from others. The Buddha said:
"Even animals fear being asked for alms; how much more so should humans?"
△ Entering a Village (20): One must not enter a village due to specific circumstances.

"Village" (*grāma*) means a multitude; "settlement" (*niveśana*) means a dwelling. It is called a "village" because it is a place where many people dwell together. [End of] the specific circumstances.
This is for the sake of the eternal endurance of the Triple Gem, or for matters of vital importance concerning one's teachers and parents;

it is not for the purpose of soliciting alms or for one's own private affairs. Unless there is such an urgent necessity, one must not lightly enter a village, lest one defile one's own six sense faculties.
Or they may be offended by others. The *Buddhaghoṣa-sūtra* states: "When bhikṣus reside in a village, though their bodies and speech are diligent, all Buddhas grieve for them.

When bhikṣus dwell in the mountains, setting aside worldly affairs and resting in peace, all Buddhas rejoice. Therefore, an ancient worthy said: "The Buddhas and Patriarchs rebuke monks who dwell in city walls;
the sages of old all hid themselves in mountain caves. From the mountain springs, the water flows out into the human world."
Go! Though the clear water remains, it becomes turbid waves;
one cannot gallop.
"Gallop" (chí) means to run at full speed.
One must not walk while swinging one's arms;
this refers to letting the hands hang down and dangling the arms. *Xinghu* states:
"One must not let the hands hang down for more than eight paces," and "one must not walk while repeatedly looking sideways at people or objects."

This refers to looking to the left and right. *Xinghu* states: "In walking, one should always look straight ahead, observing the ground for a distance of seven feet, so as not to tread upon and harm insects or ants.
One must not walk while conversing or laughing with śrāmaṇeras or children."
First, it causes one's own body and mind to be distracted; second, it prevents those who see one from developing faith and respect. The *Qinggui* states:
"One must not walk together with another hand-in-hand, nor discuss the是非 (right and wrong) of worldly affairs."
One must not walk in front of or behind a woman, nor walk in front of or behind a *bhikṣuṇī*. There must be a distinction between monastics and laypeople;
men and women must be kept separate so as not to invite the censure or slander of others and bring disgrace upon the path of the Dharma.
If one encounters them on the road, one should skillfully avoid them. As the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "If a *bhikṣu* fears an ill reputation..."
Thus, one is free from all faults; furthermore, one does not even approach eunuchs or women, nor walk a single step along the same path with them.
One must not travel before or behind, following one another, with those who are intoxicated or insane.
Wherever one travels, there will inevitably be things that cause harm. Upon encountering them on the road, one should immediately avoid them from afar, or take a different path.
In all cases, one must also keep a great distance from vehicles, horses, mad dogs, predatory beasts, and the like.
One must not look at women with lingering or lingering glances.

As the Buddha said in a verse in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "It would be better to have red-hot copper wire wound around one's eyes than to look upon the forms of women with a distracted and lustful mind."
One must not look at women from the corners of one's eyes.
As the Sūtra says: "Restrain the six sense-faculties; do not gaze upon beautiful forms. Let the eyes not look about; let the mind harbor no thoughts of lust; let the mouth utter no flirtatious words;
let one’s tracks not be sought after; do not share a boat; if you meet on the road, do not converse; and if you carry unusual items..."
Do not look around.
If you encounter a venerable elder or a close acquaintance, both should stand to one side; they shall first inquire after your well-being with a friendly greeting.
If you meet a spiritual friend, whether ordained or lay, on the road, you must both stand by the side of the path and wait until they have passed.
One should first lower one’s head, join one’s palms, and ask: "Where are you going? Once they have answered, one should say:

"May you travel well. To say "may you travel well" means: may they be free from illness, water, fire, armies, thieves, poisonous insects, and royal calamities in this present life, and may they travel back and forth between the realms of humans and devas in the future.

If one encounters performances such as theatrical illusions, strange spectacles, and the like, it is in every way improper to watch them; rather, one should walk with the body upright and the mind directed straight ahead.

By concentrating the mindfulness, the body becomes upright; by not looking about, one proceeds on a straight path. "Theatrical" refers to singing, chanting, and all manner of acrobatic or performative arts.
"Illusions" refers to sorcery that manifests various transformations to delude people. "Strange spectacles" refers to [the aforementioned].
This refers to anything that causes alarm to the heart and eyes.

Whenever one encounters a water pit or a gap in the water, one must not leap over it; if there is a path, one should walk around it. If there is no path and everyone else leaps over, then one may do so as well.
Even if one has obtained [a horse], one must first assess one's own physical capacity and wait until there are companions before attempting to leap over [obstacles].
Unless there is a medical reason or an urgent matter, one must not ride a horse; nor, even with a playful mind, may one whip it to gallop at full speed.

*Zòu* (驟) is pronounced *zōu*. To gallop a horse is called *chí* (馳); to move with extreme speed is called *zòu* (驟). According to the Great Code (*Dàlǜ*), those who are aged or infirm are permitted to ride, provided they do not ride mares.
Female mounts are to be assigned separately.
Appendix: Whenever one encounters government officials, regardless of their rank, one must always yield the way.
One may retreat to stand before someone’s doorway, stand upright beneath a eaves, or stand respectfully by the roadside; only after they have passed may one proceed.
If one encounters those engaged in fighting or quarreling, one should likewise avoid them from afar; one must not stay to watch.
To watch constitutes a loss of decorum and may even invite misfortune. The *Mahāvinaya* states:
"If one watches elephants, oxen, horses, or even chickens fighting, as well as people quarreling, one incurs an offense."
You must not return to the temple and boast about the magnificent sights you have seen in the city.
Such magnificence is a robber that ruins the human mind and a cause for the suffering of saṃsāra.

Ancient sages who were guests of the transcendent world did not allow their eyes to encounter improper sights, nor did they allow their mouths to speak the vulgar talk of the marketplace and the alleys.

To remain unstained by worldly dust is not something worthy of boasting; rather, it is only when one contemplates suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self that one truly acts in accordance with what is fitting for a son of the Śākya.
△ Section Twenty-one on Market Goods:
There is no nobility or baseness in disputes;
one must repay according to the season. One must not give less, for that would diminish the other's profit. Nor should one give too much, for that would waste the trust [placed in you].
To give as a permanent endowment is called *shichang*.
A place where women sit to sell goods,
a shop where merchandise is displayed, is called a *si*.
If you are wronged by another, employ skillful means to avoid them and do not seek justice from them;
"justice" (zhí) here refers to price. If you are being encroached upon or disputed over a purchase by another, you should simply withdraw and avoid them well.
Having already promised to purchase item A, even if item B is subsequently cheaper, one must not abandon the former to take the latter, thereby causing the original owner resentment.

This principle applies whether A comes first and B later; that is, once one has already promised to buy a certain person's goods, even if something cheaper appears later, one may not abandon that previously agreed-upon expensive item to take the later, cheaper one, causing the original owner of the goods to feel anger and regret. Furthermore, such a person is not a practitioner of the Way.
...the mind.
Be careful not to act as a guarantor and cause others to incur faults or debts.

To place one's trust in another is called "acting as a guarantor" (*pao-jen*). "Fault" (*ch'ien*) refers to transgressions; "debt" (*fu*) refers to liabilities. If one acts as a guarantor for another...
Such transgressions and debts will ultimately result in resentment and slander, thereby inviting calamity and misfortune upon oneself.
△ Twenty-second: In all actions one undertakes, one must not act according to one's own will;
whenever entering or leaving, going or returning, one should first inform the teacher.

The *Mahāvinaya* states: "There are only five matters for which one need not inform the teacher; apart from these, every single action must be reported to the teacher, and failing to do so constitutes an offense.
These five are: first, chewing a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*); second, drinking water; third, defecating; fourth, urinating;

and fifth, circumambulating a Buddha stūpa within the boundary (within forty-nine *vyāma*). The teacher shall then gauge the matter and the timing, granting permission for the disciple’s advancement or withdrawal."
When making a new *dharma-cīvara*, one must first inform the teacher. When wearing a new *dharma-cīvara*, one must first inform the teacher.
By "dharma-cīvara" is meant the *saṃkakṣikā* and the *nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī*. Even if it is not a *dharma-cīvara*, but merely a new garment, one must in all cases inform the teacher.
The teacher shall examine its provenance, as well as the color and craftsmanship of the robe, to determine whether it conforms to the Dharma or not.
One should then dye it, fashioning its color, dimensions, and measurements so that they accord with the Dharma; therefore, it is called a "Dharma robe.
When shaving the head, one must first inform the teacher, saying:
"So-and-so shall shave my head, [I,] such-and-such a person. Only after the teacher grants permission may one shave it.
When taking medicine for an illness, one must first inform the teacher.

As soon as one perceives that there is an ailment, one should immediately inform the teacher so that he may know it. Whatever medicine one intends to take, one must take it only after the teacher has granted permission.
When performing affairs on behalf of the Saṃgha, one must first inform one's teacher.
Furthermore, if the teacher has instructions to give, there would otherwise be the fault of failing to attend to them; therefore, it is necessary to inform him first.
If one intends to privately prepare items such as paper or pens, one must likewise first inform the teacher.
The use of paper and brush may hinder the primary duties of meditation and recitation; therefore, one should prepare them only after obtaining the Master’s permission.
If one intends to chant the scriptures or perform *geya* (hymns), one must first inform the Master.
*Geya* refers to the chanting of praises in Sanskrit (*brahma-svara*). Whenever one first begins to chant or recite, one must first announce it to him.
If a person receives an object as a gift, they should first inform their teacher and only then accept it. When one gives one's own property as a gift to another, one should first inform the teacher;
once the teacher has given permission, one may then give it.
The teacher must grant permission before one receives; the teacher must give only after having granted leave. Only then can one avoid criticism.

Later, fearing the fault of others following one’s own example in lending things, one should first inform the teacher when desiring to borrow from another. Only after the teacher has granted leave should one lend. If one wishes to borrow an object from another person, [one should likewise act with due care].
One must first inform one's teacher. Only when the teacher grants permission may one go.

Since one’s wisdom and insight are not yet profound, how could one possibly discern what is appropriate or inappropriate? Therefore, it is necessary to inform the teacher first. If the teacher grants leave, only then should one take [the object].
If one does not know the proper timing, errors and omissions are difficult to remedy.
When requesting permission from the teacher, whether it is granted or not, one must always perform a prostration. If permission is not granted, one must harbor no resentment.

Regarding all matters brought before the teacher, one must follow the teacher’s instructions regardless of whether they are granted or not. If a feeling of displeasure arises in the mind, one immediately incurs a transgression.

Appendix: Even for major matters—whether traveling abroad, attending lectures, joining the assembly, staying in the mountains, or undertaking projects involving external conditions—one must always inform one’s teacher;
one must not act on one's own authority.
In all matters of conduct and action, one must not act according to one's own whims; therefore, it is said that "all should be reported to the teacher.

"Traveling abroad" refers to visiting and seeking instruction from spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). "Listening to lectures" refers to hearing the exposition of the holy teachings of the Tripiṭaka. "Entering the assembly" refers to entering among the community of great monks.
"Guarding the mountain" refers to protecting the bamboo, timber, and other assets of the monastery gate. "Generating conditions" refers to undertaking and establishing [religious] projects.
Regarding temples, the commissioning of statues, and other such matters: wandering about to seek out such opportunities was originally not something a śrāmaṇera ought to do.
A śrāmaṇera should instead focus on training in meditation and recitation; once these are mastered, it will never be too late to engage in those other activities.
△ Section Twenty-Three: On Traveling Afar.
To travel afar, one must rely upon a good companion.

A "good companion" refers to a virtuous friend. The *Book of Rites* (*Liji*) states: "Those who share the same school are called companions (*peng*); those who share the same aspirations are called friends (*you*). [This is] from the *Shunzheng* (Correcting the Sequence).
The Treatise says: "A virtuous friend is the root of all practices. Thus, the *Huan-yü jīng* (Sūtra of Joyful Delight) states:
"A worthy friend is the foundation of ten thousand blessings. In this life, one avoids the prisons of kings; at death, the gates to the three miserable realms are closed."
Ascending to heaven and attaining the Way—all these are aided by the assistance of virtuous friends. Guishan said: "A long journey requires the help of good companions;
they repeatedly purify one's ears and eyes. It is said: "Those who give birth to me are my parents; those who perfect me are my friends.
One assists in benevolence through friendship and evaluates people accordingly. Thus, good friends possess the merit of mutual polishing, refining one until completion.
The function of the vessels of the Dharma is like crossing a great ocean, where the sail and the rudder must work in concert.
For this reason, the Tathāgata has commanded that you respect one another as you would the World-Honored One. Study and practice for yourselves;

like a person traveling at night without a lamp, it is better to wander alone than to associate with evil companions who will damage your right conduct. Therefore, abandon external conditions and inscribe these names [as a reminder]. Do not follow what is false.
A bad friend is as fearsome as a wolf or a tiger; a good guide and virtuous companion is as close as one's own parents.
Chengfan said: "In choosing friends, be like Yunyan, Daowu, Xuefeng, and Yantou; it would be a great fortune indeed to encounter such individuals once in a hundred generations.
Alternatively, those whose insight is slightly superior and whose aspirations and conduct are largely the same may also serve as friends. However, if there is even a slight [disparity]...
It is not so; it would be better not to have them at all. The *Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa* (Heart of the Bodhisattva Sutra) says:
"All Bodhisattvas who cultivate the supreme path should know these four essential dharmas: first, to draw near to virtuous friends; second, to hear the true Dharma;
third, to contemplate according to principle; and fourth, to practice and realize according to the Dharma. Throughout the ten directions, one...
All Great Holy Lords cultivate these four dharmas to realize Bodhi. The *Inga-kyō* (Sutra on Cause and Effect) states: "A friend has three essential dharmas:
first, upon seeing a fault, one should promptly admonish and instruct; second, upon seeing a good deed, one should deeply give rise to sympathetic joy;
third, when in the midst of suffering or calamity, one does not abandon the other. Such words as these are the maxims of the Buddhas and Patriarchs for ten thousand generations.
This is an excellent rule. How could it not be deeply believed?
Those of antiquity whose minds were not yet enlightened traveled thousands of li to seek a teacher;
those of old whose minds were not yet clear sought out wise mentors, not considering even a thousand li too far. Chengfan said:
Now, in seeking a teacher for the sake of the Dharma, there is certainly no lack of need for careful discernment.

If you have not yet clearly perceived or deeply understood them, you must be cautious not to follow the mere rumors of others and hastily judge their relative importance or intimacy. To speak according to the reality of the matter, this concerns the hall and chambers of the Patriarchs and Buddhas.
He remained silent for a long time. Furthermore, among the masters and teachers of various regions, those who seek out the wild and uncouth are rare. Appendix:
Being young in age and shallow in precepts, you are not permitted to travel far. Should you travel, you must not journey together with those of ill character.
Those who are base are evil companions. Guishan said: "Associating with the wicked grows one's evil views;

creating evil morning and night, one receives retribution in this very life, and after death, one sinks into the depths. Once one loses the human body, ten thousand kalpas will pass before it is regained."

One must seek out teachers and inquire after the Way to resolve the matter of birth and death; it is inappropriate to merely gaze at mountains and play by waters, seeking only to travel far and wide to show off to others.
Regarding unsurpassed bodhi, no one other than a wise teacher can provide guidance; therefore, one must seek a master and inquire after the Way.

On the long journey through birth and death, delusion and awakening depend upon oneself; thus, one must personally exercise discernment. What benefit do gazing at mountains and playing by waters bring to the body and mind?

What benefit is gained by showing off one's vast learning? It does not increase the flavor of the Way. For those who are truly preoccupied with birth and death, what leisure do they have for such matters?
Wherever you arrive, set down your luggage; you must not enter the hall directly. One person shall watch over the luggage while the other...
A person should first enter to inquire after [the master's] well-being and ascertain the monastery’s regulations before settling their luggage and entering the interior.

"Luggage" (xínglǐ) may be used interchangeably with "traveling provisions" (xínglǐ), or referred to as "packing bags" (zhuāngbāo); it refers to the travel satchel, which is indispensable for anyone traveling afar.
Monastic systems vary and rules differ; there is no fixed protocol, and one must act according to the specific circumstances.
Therefore, it is said that one must take its constant abiding and movement before it can be properly settled and brought inside.
△ Second, Fourth, and Fifth: The Name and Characteristics of the Robe.
The robe consists of twenty-five strips. In Sanskrit, it is called *antarvāsa*; in Chinese, it is called the "inner dwelling robe" (*zhōngsù yī*).
This refers to that which stays close to the body.
It is also called the "lower garment" (*antaravāsaka*),
meaning that among the three robes, this is the one worn most underneath.
It is also called the "variegated work robe" (*zàzuò yī*).
This refers to the garment worn when performing various manual tasks within the monastery grounds.
Whenever one performs labor or service within the temple, or travels to and fro on the roads, one should wear this robe.
The details regarding the length of the ritual procedures are fully explained in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-vinaya*.
The verse for donning the robe says: "Excellent is this garment of liberation, The supreme field of merit. I now receive it upon my head;
May I never be parted from it in life after life. *Oṃ siddhye svāhā.*
In this verse, the first two lines state the name and meaning, while the latter two lines constitute a vow, for a cause invites its corresponding fruit.
The syllable "Oṃ" and those that follow are mantra-words; they cannot be explained through conventional terminology.
Furthermore, there are many names and meanings for the three robes (*tricīvara*): they are called the "armor of patience," because they can subdue all māras; they are also called "lotus garments."
Because it is not defiled by the mire of desire, it is also called the "Dragon-Saving Robe";

because if a dragon obtains even a single thread of it, it will not be devoured by the *garuḍa* bird, it is now called the "Robe of Liberation," for through it one is liberated from the afflictions of birth and death.
It is also called the "Field of Merit Robe," because it can give rise to manifold virtues. As for its being "unsurpassed," it means that this robe is endowed with...
Regarding the aforementioned efficacy: from the heavens above to the earth below, even among the robes of the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*), none can surpass this robe.
Therefore, the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time all don this robe to realize the fruit of the Way.
Other meanings need not be recorded here at length.
The seven-strip robe: in Sanskrit, *uttarāsaṅga*; this is translated as "upper garment.
This means that among those garments worn on a regular basis, this one is worn above them.
It is also called the "Assembly-Entry Robe," meaning it is worn when entering among the community of monks.

Whenever one performs prostrations to the Buddha, practices repentance, recites sutras, practices seated meditation, attends a meal offering or a lecture, or participates in the *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā* ceremonies, one should wear this.
*Āvāsa*.
*Poṣadha*, here translated as "Prolonged Purity. *Pravāraṇā* refers to when one recognizes faults within oneself and allows the Saṃgha to address them freely.
The verse for donning the robe says: "Excellent is this garment of liberation, the robe of the unsurpassed field of merit. I now receive it upon my head, O World-Honored One..."
May the world always wear it. Oṃ. Tūṣa tūṣa svāhā. The *Jietan jing* (Sutra on the Precept Platform) states:
"The five-strip robe cuts off greed of the body; the seven-strip robe cuts off anger of the mouth;
the great robe cuts off delusion of the mind. Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Those who wear the kāṣāya cast off the three poisons."
The Buddha told Ānanda: "The disciples of all past Buddhas wore robes such as these; the disciples of all future Buddhas shall likewise wear these robes.
Just as I today cut them with a knife to form the saṃghāṭī robe, they cannot be plundered by enemies or thieves.
This is the garment of liberation, the robe of the field of merit. If there should be any sentient being who gives rise to even a single evil thought..."
If one directs the mind toward the Buddhas of the three periods, the Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats, as well as those who wear dyed robes, one incurs immeasurable transgression.
Why is this? The dyed, monastic robe is the emblem of the worthy sages (āryas).
If one can resolve to revere those who wear dyed robes, the merit obtained will be immeasurable. It was through the utmost sincerity of my faith and veneration that I attained Buddhahood. High...
The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Sengzhuan*) states: In the fifth year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, there was a disciple of Dharma Master Huiguang at Anxiang Temple.
His mother was impoverished and lacked even undergarments; she entered her son’s room, took an old cassock, and fashioned it into one for herself to wear.

While she was gathered with several neighboring women, laughing and conversing, she suddenly felt her feet grow hot, which gradually ascended until it reached her waist. In an instant, thunder crashed.
He hurled the neighbor’s wife more than a hundred paces away; her two ears were clogged with mud and earth, and she remained unconscious for a day before regaining consciousness.

As for the one who used the robe, he was subsequently struck dead by a thunderbolt; his body was scorched and curled by fire, and on his back was inscribed: "This was because he used the dharma-robe improperly.
His son collected his remains for burial, but he was again struck out of the ground. Only then did [the son] leave the corpse exposed beneath a tree.
In the end, it dissolved away. Thus we know that upholding the Dharma robes brings benefit even to dragons who have taken the Three Refuges;
this faith is not in vain. Furthermore, there was a mountain-dwelling monk who stayed overnight in a deep ravine. He shielded himself with his robe;
a strange spirit arrived, its form most terrifying, extending its arm inward to seize the one staying there. Fearing contact with the *kāṣāya*, it was obstructed and could not enter.
Thus he was able to escape and be delivered. Such various signs are difficult to describe in full.
As for the twenty-five-fold robe, its Sanskrit name is *saṃghāṭī*; this is translated here as "joined" (*hé*) or "layered" (*chóng*).
This refers to pieces that have been cut and then stitched together; it is also a re-made garment.
It is also called a "miscellaneous fragments robe" (saṃkakṣikā), because the number of strips is great.
Whenever entering a royal palace, ascending a seat to preach the Dharma, or going on alms-round in a village, one should wear this robe. Furthermore, there are nine grades of this robe;
the lower grade has three types, namely: the nine-strip, the eleven-strip, and the thirteen-strip (with two lengths and one short strip). The middle grade has three types.
That is to say, there are those with fifteen strips, seventeen strips, and nineteen strips (three long and one short). There are three grades of the superior category:
namely, twenty-one strips, twenty-three strips, and twenty-five strips (four long and one short). The verse for donning the robe says: "Excellent is this garment of liberation."
The robe of the unsurpassed field of merit, I now receive upon my head; may it extensively deliver all deluded beings.
Oṃ mahākā papoṣiṣṭe svāhā.
Sentient beings do not awaken; therefore, they are called the "multitude of deluded ones. The Buddhas have already awakened; therefore, they are titled the "Greatly Awakened.

These three robes were originally the Dharma-garments of bhikṣus. Now, wishing to enable śrāmaṇeras to know in advance the excellence of their names and characteristics, they are appended here at the end;
it is not for the purpose of having them donned. Regarding the wish of a śrāmaṇera to wear the *saṃkakṣikā* robe, [the details] are found within the Tripiṭaka.
A verse says: "How great is the robe of liberation! The field of merit garment without marks. Wearing it as one observes the precepts, one widely delivers all sentient beings.
The *Baiyi Jie-mo* (One Hundred and One Karmas) states: "For those who are śrāmaṇeras, the *man-tiao* (single-layered robe) is the proper attire;

yet there are those who arbitrarily wear the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṣāya*), which is deeply sinful and excessive. This practice has long been prevalent in the land of China, and thus it has become improper."

This is not the Dharma; do not allow it to be worn. This is the personal testimony of the Tang Tripiṭaka Master Yijing, who traveled to the Western Regions and observed the lands of the five regions of India as well as the various Vinaya texts. In none of these does a śrāmaṇera wear the cut-and-sewn robes of a bhikṣu.
I have specifically provided this instruction to dispel the delusions of a thousand ages. Since it has been stated that this is truly contrary to the Dharma, [it must be abandoned].

Who else shall take upon themselves their transgressions? This is something those who act as teachers must not fail to understand, and those who serve as disciples must likewise not fail to be cautious regarding.
*Bhikṣā-pātra*: the Sanskrit term *pātra* is here translated as "vessel of proper measure," meaning that its substance, color, and dimensions all accord with the Dharma.
Regarding the two materials for the body and the bowl— clay and iron— their color is treated by means of medicinal smoke.
For the iron bowl, one uses apricot kernels, hemp seeds, rice husks, and so forth, to fumigate it until it becomes black, the color of a pigeon, or the color of a peacock’s throat.
As for their measurements, they are divided into superior, middling, and inferior.
The superior bowl holds one *dou*; the inferior bowl holds five *sheng*; those between these two are called middling bowls. Regarding the *niṣīdana*:
in Sanskrit it is *niṣīdana*, which here is translated as "sitting mat" (*zuòjù*), and is also called the "foot-following cloth. The opening verse of its ritual manual says: "Sitting..."
Providing the *niṣīdana*, nurturing the sprout of the mind-nature, unfolding to ascend to the ground of the sages, and upholding the command of the Tathāgata:
Oṃ. Damba damba. Svāhā.
This was established for the purpose of carrying it along, for sitting and reclining, and to protect one’s body, one’s robes, and the monastic bedding.
The *Śīlālaṃkāra-sūtra* states: "The *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) is like the foundation of a stupa.

If you sit upon your body without a sitting mat, then the fivefold concentration and wisdom will have no basis from which to arise. Since it is called a "sitting mat," this is how it should be used at present.

To perform prostrations [upon these] completely violates the original regulations. Since the Vinaya sometimes prescribes that the four corners be affixed [to the mat], we do not understand why this is now misinterpreted as being for the Four Heavenly Kings, leading people to avoid placing their feet upon them.
Furthermore, there are those who step upon them with impure footwear.
To neglect one’s duties out of fear, or to treat them with such negligence as to be laughable—both are equally ridiculous. A teacher must not fail to instruct their disciples;

once corrupt practices have been established for a long time, they are difficult to reform overnight. If one intends to respect and protect the three robes (*tricīvara*) for the purpose of performing prostrations, they may be used provisionally for that purpose.
